Why do we permit them to monopolize the profits? Nor is profit the only concern. It is detrimental to order in the city. The Elders cannot repel pressure from outside. Last week, at their request, we disposed of two unlicensed dealers, did we not? Why must we act as their running dogs and undertake the dirty work?”

Japanese: 「廖どの、彼らとは協定があります」
English: “Lord Liao, we have an agreement with them.”

Japanese: 龍頭の側で食事もとらずに立ったまま状況を見守っていたジェフリー・ウォンが冷静に諫める。
English: Jeffrey Wong, who had remained standing beside the Longtou without eating, calmly admonished him.

Japanese: 「そんなことは知っている。その協定が無駄だと言っているのだ。このまま協定を守って、老人達を保護し、彼らに利益を独占させてやる必要なんかない。麻薬利権は莫大な利益を生むのは、みなよく知っているだろう？　麻薬の売買は行わないという理念は、ローズが街をダメにしていた頃の時代遅れの掟だ。YSの成長も最近はすっかり鈍化している。そろそろ解禁すべきじゃないだろうか？」
English: “I know that. I am saying the agreement is pointless. We have no need to continue honoring it, protecting the Elders, and allowing them to monopolize the profits. Every man here knows that the drug interests produce enormous returns. The principle that we do not deal in narcotics is an obsolete rule from the days when Rose was destroying the city. The growth of YS has slowed to nothing of late. Is it not time to lift the prohibition?”

Japanese: 「それは難しいでしょう。衰えたといえども、老人達の存在なくしては街のタイプBたちを管理することは不可能ですし、Y地区の平和も保たれない」
English: “That would be difficult. Even in their decline, it is impossible to manage the Type Bs of this city without the Elders, and the peace of Y District could not be maintained.”

Japanese: 「ウォン君。きみには聞いていない。……龍頭どのはどうお考えか？　今この状態で薬物取引に参入しても老人達は文句は言わないだろう。言える立場でもない。刃向かうなら戦えばいい」
English: “Mr. Wong, I did not ask you. ...What is your view, Lord Longtou? In the present circumstances, the Elders would not object if we entered the drug trade. They are in no position to object. If they resist, we can fight them.”

Japanese: 廖は言って、じっと龍頭を見つめる。彼は溜息をつき、
English: Liao stared fixedly at the Longtou. The other man sighed.

Japanese: 「そんな考えには乗れないな」
English: “I cannot support such a plan.”

Japanese: 「何故かな？　我々が売らなくとも、街には麻薬があふれており、中毒者が路上でへたばっている。目の前に落ちている金を拾わないという方針は、私には理解出来ない。そうだろう、みんな？」
English: “Why? Whether we sell them or not, drugs flood the city and addicts collapse in the streets. I cannot understand a policy of refusing to pick up money lying before one’s eyes. Surely you agree, gentlemen?”

Japanese: そして廖は仲間達を振り返るが、彼らは何も言わずに他のメンバーの出方をうかがっている。
English: Liao turned to his fellows. They said nothing, waiting instead to see how the other members would respond.

Japanese: 「ミスター・フェルナンデス、あなたはどうお考えで？　あなたのところの若い連中は麻薬でのトラブルが多い。我々で街の流通独占し、完全に管理出来るようになれば、無用のいざこざは減らせるのでは？」
English: “Mr. Fernandes, what is your view? The young men in your organization experience a great deal of trouble over drugs. If we monopolized the city’s distribution and brought it under complete control, could we not reduce needless disputes?”

Japanese: 「私はそうは思わない。……ただ、扱うかどうかに関してはどちらでもいい話だ。私たちはたとえ売るようになっても関わるつもりはない。これまで通りやっていく」
English: “I do not believe so. ...As to whether YS deals in them, I have no preference. Even if it begins to sell them, we have no intention of taking part. We will continue as before.”

Japanese: フェルナンデスは肩をすくめてそう言った。
English: Fernandes spoke with a shrug.

Japanese: 「廖さん、悪いがその意見は今日も引っ込めて貰うよ。ジェフリーが言ったように、老人達との関係は大事だ。壊すつもりはない」
English: “Liao, I am afraid you must withdraw the proposal again today. As Jeffrey said, our relationship with the Elders is important. I do not intend to destroy it.”

Japanese: 「龍頭。あなたのその弱気が、最近のYSの停滞を招いている。昔のあなただったら、そのようなつまらぬ意見は言わなかったはずだ」
English: “Longtou, that weakness of yours has brought about the recent stagnation of YS. You would never have voiced so trivial an opinion in the past.”

Japanese: 廖は捨て台詞を吐いて着席する。龍頭は表情を変えずにそれを受け流す。
English: Liao flung out the parting remark and sat down. The Longtou let it pass without changing his expression.

Japanese: 「他に、何か意見を言いたいものはあるかね？」
English: “Does anyone else wish to express an opinion?”

Japanese: 一同を見回すが、そこで口を開くものはいなかった。
English: He surveyed the room, but no one spoke.

Japanese: 「よし、それでは話させて貰おう」
English: “Very well. Then I shall proceed.”

Japanese: 龍頭はナプキンを口元に当て、痰を吐くような動作をしてから言った。
English: The Longtou pressed his napkin to his mouth and made a motion as though spitting out phlegm before he continued.

Japanese: 「今日集まって貰った一番の理由は、他でもない、私の死後の人事についてだ」
English: “The principal reason I asked you to assemble today is the question of appointments after my death.”

Japanese: 誰も声や態度に感情を出したりはしないが、その一言で、みなの雰囲気が変わったのを感じた。
English: No one allowed emotion to appear in voice or manner, yet at those words I felt the atmosphere of the room change.

Japanese: 参加者の誰しもが、龍頭がこの話題を用意していたことを半ば想像していたに違いない。経緯を何も知らない僕だって、この場で会食が始まってからなんとなくその想像はしていた。
English: Every participant must have half expected the Longtou to raise this subject. Even I, who knew nothing of the circumstances, had begun to imagine as much during the dinner.

Japanese: しかし、いざ直面すると緊張しないわけにはいかないようだった。廖なども、何気ない風をよそおってはいたが、やたらと口ひげを撫でているのがその内心が穏やかではないことを示している。
English: Faced with the moment itself, however, none seemed able to avoid tension. Liao pretended indifference, but the frequency with which he stroked his mustache suggested that he was far from calm.

Japanese: そして、僕もそうだ。龍頭が次の後継者を誰に指名するかについて、ある程度予測はついている。が、緊張するかしないかというのはそれとは別の問題だ。
English: The same was true of me. I had a reasonable idea whom the Longtou would name as his successor. Whether I could predict the choice and whether I felt tension were separate matters.

Japanese: あのYSの象徴であるクリス・ツェーが、ついに自分の死を公式に認め、己の口でその後の処置について発表するというのだ。僕はその息子という立場ではあったが、それ以上に、かつてY地区の住民だった者として特別な感慨があった。
English: Chris Tse, the symbol of YS, was at last formally acknowledging that he was going to die and declaring in his own voice what was to follow. I stood there as his son, but even more than that, I felt a particular emotion as one who had once been a resident of Y District.

Japanese: そして龍頭は口を開いた。
English: Then the Longtou spoke.

Japanese: 「おれが死んだら、その後は我が叔父であるマイケル・ツェーを龍頭として仰いでもらう」
English: “When I die, you will take my uncle Michael Tse as Longtou.”

Japanese: その言葉に、誰ともなく溜息が漏れる。
English: A sigh escaped the room, though I could not say from whom.

Japanese: まあ妥当、というか無難な人選だろう。マイケル・ツェーは人物としては特別なところのない凡庸な人間だが、香港グループのなかでは本来は龍頭よりも序列が上の人間である。このメンバーのなかでは年長者の部類だし、人柄にも角がなく、誰しもが受け入れやすいだろう。僕の想像とも一致する。
English: It was a reasonable—or at least a safe—choice. Michael Tse possessed no extraordinary qualities and was a thoroughly ordinary man, but within the Hong Kong group he had originally stood above the Longtou in rank. He was also among the older men in the room, and his mild character should make him easy for anyone to accept. The choice matched my own prediction.

Japanese: ちらと廖を見ると、腕組みをしたまま難しい顔をしている。彼にとっても予想内ではあったが、諸手を挙げて歓迎するほどの人選でもないといったところか。さすがに自分が後継者に指名されるとは考えていなかったようだ。
English: I glanced at Liao. He had folded his arms and wore a troubled expression. The appointment had probably fallen within his expectations but was hardly one he could welcome with open arms. He did not appear to have expected the succession himself.

Japanese: 「その補佐官として、二路元帥のジェフリー・ウォン」
English: “The Second Route Marshal, Jeffrey Wong, will serve as his adviser.”

Japanese: あらかじめ知っていたのだろう。その言葉にあわせて、ジェフリー・ウォンは礼をする。
English: He must have known in advance. Jeffrey Wong bowed at the words.

Japanese: これも驚くような発表ではない。しかし、次の言葉はさすがの僕も想像をしていなかった。
English: That declaration, too, contained nothing astonishing. Even I, however, had not imagined the words that followed.

Japanese: 「そしてもう一人、そこに居る謝亮（ツェー・ルオン）にも補佐を行ってもらう」
English: “A second man will assist him: Tse Leung, seated there.”

Japanese: 一同の視線が一斉に僕の顔に集中する。その表情はいずれも驚きに満ちていた。
English: Every eye in the room converged upon my face. Every face was filled with surprise.

Japanese: それはそうだろう。僕だってさすがに驚く。
English: Naturally. Even I was surprised.

Japanese: 「いいな、亮」
English: “Understood, Leung?”

Japanese: 「初耳ですが？」
English: “This is the first I have heard of it.”

Japanese: 念を押す龍頭に、僕は怪訝に問い返す。
English: I answered the Longtou’s demand for confirmation with a puzzled question.

Japanese: 「そりゃ、考えを口にしたのは今が初めてだから当たり前だろう？　ジェフリーと共に叔父どのの補佐をしながら、仕事を覚えるんだ。そして、ゆくゆくはお前が龍頭となれ」
English: “Naturally. This is the first time I have spoken the thought aloud. You will learn the work while assisting my uncle together with Jeffrey. In time, you will become Longtou.”

Japanese: 龍頭は、口元に笑みさえ浮かべながらそう言った。
English: The Longtou said it with a smile at the corners of his mouth.

Japanese: どういうつもりなのか？　こんな場所で、僕を後継者に指名することが、彼にとって何の意味があるのか。
English: What did he intend? What meaning could it have for him to nominate me as his successor in a place like this?

Japanese: しかし、なんというペテン師だろう。あの場面では、お前には能力がないだのなんだのと散々罵っておいたのに。
English: What a swindler he was. When we spoke before, he had heaped abuse on me, saying I had no ability and the like.

Japanese: 人を馬鹿にするにもほどがある。今この場で病人の顔に手元のコーヒーカップの中身をぶちまけてやったらさぞかし痛快だろうが、すんでのところでこらえた。
English: There were limits to how thoroughly one could mock another human being. It would have been wonderfully satisfying to fling the contents of my coffee cup into the sick man’s face then and there, but I stopped myself at the final instant.

Japanese: 「まったく心外だ！」
English: “This is entirely unacceptable!”

Japanese: 廖志明が大声で怒るのは、無理もない話だろうと僕も思う。
English: I thought Liao Chi-ming had every reason to raise his voice in anger.

Japanese: 「マイケルどのはまだわかる。古くからこの地で一家を構える功労者だ。しかし、その話だと、要するに息子どのが就任するまでの繋ぎではないか！　確かに小謝は評判の良い若者だが、そういう問題ではない。これでは貴族か何かの世襲だ！　龍頭、思い上がってはいかんぞ。我らは同志であって、龍頭の家来ではない。きみの個人的なファミリーである旧義勝の相続なら勝手にやればいいが、我らの連合であるYSの龍頭にするとは何事だ。そのような考えでいるのならば、私はYSに協力することは出来ない」
English: “I can understand Lord Michael. He is a distinguished man whose House has stood in this place since long ago. But in the plan you describe, is he not merely an interim holder until your son assumes office? Siu Tse is certainly a well-regarded young man, but that is not the issue. This is hereditary succession fit for an aristocracy! Longtou, you must not grow conceited. We are your comrades, not your retainers. If you wish your personal Family, the old Yisheng, to pass by inheritance, that is your affair. But what is this talk of making him Longtou of YS, our federation? If that is your thinking, I cannot cooperate with YS.”

Japanese: 「それは、この龍頭に逆らい、YSに反逆するということかい？」
English: “Do you mean to defy this Longtou and rebel against YS?”

Japanese: 龍頭はジロリと廖を睨み付ける。それは往年の迫力に満ちたもので、廖も気圧されたのか、言いよどむ。
English: The Longtou fixed Liao with a glare. It possessed all the force of his prime, and Liao, perhaps overawed by it, faltered.

Japanese: 「反逆は死で償うと決まっている。この死にかけより早く死にたくはないだろう？　撤回されよ」
English: “The settled penalty for rebellion is death. You would not wish to die before this dying man, would you? Retract your words.”

Japanese: 「……私を脅すのか？　それならやめておいた方が良い」
English: “...Are you threatening me? If so, you would be wiser not to.”

Japanese: 廖は表情を固くして睨み付ける。一方龍頭も冷笑を顔に貼り付けたまま黙って廖の顔を見つめている。
English: Liao’s face hardened as he glared. The Longtou, meanwhile, stared back in silence, a sneer still fixed upon his face.

Japanese: 「それにこれは反逆ではない。ただYSのために個人的な意見を述べたまでだ」
English: “Besides, this is not rebellion. I have merely expressed my personal opinion for the sake of YS.”

Japanese: にらみ合いは暫く続いたが、結局根負けして廖が先にそう言った。
English: The two men stared at one another for some time. In the end, Liao yielded first and spoke those words.

Japanese: 「それならば結構」
English: “Then very well.”

Japanese: 龍頭は笑い、
English: The Longtou laughed.

Japanese: 「他に、何か意見があるものはいるか？　これは重大な話だ、廖どののように忌憚のない意見を述べて貰ってかまわない」
English: “Does anyone else have an opinion? This is a matter of great importance. You may speak as frankly as Lord Liao.”

Japanese: このようなやりとりを見せられて、あえて口を開くものは存在しないかと思われたが、
English: After witnessing that exchange, no one appeared likely to venture a word.

Japanese: 「それでは、この話は……」
English: “In that case, the matter is—”

Japanese: 龍頭がそうまとめかけたところで、意外にもフェルナンデスが口を開いた。
English: The Longtou had begun to conclude the discussion when, unexpectedly, Fernandes spoke.

Japanese: 「意見ってわけじゃないが……」
English: “This is not an opinion, exactly...”

Japanese: フェルナンデスは普段からしわだらけの顔に、深いしわをさらに増やしている。
English: Fernandes’s ordinarily wrinkled face had acquired still deeper lines.

Japanese: 「クリス・ツェー。これは横暴というものだよ」
English: “Chris Tse. This is tyranny.”

Japanese: 全くその通りだ、と僕は同調したかった。
English: I wished I could announce my complete agreement.

Japanese: 龍頭はただ笑って受け流すと、
English: The Longtou dismissed it with a laugh.

Japanese: 「それは感想であって、意見ではないようだな。意見がないのなら、私はこのへんで席を外させていただく。みなはいつも通り、好きに歓談していってくれたまえ」
English: “That sounds like an impression, not an opinion. If there are no opinions, I shall excuse myself. The rest of you may remain and converse as you please, in the usual fashion.”

Japanese: そして、ジェフリー・ウォンと共に部屋を出て行った。
English: Then he left the room with Jeffrey Wong.

Japanese: 「この素晴らしい提案を、馬明は知っていたのかい？」
English: “Did you know about this marvelous proposal, Ma Ming?”

Japanese: 部屋を出てから、僕はそう訊ねた。
English: I asked the question once we were outside the room.

Japanese: 「知らなかった。おれの方からは提案していたが、兄貴はうんともすんとも言わなかったんだ。いつか知らんが、ジェフリーと二人で決めたんだろう。お前と親しいおれにはわざと隠していたのかな？　それにしても、まったく驚いた」
English: “I didn’t. I had proposed it myself, but Big Brother never gave me so much as a yes or no. He and Jeffrey must have decided at some point. Perhaps they deliberately concealed it from me because you and I are close. In any case, I was completely astonished.”

Japanese: 馬明は大げさにかぶりを振る。嘘をついているような態度ではない。
English: Ma Ming shook his head with theatrical emphasis. His manner did not suggest a lie.

Japanese: 「しかし、意見としては大賛成だ。なあ小謝、言ったろう？　兄貴は本心ではお前に継いで欲しいんだって」
English: “But I support the decision wholeheartedly. Siu Tse, didn’t I tell you? In his heart, Big Brother wants you to succeed him.”

Japanese: そう言って大きなてのひらで僕の背中をバンバンと叩く。あんな場でも酒を飲みまくっていた酔っ払いのひどい馬鹿力で、僕はむせながらそれを振り払い、
English: With that, he struck me repeatedly on the back with his great palm. The drunken brute had continued drinking even in that room and possessed monstrous strength. Coughing, I threw off his hand.

Japanese: 「冗談じゃない。これじゃ僕がピエロだ」
English: “Do not be absurd. He has made me a clown.”

Japanese: 今でもさっきの場面を思い出すと苦い思いがするが、それとは別に気になることがある。
English: The memory of that scene still left a bitter taste. Yet a separate matter troubled me.

Japanese: クリス・ツェーと言えばＹＳの独裁者だったはずだ。フェルナンデスは昔からあんな調子だが、少なくとも、僕の記憶では、廖や他の幹部達はもっと龍頭を恐れていたはずだ。
English: Chris Tse was supposed to be the dictator of YS. Fernandes had always behaved as he did today, but in my memory, Liao and the other officers had once feared the Longtou far more.

Japanese: 龍頭が部屋を去ったすぐ後にフェルナンデスは部屋を去ったが、他の連中は残り、今さっきこの場で行われた龍頭の発言について不満を述べ合っていたが、あんなことはかつてのＹＳでは考えられない。その場には僕や馬明もいたのだ。
English: Fernandes departed shortly after the Longtou. The others remained and exchanged complaints about what the Longtou had just announced, though such conduct would have been unthinkable in the YS of the past. Ma Ming and I were still present in the room.

Japanese: 影響力が落ちたのは聞いていたが、ここまでとは思わなかった。
English: I had heard that his influence had declined, but I had not imagined matters had gone this far.

Japanese: 「やっぱり、病人というものはなめられるんだね」
English: “People really do look down on the sick.”

Japanese: 僕がそのことについて話すと、
English: When I raised the subject,

Japanese: 「兄貴が寝込むようになってから、ずっとあんな調子だよ」
English: “They’ve been like that ever since Big Brother became bedridden.”

Japanese: 馬明も、やるせないといった表情で溜息をついた。
English: Ma Ming sighed with an expression of helpless sorrow.

Japanese: 僕の父、クリス・ツェーが死ねばＹＳは間違いなく混乱状態に陥るだろう。
English: When my father, Chris Tse, died, YS would unquestionably fall into disorder.

Japanese: 今日父が口にした死後の人事処理についても、そのように履行されるかどうか。
English: Even the appointments my father had announced today might not be carried out as he described.

Japanese: クリス・ツェーに限らない。死んでしまえば、誰のものであれその言葉の重みなどはなくなる。彼の後を引き継ぐ者におさえつけるだけの力がなければ、平気で反故にするはずだ。
English: This was not unique to Chris Tse. Once a man dies, whatever his identity, his words lose their weight. Unless the successor possesses enough power to hold the others down, they will break their promises without a thought.

Japanese: それが、こういった弱肉強食の世界に生きる連中のシンプルな行動法則であるのは、この街の人間なら誰でも知っている。
English: Anyone from this city knew that to be the simple law governing men who lived in a world where the strong devoured the weak.

Japanese: そんな状況を父が把握していなかったとは思えない。なのに、あのような話を根回しもなく敢行したのはどういうことか？　かつての独裁者だったころならわかるが、もはや威光のない父が、あんなかたちで何の実績もない息子を事実上の後継者に指名すれば、廖志明やジョゼ・フェルナンデスのような古くからの盟友が反発するのは当然だ。事実みな面食らっていた。この間会った時は、父自身がその話をしていたじゃないか。
English: I could not believe that my father had failed to understand the situation. Why, then, had he made such a declaration without preparing the others? It would have been understandable when he was still a dictator. Now that his prestige was gone, naming a son with no achievements as his effective successor in such a fashion would naturally provoke old allies like Liao Chi-ming and José Fernandes. Indeed, everyone had been taken aback. My father himself had warned me of that very matter when we last spoke.

Japanese: 病が冷静な判断力を奪ったのか。そうでなければ、会食での宣言は、一同にではなく僕に向けての言葉で、何かを伝えようとしたのか。そうだとしてもその意図はわからないけれども、話しているときの父の表情を思い出すとなんとなくそんな感じがする。
English: Had illness robbed him of dispassionate judgment? Or was the declaration at dinner directed not toward the assembled officers, but toward me? Had he been trying to tell me something? Even if so, I could not understand his intention. Yet when I recalled his expression as he spoke, that possibility somehow felt true.

Japanese: 相談もなく指名されたことはやっぱり不本意ではあるが、ああいう形で虚しい宣言をせざるを得なかった状況を思うと寂しいような気持だ。
English: I remained displeased at being nominated without consultation. But when I considered the circumstances that had forced him to make such an empty declaration, I also felt something resembling sadness.

Japanese: そして、まだ生きている父を既に死んだもののように扱っているＹＳの連中に対する不快感もある。
English: I was also disgusted by the men of YS, who treated my still-living father as though he were already dead.

Japanese: 「なあ馬明」
English: “Ma Ming.”

Japanese: 「なんだ」
English: “What is it?”

Japanese: 「本当に、僕にクリス・ツェー亡き後のYSを指揮する能力があると思うかい？」
English: “Do you truly believe I have the ability to command YS after Chris Tse is gone?”

Japanese: 「もちろんだとも」
English: “Of course.”

Japanese: 馬明は胸を張るが、僕は全然心強くはならなかった。
English: Ma Ming thrust out his chest, but I did not find him reassuring in the least.

Japanese: 心が千々に乱れたままでは、考えもまとまらない。僕は歩くことで思考を整理するタイプで、途中で車をおろしてもらうとあてもなく滑走路通りのネオンに濡れながら行ったり来たりしていた。
English: With my mind in turmoil, I could reach no coherent conclusion. Walking has always helped me put my thoughts in order. I had the driver let me out partway and wandered aimlessly back and forth, drenched in the neon of Runway Street.

Japanese: 先日猛獣の凄惨な狩り場となったこの通りは、何もなかったかのような活況を呈している。Y地区で起きた事件は基本的に報道されることはない。通行するほとんどの客たちはそんな事件があったことさえ知らないだろうし、この通りでものを売る人々はどんな事件があっても何食わぬ顔をして営業することに慣れている。
English: The street, so recently the site of a beast’s grisly hunt, bustled as though nothing had happened. Incidents in Y District were almost never reported. Most visitors passing through probably did not even know one had occurred, and the people who sold their wares here were accustomed to continuing business with unconcerned faces after any event whatsoever.

Japanese: この街に満ちた混沌とした生命力は、どんな出来事も飲み込んでしまう。やがて父が死んで、街のギャング達に混乱が訪れたとしても、通りに店を並べる彼らの何人かがそれに巻き込まれたとしても、不幸な当事者以外は笑顔で客引きの声を上げつつけるのだろう。そうであって欲しいと思う。
English: The chaotic vitality that filled this city swallowed every occurrence. In time, my father would die and disorder would come to the city’s gangs. Some of the people lining the streets with shops might become entangled in it. Even then, everyone but the unfortunate parties themselves would surely go on smiling and calling to customers. I hoped they would.

Japanese: 僕はここで、何かが出来るのだろうか？　そしてそれは、いま自分がやろうとしていることを中断するほどの価値があるのだろうか？
English: Was there anything I could do here? And would it be worth interrupting what I was now trying to accomplish?

Japanese: 考えがまとまらないでいると、ポケット越しに携帯電話の振動が伝わった。
English: As I failed to bring my thoughts together, I felt my phone vibrate in my pocket.

Japanese: 『リョウさん？』
English: “Ryo?”

Japanese: 汐家の自宅からかかってきた電話の声は、汐松子のものだった。
English: Matsuko Shio was calling from the Shio house.

Japanese: そして僕は、汐家にサンプルを預けていたことを思い出す。
English: I remembered that I had left the sample with the Shios.

Japanese: まったく、どれだけ沢山の出来事が一片に到来してしまったのだろう！
English: How very many events had arrived at once!

Japanese: 「どうしたの？」
English: “What is it?”

Japanese: 『お父さんから連絡があって、今夜は遅くなるから、うちに来て待ってて欲しいということです』
English: “Father contacted me. He says he will be late tonight and wants you to come here and wait.”

Japanese: 「わかったよ。今から行く」
English: “All right. I will come now.”

Japanese: 『料理を用意して、待ってますからね！』
English: “I’ll have dinner ready and waiting!”

Japanese: はしゃぐ松子の声に、
English: Hearing the excitement in Matsuko’s voice,

Japanese: 「うん」
English: “All right.”

Japanese: とだけ返し、僕は通話を切った。
English: I gave only that reply, then ended the call.

Japanese: 「今さっき電話があって……」
English: “He just telephoned...”

Japanese: 勝手知ったる汐家に上がり込み、上着を脱いだところで松子はそう切り出した。
English: I let myself into the Shio house without ceremony. As I removed my coat, Matsuko began to explain.

Japanese: 「お父さん、やっぱり今日は帰ってこないんだそうです。……どうしますか？」
English: “Father says he will not be coming home tonight after all. ...What would you like to do?”

Japanese: 彼女は上目遣いで僕を見る。
English: She glanced up at me.

Japanese: 「泊まっていくよ」
English: “I will stay the night.”

Japanese: 「そうですね。それがいいです。久しぶりですし」
English: “Yes. That would be best. It has been such a long time.”

Japanese: 彼女は表情をキラキラとさせて一人で何度も頷くと、
English: Her expression shone as she nodded to herself several times.

Japanese: 「じゃあ、用意していた料理を持って来ます」
English: “Then I’ll bring the food I prepared.”

Japanese: キッチンへ小走りで向かった。
English: She trotted off to the kitchen.

Japanese: 彼女の手料理を食べ、その後バスルームを交互に使った。
English: I ate the dinner she had cooked, and afterward we took turns using the bathroom.

Japanese: リビングルームで汐さんがコレクションしているクラッシックのアナログレコードを流し、汐さんのとっておきのワインを勝手に開け僕と松子は久しぶりに語らった。
English: We played one of the classical records from Mr. Shio’s vinyl collection in the living room, opened one of his prized bottles of wine without permission, and talked together for the first time in many months.

Japanese: 僕は学校でのエピソードをいくつか話して、教授達は変人ばかりだと言ったり、実験での自分の失敗談などを面白おかしく脚色して話すと彼女はそのたびにころころと笑った。
English: I told several stories of life at school, described all the professors as eccentrics, and embellished my failures in the laboratory for comic effect. Each one sent her into peals of laughter.

Japanese: 彼女の方は、今働いている児童擁護施設での子供とのやりとりを話してくれた。
English: For her part, she told me about her interactions with the children at the child welfare facility where she now worked.

Japanese: 「楽しくって、楽しくって、仕方がないんです。今が一番人生で充実しているかもしれません」
English: “It’s so much fun—so much fun I can hardly stand it. This may be the most fulfilling time of my life.”

Japanese: 興奮気味にそう語る。
English: She spoke with some excitement.

Japanese: 松子が楽しそうにしているなら、僕もとても嬉しい。僕は子供の頃、彼女を楽しい気分にしようと、どれだけ真剣に考えたことか。
English: If Matsuko was happy, then I was delighted as well. When we were children, how earnestly I had tried to think of ways to make her happy.

Japanese: あの時出来なかったことが、こうして自力で果たされてしまったことを思うと、少し悔しいような気もするけれど。
English: Though when I considered that she had accomplished by herself what I had been unable to do then, I felt a little frustrated as well.

Japanese: 僕たちは二人並んでソファに腰をおろしていた。
English: We sat side by side on the sofa.

Japanese: 間接照明の淡い光が、すべてのものをぼんやりと夜の闇のなかに生き物のように浮かび上がらせている。窓の外からは、時々トラックが通るゴトゴトという音がきこえる。シオクリーンは深夜も営業している。
English: The soft light of the indirect lamps brought every object dimly to life within the darkness of the night. From outside the window came the occasional rumble of a passing truck. Shio Clean operated into the small hours.

Japanese: 彼女の髪からシャンプーの匂いがした。触れてはいないけれども、すぐそばにいるから体温を感じる。その手にしたグラスのワインはあまり減っていないが、その元々は白い頬は、首筋は、パジャマの襟から覗く胸元はピンク色に染まっている。
English: I could smell shampoo in her hair. We were not touching, but she sat so near that I could feel the heat of her body. The wine in her glass had scarcely diminished, yet her naturally pale cheeks, the line of her neck, and the skin visible beneath the collar of her pajamas had all turned pink.

Japanese: おそらく僕も赤くなっているのだろう。酔いが、さきほどの件で疲れていた脳を適度にほぐしてくれている。
English: I was probably red as well. The wine was pleasantly relaxing my mind after the strain of what had happened earlier.

Japanese: 「よっぽど楽しいんだね。よく喋るようになったし、明るくなった」
English: “You must enjoy it tremendously. You speak much more now, and you have grown brighter.”

Japanese: 「いつもそんなことばっかり言うんですね」
English: “You always say things like that.”

Japanese: 松子はまっすぐ僕を見ながら笑う。その瞳にはいつもつけているカラーコンタクトはなく、彼女本来の金属的な金色に輝いている。
English: Matsuko smiled as she looked directly at me. She was not wearing her customary colored contact lenses, and her eyes shone with their natural, metallic gold.

Japanese: 「だって、驚きだよ。昔は素直で従順だけど、従順すぎてなんでも我慢して、人間味が薄かった。心を表に出さなすぎて、本当に心配したんだから」
English: “Because the difference astonishes me. You were always honest and obedient, but far too obedient. You put up with everything and hardly seemed human. You kept your feelings so entirely hidden that I was truly worried.”

Japanese: 率直に言うと、彼女は首をひねってから、
English: At my frank words, she tilted her head.

Japanese: 「……その時と根っこはあまりかわってはいないと思います。難しいところです」
English: “...Deep down, I don’t think I’ve changed very much since then. It’s difficult to explain.”

Japanese: そう言って溜息をつくと、暑そうに胸元を手のひらで煽った。アルコールが体を火照らせているのだろう。
English: She sighed, then fanned the front of her chest with one hand as though she were hot. The alcohol had probably warmed her body.

Japanese: 「でも、たとえばあの頃の僕やきみに、子供の面倒見て目を輝かせているなんてこと教えてやっても絶対に信じないよ」
English: “Even so, if someone had told the children we were that one day you would care for children with your eyes shining, neither of us would ever have believed it.”

Japanese: 「そうでしょうね。自分でも驚きです……。でも、本当に楽しいんです。ああいうところで、誰かを助けるのって、自分に貴い価値が生まれたような気がします」
English: “No, we would not. I am surprised myself... But I truly enjoy it. When I help someone in a place like that, I feel as though I have gained some precious worth of my own.”

Japanese: 彼女は真面目な横顔で言ってから、ちらと僕の表情を確認するようにこちらを振り返り、そしてまた恥ずかしがるように視線をそらして言葉を続ける。
English: She said this with a serious expression, then turned to glance at me as though checking my reaction. Looking away again in embarrassment, she continued.

Japanese: 「誰かを助けるその手というのは、とても平等なんですよ」
English: “All hands that help someone are equal.”

Japanese: 「手が平等？」
English: “They’re equal?”

Japanese: 彼女はこくりと頷き、
English: She gave a small nod.

Japanese: 「たとえばパンを渡す手、たとえば凍えるからだに毛布を掛けてあげる手、これは誰のどんな手によるものであっても、相手を飢えや寒さから守ることが出来るんです。それまでどんな恐ろしい行為を重ねてきた人間でも、おぞましい正体を持つ人間でも、その手の価値は、パンを受け取る人にしてみれば平等です。……神様の手みたいに平等なんです。私もそこで、誰かに何かをしてあげているときだけは、自分じゃない、誰でもない、ただの善意の塊になっているような気がします」
English: “A hand that gives someone bread, for example, or one that lays a blanket over a freezing body. No matter whose hand it is or what kind of hand it may be, it can protect someone from hunger or cold. The hand may belong to a person who has committed any number of terrible acts, or to someone with a horrifying true nature. But to the person receiving the bread, the value of every such hand is equal. ...They are all equal, like the hands of God. And when I do something for someone there, I feel that I am no longer myself, no longer anyone at all, but simply goodwill itself.”

Japanese: 「そうなんだ。少し危うい気がするけど」
English: “I see. Though it strikes me as a little dangerous.”

Japanese: 松子は元々自己が希薄だ。生い立ちを思えば仕方がないことだが。
English: To my eyes, Matsuko had always possessed only a faint sense of self. Given the history I knew, perhaps that was inevitable.

Japanese: どんなときでも自分が傷つくことを恐れないし、自分が得をしようともしない。要するに、僕とまるきり正反対だ。
English: She never appeared afraid of being hurt and never tried to secure some advantage for herself. In short, she was my complete opposite.

Japanese: 僕はそこを尊敬してはいるけれど、寂しく感じるときもあるし、もっと自分を強く持って欲しいと感じることもある。
English: I respected that quality, but at times it made me lonely. At others, I wished that she would assert herself more strongly.

Japanese: 「それでも、いいことは、いいことだと思う。前も人には親切だったけど、どこか破滅的な感じがしたからね。今はすくなくともそれは感じない」
English: “Even so, I believe that something good is good. You were kind to others before, but there was something self-destructive in it. At least, I no longer feel that from you.”

Japanese: 僕の言葉に松子は嬉しそうに微笑む。そんなふうに、自然と喜びがあふれて表情になるのも、前の松子には少なかったことだ。
English: Matsuko smiled happily at my words. Such spontaneous pleasure overflowing into expression had also been rare in the Matsuko I remembered.

Japanese: それを言うと彼女は照れ笑いを浮かべる。
English: When I said so, she gave an embarrassed laugh.

Japanese: 「感情が出るようになったというのも、その仕事の影響があると思います」
English: “I think the work has also helped me show my feelings.”

Japanese: 「そうかい？」
English: “Has it?”

Japanese: 「はい。ああいうところの子供って、つらい体験をしているから、みんなひねくれていたり、とても卑屈だったりするんですよ。そういう子たち相手だと、何があってもニコニコ笑って接しているだけじゃなかなか信頼関係が築けないんです。悪いことをしたら、怒ってるっていう感情を見せて、哀しいことをしたら、哀しい顔を見せる。それがとても大事なんです。……仕事場でそれを心がけるようにしてたから、普段の生活も変わったのかも」
English: “Yes. The children in places like that have been through terrible things, so they may become bitter and contrary, or painfully unsure of themselves. You cannot readily build a relationship of trust with children like that by doing nothing but smiling sweetly, whatever happens. When they do something wrong, you must show them that you are angry. When they do something hurtful, you must show them that you are sad. That is very important. ...I made a conscious effort to do so at work. Perhaps that changed the rest of my life as well.”

Japanese: 松子は苦笑して、そしてまた真剣な顔になる。
English: Matsuko gave a wry smile, then grew serious again.

Japanese: 「いまの職場は、とてもいろいろなことを教えてくれます。お給料貰っているのが申し訳ないくらい。この先、いろんなことが理解出来るようになって、そうすれば、私もいつか、いろんなことを素直に受け入れられるようになるのかも……。リョウさんも、体験してみたらどうです？　私と同じようなことが起きるかもしれません」
English: “My present workplace teaches me so many things that I almost feel guilty accepting a salary. Perhaps, as I learn to understand more and more, I will someday be able to accept all kinds of things as they are... Why don’t you try it too, Ryo? Perhaps something similar would happen to you.”

Japanese: 「どうだろう」
English: “I wonder.”

Japanese: 僕は首をひねって、
English: I tilted my head.

Japanese: 「僕は、誰かのためだけに何かをしようとは、もう思わない。それは結局、とても悲しいことにしかならないから。少なくとも僕にとっては」
English: “I no longer intend to do anything solely for another person. In the end, it only brings terrible sadness. At least, that is true for me.”

Japanese: 「そうなのですか？」
English: “Is it?”

Japanese: 「……僕らは似ているけれど、決定的な違いがある。きみは何かになりたいのだろうけど、僕は何ものにもなりたくないんだ。人生を何かで一杯にしようとは思わない。それが素敵なものであったとしても、詰め込まなければ空っぽだとしてもだ」

English: The hospital treated people who had developed the psychiatric symptoms associated with Type B, all of whom had become unable to live in society for one reason or another.

Japanese: 彼らはその症状の内容や性別によって分類されており、生活状況も異なっている。たとえば比較的症状の軽い女性患者はB病棟の一階で暮らし、病院内の施設を自由に利用することが出来る。急性期で症状が安定しないが集団生活を営める状態である男性患者はA病棟の二階で暮らし、棟の外に出る扉には鍵がかけられている。
English: They were classified by the nature of their symptoms and by sex, and their living conditions varied accordingly. Female patients with comparatively mild symptoms, for example, lived on the first floor of Ward B and could freely use the facilities within the hospital. Male patients in the acute stage, whose symptoms remained unstable but who could still live in a group, resided on the second floor of Ward A, where the door leading out of the building was locked.

Japanese: 能見美紗が勤務しているのは、B病棟の三階。病がある程度進行して慢性化し、症状が安定した女性患者達が暮らす棟であった。
English: Misa Nomi worked on the third floor of Ward B. It housed female patients whose illness had progressed to a certain degree, become chronic, and then stabilized.

Japanese: 美紗は二十六才のまだ若い看護師だが、なぜこんな施設で働くことになってしまったのかと、時に自分の人生を不思議に思う。
English: Misa was still a young nurse at twenty-six. At times she wondered at the course of a life that had brought her to work in a facility like this.

Japanese: 親の入院を見舞いに行った時、看護師の優しい振る舞いとてきぱきと働くさまにいたく感動した、というストーリーは少女が看護師になる理由としてはごく平凡なものだろう。そして希望したものと違う診療科に配属される、というのも珍しくはないストーリーかもしれない。
English: The story of a girl visiting a hospitalized parent, being deeply moved by the nurses’ kindness and brisk efficiency, and deciding to become a nurse herself was perfectly commonplace. Assignment to a department other than the one she desired might be an equally common development.

Japanese: しかし、タイプB専用病棟――しかも悪名高い『Y地区収容所』に勤務することになるというのは、看護学生であった頃の美紗に想像しろといってもそう容易に思いつくものではなかったろう。
English: But it would not have been easy for Misa as a nursing student to imagine that she would work in a ward exclusively for Type Bs—and at the infamous ‘Y District Internment Center,’ no less.

Japanese: この病院は、よその病院で面倒を見切れなくなった患者や、社会で問題を起こして行政によって強制的に入院させられた患者などを積極的に受け入れている。
English: The hospital actively accepted patients whom other hospitals could no longer manage, as well as those who had caused problems in society and been committed by the authorities.

Japanese: 同じような閉鎖施設であっても、例えば一般的な精神科の患者は、症状がかなり重くともある程度の年齢になれば老人ホームなどに移ることが出来るケースが多いが、タイプBのようなミュータントは、その肉体能力の高さのために、ある程度以上病気が進行してしまうと退院することが出来ない。つまり、この病院に送られた患者は、そのほとんどが一生病院の敷地から一歩も出ることがなく生涯を終えるのである。
English: Even in a similarly closed facility, an ordinary psychiatric patient, however severe the symptoms, could often transfer to a nursing home or similar institution upon reaching a certain age. Mutants such as Type Bs, however, possessed such great physical abilities that once the illness progressed beyond a certain point, they could no longer be discharged. In other words, most patients sent here would end their lives without ever taking another step beyond the hospital grounds.

Japanese: これが、この病院が収容所と呼ばれる所以であった。
English: That was why the hospital was called an internment center.

Japanese: このような施設は日本に数カ所あり、いずれも地名＋収容所といった形で呼称されている。それらは、タイプB自体の世間での悪いイメージと相まって、とてつもなく非人間的な施設だと思われている。
English: Several such facilities existed throughout Japan, and all were known by names combining their location with ‘internment center.’ Together with the public’s poor image of Type Bs themselves, those names led people to imagine institutions of extraordinary inhumanity.

Japanese: 実際、美紗もそうだった。
English: Misa herself had once imagined the same.

Japanese: タイプBについても、看護学校で習う程度のことしか知らなかったし、最初に就職した病院でも扱うことがなかった。そもそも普通に暮らしていて、AだろうがBだろうが、ミュータント自体と出会うという場面に遭遇することは滅多にない。
English: She had known no more about Type Bs than nursing school taught and had never treated one at her first hospital. Indeed, in the course of an ordinary life, one rarely encountered a mutant at all, whether A or B.

Japanese: だから、タイプBしかいないこの病院に勤務し、さらにBだけでなくAまでも街を闊歩しているY地区に暮らすというのは、全く美紗にとっては考えられないことで、それまで働いていた救急病院から異動を命じられた時には母の前で泣きついたものだった。そしてそれは、彼女が特別に弱いというよりも、ごく当然の反応と言うべきだろう。
English: Working at a hospital containing only Type Bs, and living in Y District, where not only Bs but even As walked openly through the city, had been utterly unimaginable to Misa. When the emergency hospital where she had previously worked ordered her transfer, she had wept before her mother. That response was not evidence of any exceptional weakness. It was entirely natural.

Japanese: その日、美紗は夜勤明けの朝を迎えていた。
English: That morning, Misa was finishing a night shift.

Japanese: 何年やっても夜勤というものに慣れることが出来ない。申し送りの時間はいつも、うつらうつら、その精神は半ば夢の世界にある。
English: However many years she worked them, she could never grow accustomed to night shifts. During handover, she always drifted on the edge of sleep, her mind already halfway into the world of dreams.

Japanese: この病院はとにかく申し送りが長い。今時、カーデックスなんて骨董品、他のどこの病院が使っているのだろう？　いくら病院が古いからって、設備やシステムは新しいものに変えて行けばいいのに、この塀のなかにあるものはすべてが時が止まってしまうものらしい。道具だけでなくスタッフも患者も、いつまでも古い時間のなかにいる。これって公立病院だから？
English: Handover at this hospital was interminable. What other hospital still used an antique like a Kardex these days? The hospital itself might be old, but surely the equipment and systems could be replaced. Apparently, everything inside these walls stopped in time. Not merely the tools, but the staff and patients as well, remained forever within some older age. Was this what came of being a public hospital?

Japanese: 前の病院だったら数分で終わった申し送りが、カーデックスを使うと、とてつもなく長く、眠気と戦う美紗の精神にとっては永劫とも思える時間だった。
English: At her previous hospital, handover had taken only a few minutes. With a Kardex, it grew monstrously long—an eternity to Misa’s mind as she fought against sleep.

Japanese: 「……藤田真由美（※所々P音入れる。以下患者名は同様）さん。kot（コート）マイナス三日で昨日GE（ジーイー）施行。反応便多量。日中はおかわりなく過ごされています。夜間良眠。……本田晃子さん。昨日の十一時にヘッドガードをつけずに転倒しています。腫脹や発赤はなく、バイタル正常。現在は観察室で一般状態観察中です。本日の午前にドクターが来て、それで問題がなければ解放になる見通しです。夜間良眠。……古川保美さん。この方は現在拘束中ですが、体動が激しく、昨日日勤帯の十三時三十分にバルーンが抜けていたのでさしなおそうとしたのですが、拒否が激しく職員を怒鳴りつけ……」
English: “...Mayumi Fujita. Kot minus three days; GE administered yesterday, with a large amount of stool in response. No changes during the day. Slept well overnight. ...Akiko Honda. Fell at eleven yesterday without her head guard. No swelling or redness, vital signs normal. She is currently under observation in the observation room. The doctor will examine her this morning, and if there is no problem, we expect to release her from observation. Slept well overnight. ...Yasumi Furukawa. She is presently under restraint, but has been moving violently. At thirteen thirty on yesterday’s day shift, we found that her balloon catheter had come out. When we attempted to reinsert it, she resisted fiercely and shouted at the staff...”

Japanese: 日勤者たちの前で、昨夜一緒に夜勤をつとめた同僚が看護記録を読み上げる。その声を、注意して聞こうとすればするほど、眠気が意識を現実から遠ざける。
English: Before the day staff, the colleague who had worked the night shift with her read aloud from the nursing record. The more carefully Misa tried to listen, the farther sleep carried her consciousness from reality.

Japanese: これなら自分の申し送りを後にすればよかった。先に済ませてしまったものだから、完全に緊張感がなくなってしまって、睡魔に抵抗することが難しい。
English: She should have saved her own report for later. Having finished it first, she had lost every trace of tension, and resisting sleep had become nearly impossible.

Japanese: 「ねえ、この人はもうツナギを外してもいいんじゃないかしら？　金眼を見せることもなくなったし、もともと出来る人じゃない。なんだか、ツナギを着せてから甘えちゃって、どんどんADLが低下している気がするの」
English: “Do you not think we could take her out of the coverall now? She has stopped showing the golden eyes, and she was capable enough to begin with. Since we put her in the coverall, she seems to have become dependent on us, and her ADLs keep declining.”

Japanese: Ｔという患者のところで、申し送りを遮って、前島ナースが提案する。この病棟でも有数のベテラン看護師は、いつもこうして色々な口を挟む。熱心なのはいいのだが、ここで即席のカンファレンスが始まってしまうと、申し送りが長引き、夜勤者の帰宅が遅れる原因となるのだ。
English: At the entry for a patient identified as T, Nurse Maejima interrupted handover with the proposal. One of the ward’s most senior nurses, she was forever interjecting this way. Her dedication was admirable, but when an impromptu conference began here, handover ran long and the night staff went home late.

Japanese: （また始まっちゃった）
English: (Here we go again.)

Japanese: 美紗が内心でうんざりしつつ、うっかりあくびをしてしまうと、隣の吉田主任がキッと睨む。
English: Misa, inwardly exasperated, accidentally yawned. Chief Yoshida, sitting beside her, fixed her with a glare.

Japanese: この病棟の看護師の年齢は幅広く、美紗のような二十代の若いものもいれば、前島ナースのような五十代もおり、もっと年配の、七十代の看護師なども活躍している。男女の比率は男性四割、女性六割といった具合で、比率としては男性が少ないわけではないが、この病院の業務内容を考えるとまだ足りない。
English: The nurses on this ward ranged widely in age. Some, like Misa, were in their twenties; Nurse Maejima was in her fifties; and still older nurses in their seventies remained active. Men made up roughly forty percent of the staff and women sixty. That hardly made male nurses rare, but considering the work performed at this hospital, there were still too few.

Japanese: 男性看護師の多くはもっと乱暴な患者を扱う病棟に配属されているのと、このB棟三階は女子病棟だということもあり、男性看護師は一人しかおらず、看護助手も男性は二人しかいない。
English: Many of the male nurses were assigned to wards with more violent patients, and the third floor of Ward B was a women’s ward. As a result, it had only one male nurse and two male nursing assistants.

Japanese: どうしても男手が足りない時は他の病棟から応援を頼むことになるが、この病棟では患者が不穏になって手を付けられない、などということはこの病棟では希である。ほとんどは、横になったまま動かない患者を車椅子に乗せたり、書類の詰まった段ボールを棚から下ろしたりといった力仕事のために男性が必要になるといった程度だ。実際のところ、女性だけでもほとんどの仕事はまわる。
English: When extra help from male staff was absolutely necessary, the ward requested assistance from elsewhere. Yet patients becoming so agitated as to be unmanageable was rare here. Men were generally needed only for physical tasks such as moving a patient who lay still and would not move into a wheelchair, or lowering a carton packed with documents from a shelf. In practice, women could perform nearly all the work themselves.

Japanese: （人手不足の愚痴を言うなら、こういう時間のロスを減らすよう努力すればいいのになあ……）
English: (If everyone is going to complain about understaffing, they might at least try to reduce wasted time like this...)

Japanese: 美紗はあくびをかみ殺しながら、Ｔのツナギを外すかどうかで議論する先輩達の話を聞いた。
English: Suppressing another yawn, Misa listened to her seniors debate whether to remove T’s coverall.

Japanese: Tは定期的に症状が悪化するのだが、今回は一ヶ月ほど前に発作が出て、それいらい調子が良くない。
English: T’s condition periodically deteriorated. The present episode had begun about a month earlier, and she had remained unwell ever since.

Japanese: タイプＢ発作は、多くの場合幻聴や幻覚を伴うもので、彼女の症状もまたそのようなものだ。元々自分でトイレに行って大便をするという能力に難のある患者だったのだが、それでも出来なくはなかった。今回のように具合が悪くなるとほとんど垂れ流し状態となり、しかも幻聴に指示されたと言って大便のついた下着で顔を拭いたりもする。
English: Type B episodes were often accompanied by auditory and visual hallucinations, and T experienced both. She had always struggled to use the toilet for a bowel movement, though she had not been entirely incapable of it. When her condition declined as it had now, she became almost wholly incontinent. She might also claim that a voice instructed her to wipe her face with underwear soiled by feces, and obey it.

Japanese: だから、彼女は調子が悪くなると毎回ツナギを着せられることになる。
English: Whenever her condition worsened, she was therefore placed in a coverall.

Japanese: こうした現場で扱われるツナギというのは、見た目は工務員などが着る上下が繋がった衣服であるが、ファスナーを開くには専用の金具が必要で、患者は自分で脱ぐことが出来ないようになっている。身体をかきむしってしまう癖のある患者や、おむつを穿かせても汚れると勝手に自分で外して病棟を汚してしまうＴのような患者に着せる、一種の拘束衣である。
English: The garment called a coverall in facilities like this resembled the one-piece clothing worn by construction workers. Opening its zipper required a special implement, preventing the patient from removing it herself. It was a form of restraint used for patients who habitually scratched at their bodies and for patients like T, who removed a soiled diaper on her own and fouled the ward.

Japanese: 着せてから時間が過ぎ、今はＴは落ち着きを取り戻し、幻聴を訴えることも減った。このままツナギとおむつの生活を付け続けていると、今まで不完全ながらもある程度は自分でトイレに行けていたのが、いけなくなってしまうかもしれない。だから、そろそろ外した方がいいのではないか、というのが前島ナースの提案だった。
English: Some time had passed since T was placed in the coverall. She had now recovered her calm and reported fewer voices. If she remained indefinitely in a coverall and diaper, she might lose what imperfect ability she had retained to use the toilet herself. Nurse Maejima was therefore proposing that it might be time to remove it.

Japanese: それに対して、Ｔの担当である水村ナースはまだ早いのではないかと慎重な意見を口にし、また別のナースは、Ｔは何度も繰り返すのだから、もう諦めて、おむつで生活をさせるべきだと言う。
English: Nurse Mizumura, who was responsible for T, cautiously argued that it might still be too early. Another nurse said that T had repeated the pattern many times and that they should accept the loss and have her live in diapers.

Japanese: こうした意見の対立はくだらないように思われるかもしれないが、この病棟では重要なやりとりだ。
English: The disagreement might sound trivial, but on this ward it was an important exchange.

Japanese: 一度精神レベルが落ちたタイプＢというものはもう回復しない。だから、B棟三階の入院患者の多くは退院を目的とはしていない。残された能力のなかで、少しでも生活能力を維持することが目的だ。
English: Once a Type B patient’s mental functioning declined, it did not recover. Most patients on the third floor of Ward B were therefore not working toward discharge. The objective was to preserve as much ability for daily life as possible from what remained.

Japanese: たとえば、Tのようにトイレで排便出来る状態を保つのが目的だったら、他の患者だと、入浴時に自分で体を洗うのを目的にしたり、与薬時にコップ一杯の水で薬を飲めるようになることを目指したりしている。
English: For T, that might mean preserving the ability to have a bowel movement in the toilet. Another patient might aim to wash her own body at bath time, or to drink her medicine with a full glass of water when it was dispensed.

Japanese: 急性病棟だったら、人によっては退院を目指せる場合もあるし、暴力や危険行為をやめさせるといったような話題が主になるのだろうが、この慢性病棟で、こうした細々としたことが話題の中心となるのは仕方がないことだ。
English: In an acute ward, some patients might be able to work toward discharge, and discussion would probably center on stopping violence or dangerous behavior. On this chronic ward, there was no avoiding the fact that such tiny bodily acts occupied the center of attention.

Japanese: それは美紗だってわかってはいるが、何も朝の申し送り時にはやらなくても、と思うのが正直なところであった。
English: Misa understood that. Her honest feeling, however, was that the discussion did not have to occur during morning handover.

Japanese: 彼女の見るところ、この病棟のベテラン看護師たちは患者に対する愛着がありすぎて、それはまるで我が子に対するかのような態度である。
English: As Misa saw it, the veteran nurses on this ward were excessively attached to the patients. They treated them almost like their own children.

Japanese: 今年で四十五才になる藤原ナースは自分の受け持ち患者のことをよく「ウチの子」と呼ぶ。なかでも、Ｒという患者に対しては特別な愛着を持っている。十五才の時に最初の発作が起き、十八才で最初の病院で入院した彼女は、十年前にこの病院へ転院してきたとき以来、藤原ナースがずっと受け持っている。
English: Nurse Fujiwara, who turned forty-five that year, often called the patients assigned to her ‘my children.’ She was especially attached to a patient identified as R. R had experienced her first episode at fifteen and entered her first hospital at eighteen. Nurse Fujiwara had been responsible for her ever since she transferred here ten years earlier.

Japanese: 症状がすっかり進行してしまったＲは、知能レベルがすっかり退行してしまって、妄想による迷惑行為も多く、病棟でもしばしばトラブルメーカーとなったが、問題のある患者ほど可愛いものらしい。また、独特の愛嬌もある。
English: R’s condition was now far advanced. Her intellectual functioning had regressed, and her delusions frequently led her to troublesome behavior, making her a regular source of conflict on the ward. Apparently, the more troublesome the patient, the more endearing she became. R also possessed a peculiar charm.

Japanese: 藤原ナースはＲが問題を起こすたびに、他の職員に「うちの子がすみません」と謝り、Ｒを厳しくしかる。Ｒはそのたびにしゅんとするが、学習能力というものが失われてしまっているために結局また繰り返す。
English: Whenever R caused trouble, Nurse Fujiwara apologized to the other staff—‘I’m sorry about my child’—and scolded R severely. R wilted every time, but as her ability to learn had been lost, she eventually repeated the behavior.

Japanese: Ｒは今年でもう五十九才になり、藤原ナースよりも年上だが、彼女のことを「お母さん」と呼んでいる。実際、度重なる発作によって記憶が壊れている彼女は本当の母親と区別がついていないのかもしれない。母親だとすれば、そうとう口うるさい母親だと感じているだろう。が、体調が悪いときや、妄想に混乱させられているときは、誰よりも早く気がついて手助けをしてくれる、最も頼りになる相手だと感じているに違いない。
English: R was now fifty-nine, older than Nurse Fujiwara, but called her ‘Mother.’ Repeated episodes had damaged her memory, and perhaps she could no longer distinguish the nurse from her actual mother. If R did see her as a mother, she probably found her a terribly nagging one. Yet when her health declined or a delusion left her confused, R must also have regarded the nurse as the person she could rely upon above all others—the first to notice and offer help.

Japanese: 若い美紗は、こうした患者と看護師の関係を初めて知った時、医療現場としては行き過ぎたものだと感じた。
English: When the young Misa first learned of such relationships between patients and nurses, she thought them excessive for a medical setting.

Japanese: けれど、自分もそこで働くようになって印象がややかわった。ほとんど回復の見込みがない、悪くなってゆくだけの患者たちが、残された人生のすべてを『暮らしてゆく』この場所は、いわゆる一般的な医療現場とも違うのかもしれない。
English: After she began working there herself, her impression changed somewhat. Perhaps a place where patients with almost no hope of recovery, patients who would only deteriorate, spent all the remainder of their lives ‘living’ was different from what people ordinarily called a medical setting.

Japanese: おむつの件が結局現状維持のまま保留しようという話でまとまりつつあるその時、デイルームから激しい物音がした。
English: The discussion was moving toward postponing a decision on the diaper and maintaining the current arrangement when a violent noise came from the dayroom.
“What was that?”

Japanese: 看護師達は驚き、立ち上がる。
English: The nurses jumped to their feet.

Japanese: 看護師達が業務を執り行う看護室は透明で丈夫なアクリルボードによって患者達の生活空間と仕切られ、デイルームの様子が一望出来るようになっている。
English: The nurses’ station where they performed their duties was separated from the patients’ living space by a transparent sheet of durable acrylic, allowing an unobstructed view of the dayroom.

Japanese: 美紗も立ち上がって眺めると、患者のＦが尻餅をつき、その前にＵが仁王立ちをして、顔を真っ赤にしているのが見えた。Ｆの側には空になったマグカップがあり、水が飛び散っている。そして椅子がひっくり返っているところなどを見ると、二人の間で何かあって、席に着いていたＦが椅子ごと倒れたという状況がうかがえる。
English: Misa stood and looked. Patient F was sitting on the floor after a fall, while U stood planted before her, face crimson. An empty mug lay near F, with water splashed around it. A chair had also overturned, suggesting that something had occurred between them and that F had fallen backward with her chair.

Japanese: 暴力行為が行われたのだろうか？　男子病棟では多いが、この病棟ではそこまで頻繁には発生しないトラブルである。
English: Had there been violence? Such trouble was common on the men’s wards, but occurred far less frequently here.

Japanese: 看護助手の林田がベルトからチェーンで繋がれた鍵でドアを開けてデイルームに出ると、看護師達もそれに続く。
English: Nursing assistant Hayashida opened the door with a key chained to his belt and stepped into the dayroom. The nurses followed.

Japanese: 「ヒロちゃん、どうしたんだい？」
English: “Hiro, what happened?”

Japanese: 林田が興奮するUにニックネームで呼びかける。
English: Hayashida addressed the agitated U by her nickname.

Japanese: Uは十代のまだ若い患者で、青白く痩せている。薬の副作用によって足元がおぼつかずによく転ぶため、頭にはボクシングで使うようなヘッドガードを装着している。顔立ちは整っており、本来ならかわいげのある少女なのだろうが、身だしなみは全く整えられておらず、髪の毛はぼさぼさにはね、口もとは産毛がちょろちょろと伸びており、そして、その目は金色に輝いていた。
English: U was a young patient in her teens, thin and deathly pale. Side effects from her medication made her unsteady and prone to falls, so she wore a padded head guard like those used in boxing. Her features were regular, and under other circumstances she might have been an appealing girl. Yet her appearance was completely neglected. Her hair stuck out in untidy tufts, fine hairs straggled above her mouth, and her eyes shone gold.

Japanese: 「おいおい、目が金色になってるぞ」
English: “Now, now. Your eyes have gone gold.”

Japanese: 林田はUを落ち着かせるような笑顔を浮かべつつ、Fとの間に自分の身体を入れた。
English: Hayashida stepped between U and F, wearing a smile meant to calm her.

Japanese: 「ねえヒロミちゃん落ち着いて。フクちゃんに何かしたの？」
English: “Hiromi, try to calm down. Did you do something to Fuku?”

Japanese: 美紗は林田を睨み付けて威嚇的な態度をとるUに近づき、そう言った。
English: Misa approached U, who was glaring threateningly at Hayashida, and spoke to her.

Japanese: 彼は美紗の担当する患者であった。
English: She was one of Misa’s assigned patients.

Japanese: 美紗は三人の患者を担当しているが、Uはその中で最も若く、最も難しい患者である。
English: Misa was responsible for three patients. U was both the youngest and the most difficult.

Japanese: 被毒妄想があり、しばしば食事に毒が入っていると訴えて手を付けずに捨ててしまう。それが続くとすぐに栄養失調寸前まで陥り、仕方なくベッドに拘束をして点滴をすることになる。
English: She experienced delusions of poisoning and frequently insisted that her food contained poison, throwing it away untouched. When that continued, she soon became dangerously malnourished, leaving the staff no choice but to restrain her in bed and administer an intravenous drip.

Japanese: 夜は眠らず、病棟内を徘徊して、他の患者の私物を漁る。
English: At night, she did not sleep. She wandered the ward and searched through the other patients’ belongings.

Japanese: トイレットペーパーを適切な量使うことが出来ず、他の患者のようにロールを持たせると丸ごと流してつまらせてしまう。そのくせロールを与えないと不穏になって、幻聴が活発化する。
English: She could not use an appropriate amount of toilet paper. If given a roll like the other patients, she flushed the entire thing and blocked the toilet. Yet withholding the roll made her agitated and caused the voices she heard to grow more active.

Japanese: 普段から落ち着きがなく、他患に同じことを何度も繰り返し質問し、相手を怒らせてしまうことも多い。
English: She was habitually restless and often angered the other patients by asking them the same question again and again.

Japanese: しかし、こんな風に自分が興奮して他人に何かをするということは滅多になかったので、美紗としても意外な思いであった。迷惑行為が頻回なわりには愛嬌があり、病棟最年少ということもあって職員にも他の患者にも可愛がられていた。
English: Even so, it was rare for her to grow agitated and do something to another person in this way, and Misa found the incident surprising. For all the frequency of her troublesome behavior, she had an endearing quality. As the youngest patient on the ward, she was doted upon by staff and patients alike.

Japanese: 「大丈夫？　何かきこえちゃった？　こわくない？」
English: “Are you all right? Did you hear something? Are you frightened?”

Japanese: Uの目はうつろで、美紗の方に視線をやりはするが、問いかけに対する返事はない。
English: U’s eyes were vacant. She looked toward Misa, but gave no answer to the questions.

Japanese: 元々意志の疎通がはかりにくいタイプで言葉に対する反応が薄いのだが、今はさらに一段と鈍いようだ。
English: Communication had always been difficult for her, and she responded only weakly to words. At present, her responses seemed duller still.

Japanese: 「とりあえず、向こうの椅子に腰掛けようか」
English: “Why don’t we sit in the chair over there for now?”

Japanese: 林田が手を引こうとするのを、Uは乱暴にふりほどく。
English: When Hayashida tried to take her hand, U shook him off violently.

Japanese: 「能見さん、こりゃダメだ。頓服使ったほうがいいんじゃない？」
English: “Ms. Nomi, this is no good. Don’t you think we should use a PRN?”

Japanese: 林田は美紗を振り返って苦笑する。
English: Hayashida looked back at Misa with a wry smile.

Japanese: 「この子、今は何も出てないんです」
English: “She has nothing ordered right now.”

Japanese: 美紗は首を横に振る。
English: Misa shook her head.

Japanese: 「ああそうか。主治医が安田先生にかわったんだっけ」
English: “Oh, right. Dr. Yasuda took over as her attending physician, didn’t he?”

Japanese: 林田は納得したように頷く。安田医師は、この病院内ではなかなか薬を出さない医者として有名であった。
English: Hayashida nodded in understanding. Within the hospital, Dr. Yasuda was famous for his reluctance to prescribe medication.

Japanese: その背後では看護師たちが、倒れたFの身体を調べている。
English: Behind him, the nurses were examining F where she had fallen.

Japanese: 「出血も腫脹もないようですねえ」
English: “There does not appear to be any bleeding or swelling.”

Japanese: 服をめくって肌の外傷を調べていた前島ナースがのんびりした口調でそう報告する。
English: Nurse Maejima, who had lifted F’s clothes to inspect the skin for injuries, reported in a leisurely voice.

Japanese: 「血圧もプルスも正常です」
English: “Blood pressure and pulse are both normal.”

Japanese: 水村ナースが落ち着いた声でそう伝える。
English: Nurse Mizumura delivered the finding calmly.

Japanese: 「大丈夫？　どこか痛いところはない？」
English: “Are you all right? Does it hurt anywhere?”

Japanese: 主任がそう尋ねても、Fは反応をせず呆然と目を見開いている。Fは四十を越えた背の低い女で、こちらはUと違っておしゃべりで、他人の言葉にはいつも機敏に反応するのだが、どうやらショックから抜け出せないでいるらしい。
English: Even when the chief asked, F did not respond. She stared blankly with her eyes wide open. F was a short woman over forty. Unlike U, she was talkative and ordinarily responded quickly to the words of others, but she apparently had not yet recovered from the shock.

Japanese: 「フクちゃん。一体何があったの？　すごい音がしたからみんなびっくりしちゃった」
English: “Fuku, what in the world happened? There was such a loud noise that you startled everyone.”

Japanese: 主任はFの前にしゃがみ込んで優しくそう問いかけると、Fは堰が切れたように早口で喋り出した。
English: The chief crouched before F and questioned her gently. As if a dam had burst, F began speaking in a rapid torrent.

Japanese: 「こ、こいつがよう！　この馬鹿女が、急に近づいて来て、アタシを突き飛ばしたんだよ。ほら、目がキンキラになってるじゃないの？　前も、アタシのことやたらとつけ回してよ。こわくてしかたねえよ。こいつ、人殺したことあるんだろう？　それでここに入ってるんだろ。ねえ主任さん、保護室に入れてくれよ」
English: “I-it was her! This stupid bitch came up out of nowhere and shoved me. Look, can’t you see her eyes glittering gold? She followed me everywhere before, too. She scares the hell out of me. She killed somebody, didn’t she? That’s why she’s in here. Chief, put her in the seclusion room.”

Japanese: 「フクちゃん、人のことをそんな風に言っちゃダメだって、いつも言ってるでしょう。それにちょっと声が大きいわ」
English: “Fuku, I am always telling you not to speak about people that way. And your voice is a little loud.”

Japanese: 「でもよう、本当のことじゃねえか。……あー、やだやだ。こんなおかしい病院、やだねえ！　主任さん、いつになったら私は退院出来るんだい？　いい加減、アタシをここに閉じ込めるのは勘弁してほしいよ。せめてよその病院で受診させてくれないかねえ？　ここは藪医者ばかりだから、私を病人にするのさ。そうして、アタシをここで死なせて財産を奪おうとしている……」
English: “But it’s true, isn’t it? ...Ah, no, no. I hate this lunatic hospital! Chief, when are you going to let me out? I’ve had enough of you locking me in here. Couldn’t you at least have me examined at another hospital? This place is full of quacks. They’re the ones making me sick. They mean to let me die here and steal my fortune...”

Japanese: Fは病識がない……つまり、自分がおかしいという自覚が全くない患者で、ことあるごとに職員が騙して自分を入院させていると訴える。もちろん、狙われていると本人が言う財産などあるはずもない。
English: F lacked insight into her illness—that is, she possessed no awareness that anything was wrong with her. At every opportunity, she claimed that the staff had deceived her and arranged her hospitalization. Of course, the fortune she claimed they were after did not exist.

Japanese: 「その話は後にしてね」
English: “We will discuss that later.”

Japanese: 主任は困ったような顔でそう言うと、
English: The chief answered with a troubled expression.

Japanese: 「フクちゃん、立てる？　立てるなら、ちょっとお部屋に戻っててちょうだい。あ、その前に、お薬飲んで行きなさいね。あなたもちょっと興奮してる。このままじゃ、あなたもまた悪くなっちゃうわ」
English: “Fuku, can you stand? If you can, go back to your room for a little while. Ah—but take some medicine first. You are rather agitated yourself. At this rate, your condition will deteriorate again.”

Japanese: 「薬なんかいらねえよ」
English: “I don’t need any medicine.”

Japanese: Fは一旦は断ったが、水村ナースから頓服薬とコップを差し出すと、渋々それを服用した。そして、Uに向かってわざと舌打ちをしてからデイルームを出て行く。
English: F refused at first, but when Nurse Mizumura offered her a PRN medication and a glass, she swallowed it reluctantly. Then she made an ostentatious click of her tongue at U and left the dayroom.

Japanese: 「本当に、福沢さんを突き飛ばしたりしたの？」
English: “Did you truly push Ms. Fukuzawa?”

Japanese: Fが出て行ってから、美紗は相変わらずその場に立ち尽くすUにそう尋ねる。Uの唇は震え、何か言おうと一端は開くが、結局声を発することなくまた閉じた。その端から、唾液がこぼれて顎を伝う。
English: After F left, Misa questioned U, who remained standing in the same place. U’s lips trembled. She opened them once, as if trying to speak, but closed them again without producing a sound. Saliva spilled from one corner and ran down her chin.

Japanese: 「ねえ、どうしてそんなことをしたの？　押されたら、福沢さんもびっくりしちゃうでしょう。理由を教えてくれない？」
English: “Why did you do that? You must have frightened Ms. Fukuzawa when you pushed her. Won’t you tell me why?”

Japanese: Uの唇は再び震え、そして今度はやっと言葉が出た。
English: U’s lips trembled again. This time, words finally emerged.

Japanese: 「……だ、だまれ」
English: “...S-shut up.”

Japanese: 「まあ」
English: “Oh.”

Japanese: 美紗が言葉を失って固まってしまうと、林田がなれなれしくUの肩に腕を回し、
English: Misa froze, at a loss for words. Hayashida casually put an arm around U’s shoulders.

Japanese: 「ヒロちゃん、きみはちょっと興奮しすぎているなあ。それとも若い看護師さん相手だとテレちゃうのかな？　向こうでこの林田さんと、ちょっと落ち着いて話をしない？」
English: “Hiro, you’re much too worked up. Or are you shy around a young nurse? Why don’t you come sit over there and have a quiet talk with yours truly?”

Japanese: すると、美紗に対してあれだけ頑なだったUは、あっさりと頷く。
English: U, who had been so closed off with Misa, nodded readily.

Japanese: 「よし、じゃあ行こう」
English: “Good. Let’s go.”

Japanese: 林田は美紗に目配せをしてから、肩を組んだままUと並んでデイルームの向こうの長椅子に腰をかける。
English: Hayashida signaled to Misa with his eyes, then walked U across the dayroom with his arm still around her shoulders. They sat together on a bench.
“Whew...”

Japanese: 看護室に戻ってから、美紗は大きく溜息をつく。
English: Back in the nurses’ station, Misa heaved a long sigh.

Japanese: Uに「だまれ」と言われたことがショックであった。
English: Being told to shut up by U had shocked her.

Japanese: 彼は普段そんな暴言を口にする人物ではない。それなりにうまくやっており、担当看護師として信頼関係を築けたと思っていたのだ。
English: She did not ordinarily use such abusive language. Misa had thought the two of them got along reasonably well and that, as her primary nurse, she had built up a relationship of trust.

Japanese: 一方、助手の林田に対してはあんなに興奮した状況でも意志の疎通がとれている。林田は助手とは言え自分よりベテランであるし、患者との接し方には定評があり、この病棟の誰よりも不穏になった患者を落ち着かせるのがうまく、困ったときは主任や他のベテラン看護師でも彼を頼りにする。
English: Yet even in that state of agitation, U had communicated with the assistant Hayashida. He might be an assistant, but he had more experience than Misa and an excellent reputation for his manner with patients. No one on the ward was better at calming an agitated patient. When trouble arose, even the chief and the other veteran nurses relied upon him.

Japanese: そういった人物と比べるのは間違いなのかもしれないが、やはりこうした重要な場面で何も出来ないことに、美紗は無力感を覚える。若くして症状の重いUは最も力を入れている患者で、その人物との間にこんなことがあると、自分は向いていないのではないかと、溜息ばかりが出るのである。
English: Perhaps it was wrong to compare herself with a man like that. Even so, her inability to do anything at such a crucial moment filled Misa with helplessness. U, a young patient with severe symptoms, was the patient to whom she devoted the most effort. When something like this happened between them, Misa could do nothing but sigh and wonder whether she was unsuited to the work.

Japanese: 落ち込む美紗の目の前では主任が主治医に報告の電話をし、水村ナースと前島ナースが今起きたことについて話し合っている。
English: As Misa stood there dejected, the chief telephoned the attending physician to report the incident, while Nurses Mizumura and Maejima discussed what had happened.

Japanese: 「まったく、フクちゃんのあの態度をみた？　最後にわざとらしく舌打ちなんかしちゃってさ。ああいうことばっかりしてるから、色んな人のトラブルに巻き込まれるのよ。今回も、本当に何もしなかったのかしらねえ。この間吉田さんに頭をはたかれたのも、あの人が嫌味みたいなこと言ったからでしょ。まったく、イジワルババアなんだから」
English: “Honestly, did you see Fuku’s behavior? That ostentatious click of her tongue at the end! She does things like that constantly, and then wonders why she gets caught up in trouble with everyone. Did she truly do nothing this time, I wonder? The last time Ms. Yoshida slapped her head, it was because she said something spiteful, wasn’t it? Honestly, what a vicious old bitch.”

Japanese: Fはこの病棟のなかでは意思の疎通もとりやすく、知能も正常に近いまま残されている、いわゆる「出来る」グループに属するが、だからといって面倒のない患者というわけではない。
English: Within the ward, F belonged to the so-called ‘capable’ group. Communication with her was comparatively easy, and her intelligence remained close to normal. That did not make her an easy patient.

Japanese: 知能の程度が下がり、人格が荒廃し、身のまわりのことが出来なくなってしまった患者は手間がかかるが、知能が残ったままの患者はそれはそれで別の苦労がある。
English: Patients whose intelligence had declined, whose personalities had deteriorated, and who could no longer tend to themselves demanded considerable work. Those who retained their intelligence presented hardships of another kind.

Japanese: Fの場合、口が達者で屁理屈ばかりを言い、普段から女性看護師に対しても暴言が多い。そして具合が悪くなると、「自分は神だ」というような妄想に取り憑かれ、普段よりも一層他人に非常に尊大に振る舞ったり、命令をするようになる。そして受け入れられないと、金切り声で暴言を吐く。こうなってしまうと誰も手が付けられず、隔離部屋に閉じ込めなくてはならない。そのため、彼女は昔から保護室の常連であった。
English: In F’s case, she was glib, endlessly argumentative, and habitually abusive even toward the female nurses. When her condition worsened, she became possessed by delusions such as the belief that she was a god. She then treated others with even greater arrogance than usual and issued commands. If they refused her, she shrieked abuse. Once matters reached that point, no one could manage her, and she had to be locked in a seclusion room. She had therefore been a regular occupant of those rooms for many years.

Japanese: 「声が大きいから、他の患者さんを刺激しやすいのかもしれませんね。でも、内田さんにはちょっとびっくりしましたね。最近ちょっと具合が悪かったけど、突き飛ばすなんて……」
English: “Perhaps her loud voice makes it easy for her to agitate the other patients. But Ms. Uchida did surprise me. She has been a little unwell lately, but to push someone...”

Japanese: 「彼女も保護室になっちゃうのかねえ」
English: “Do you think she will end up in seclusion too?”

Japanese: この病棟は暴力行為がない、と言ってもあくまでも比較の話であって、やはり人が共同生活すればたまには発生することもある。
English: When people said violence did not occur on this ward, they spoke only in relative terms. Wherever people lived together, it was bound to happen occasionally.

Japanese: Uは問題行動も多く手間のかかる患者であるが、普段は素直で言うことを聞く大人しい少女で、患者間のもめ事では被害者になりやすく、今回のように加害側の立場になった場合でも職員は同情的だ。
English: U displayed many problem behaviors and required a great deal of work, but ordinarily she was an obedient, compliant, quiet girl. In disputes among patients, she was more often the victim. Even now, when she had become the aggressor, the staff were sympathetic toward her.

Japanese: 建前上はあってはならないことだし、それで対応が変わるということも基本的にはないのだが、人情として職員にも患者に対する好悪というものはある。
English: Officially, such preference should not have existed, and as a rule it did not change the care provided. But staff were human, and they too liked and disliked particular patients.

Japanese: 家族には見捨てられ、財産もなく、生活保護で暮らすような何も持たない患者ばかりだが、人柄が素直ならば、こんな場所でも人に愛される。
English: The ward was filled with patients who possessed nothing—abandoned by family, without property, and living on public assistance. Yet if their nature was open and sincere, they could be loved even in a place like this.

Japanese: 美紗はここに来てから、最終的な人間の武器というものは、この人間性ではないかと思うようになった。いつか自分が老人になり、どこかの施設に入った時に、周りの人間に愛されるような性格になれれば幸福に過ごせるだろう。
English: Since coming here, Misa had begun to think that a person’s ultimate weapon might be their character. If she herself grew old and entered some facility, she could live happily if she became someone the people around her loved.

Japanese: 「かわいいお祖母ちゃんにならなくちゃいけない！」
English: “I must become a cute old lady!”

Japanese: というのが、最近美紗がよく口にするフレーズである。
English: It was a phrase Misa often used these days.

Japanese: さて、Uが加害者になることが珍しいとは言え、看護師の日常は忙しい。これくらいのトラブルでいちいち業務を滞らせてなどいられないのだ。主任がドクターへの電話を終えると、すぐに雑談は打ち切られ、申し送りが再開される。
English: U becoming the aggressor might be unusual, but a nurse’s day was busy. They could not bring the work to a halt over trouble of this degree. The moment the chief ended her call with the doctor, the conversation ceased and handover resumed.

Japanese: そして申し送りが終わる頃、林田が鍵を開けて戻ってきた。
English: As handover drew to its close, Hayashida unlocked the door and returned.

Japanese: 「いやー、あの子、妄想バリバリだよ。困っちゃったなあ」
English: “Whew, she’s completely in the grip of those delusions. What a pickle.”

Japanese: 彼は困ったようには見えない笑顔を浮かべながら言った。よく日に焼けたその黒い顔に浮かべる笑顔は、他の棟を歩くと女性患者たちが騒ぐほどさわやかなもので、女性職員の間にも密かな人気がある。
English: He wore a smile that did not look troubled in the least. His smile was so bright against his deeply tanned face that the female patients raised a commotion whenever he walked through another building. He was quietly popular among the female staff as well.

Japanese: かつては東京のマリンスポーツのグッズを売る店で従業員をしていたらしい。それがどうしてこんな街のこんな施設で働くようになったのかは誰も知らないが、今は頼りになる職員の一人である。
English: He had apparently once worked at a shop selling marine-sports equipment in Tokyo. No one knew how that had led him to a facility like this in a city like this one, but he was now among the most dependable members of staff.

Japanese: 「例の『グレートホール』が始まってますねえ。『グレートホールが私を呼んでる』とか『グレートホールに帰らなきゃいけない』とか、そればっかり言ってる。それで、福沢さんは、グレートホールから出て来た悪魔の化身なんだって。とりあえずいつもの絵本を渡したらそれを読んでくれたけど、あの調子じゃまた繰り返すんじゃないですかねえ。あくまでも私としての個人的な感想ですが」
English: “That Great Hole business has started again. ‘The Great Hole is calling me.’ ‘I have to go back to the Great Hole.’ She says nothing else. And apparently Ms. Fukuzawa is the incarnation of a demon that came out of the Great Hole. I gave her the usual picture book for the moment, and she did read it. But in her present condition, I expect she will repeat the behavior. That is, of course, only my personal opinion.”

Japanese: 「そうですか。いつもありがとうね林田さん」
English: “I see. Thank you as always, Mr. Hayashida.”

Japanese: ドクターとの電話を終えた主任は難しい顔でそうねぎらう。
English: The chief, finished with her call to the doctor, thanked him with a troubled expression.

Japanese: 「もうすぐ先生が来て内田さんを診てくださるけど、多分保護室に隔離することになると思うわ」
English: “The doctor will be here shortly to examine Ms. Uchida, but I expect that he will order her secluded in a protective room.”

Japanese: 「ああ、それがいいですねえ。私は賛成です。じゃあちょっくら保護室の準備をしてきます」
English: “Ah, that would be best. I agree. I’ll go prepare a room.”

Japanese: 「お願いね」
English: “Please do.”

Japanese: それから申し送りが終わり、朝の与薬も終わって夜勤者が帰り支度を始める頃、Uの主治医である安田医師がやって来て、主任が言ったとおりUを保護室に隔離するよう指示を出した。
English: Handover ended, as did the morning medication round. Around the time the night staff began preparing to leave, Dr. Yasuda, U’s attending physician, arrived and—just as the chief had predicted—ordered her secluded in a protective room.

Japanese: そして美紗は今日最後の仕事としてUを保護室に連れて行くこととなった。
English: Misa’s final duty of the day was therefore to take U there.

Japanese: 保護室とは別名Zルームとも言い、患者を隔離するための鍵のついた個室である。妄想が活発化して落ち着きがなくなった患者や、他の患者とトラブルを起こして集団のなかに居づらくなった患者などをこの部屋で一時的に保護し、状態の安定をはかる。
English: The protective rooms, also known as Z-rooms, were locked private rooms used for seclusion. Staff temporarily secluded patients there when intensified delusions left them restless or conflict with another patient made remaining in the group difficult, in an effort to stabilize their condition.

Japanese: 部屋にはマットレスが一枚と、洋式便器、そしてそれを隠す衝立があるだけで、他には何もない。窓は二重になっていて、磨りガラスに手が届いて割ったりしないように手前には鉄格子がはまっている。天井には監視カメラが設置され、部屋の様子は看護室のモニターから２４時間確認出来るようになっている。
English: Each room contained only a mattress, a Western-style toilet, and a screen to conceal it. The windows were double layered, with iron bars on the inside to keep patients from reaching and breaking the frosted glass. A surveillance camera was mounted in the ceiling, and the room could be monitored from the nurses’ station twenty-four hours a day.

Japanese: A棟三階には六室設置されており、現在はそのうち三室が使用されていた。美紗が鍵を開けて廊下に足を踏み入れると、そのと扉が開く音に一番奥の部屋の患者が反応する。
English: There were six rooms on the third floor of Ward A, three of which were currently occupied. When Misa unlocked the door and stepped into the corridor, the sound of it opening drew a response from the patient in the room farthest away.

Japanese: 「水ぅう！　水を頂戴よお！」
English: “Water! Give me water!”

Japanese: 水中毒で保護室に隔離されたその患者がドアをドンドンと叩く。その音は廊下に響き、顔を顰めたくなるほどだ。
English: The patient, who had been secluded for water intoxication, pounded on the door. The sound echoed down the corridor loudly enough to make anyone grimace.

Japanese: 「おい、うるせえな。黙ってろよ！」
English: “Hey, shut the hell up! You’re too loud!”

Japanese: 音に耐えかねたその隣の、暴力行為が原因で隔離されている患者が怒鳴り返す。
English: Unable to endure the noise, the patient in the next room, who had been secluded for violence, shouted back.

Japanese: 美紗も初めて入った頃は、この空間の雰囲気に圧倒されたものだが、今は入っている患者達のこともよく知っており、普段は雑談などもし、無用に恐れるような必要がないことを理解している。
English: When Misa first began working here, the atmosphere of this space had overwhelmed her. Now she knew the patients inside well, often chatted casually with them, and understood that she had no reason to fear them unnecessarily.

Japanese: 「飛川さん、そんな乱暴な口きかないでね。そんな物言いしてるとまた出られなくなっちゃうわよ。牛野さん、あなたはちょっと水を飲み過ぎ。看護師さん達はちゃんと量計って出してるんだから。もうすこし時間が経ったら、日勤の人が持って来てくれるから待っててね」
English: “Ms. Hikawa, don’t talk like that. If you keep it up, they won’t let you out again. Ms. Ushino, you’ve been drinking too much water. The nurses measure out the right amount for you. Wait a little longer, and someone from the day shift will bring it.”

Japanese: 美紗は廊下の奥に向かって大きな声でそう呼びかける。
English: Misa raised her voice toward the far end of the corridor.

Japanese: 「そんなこと言ったって、喉がかわいたんだよう」
English: “But I’m thirsty!”

Japanese: 「可哀想な声出したってダメよ。なんでそこに入ったか覚えてるでしょう？　ここで飲み過ぎたら、また出られなくなっちゃうわ。……さあ、ヒロミちゃん、入って」
English: “That pitiful voice isn’t going to work. You remember why you’re in there, don’t you? If you drink too much here, they won’t let you out again. ...Now, Hiromi, go inside.”

Japanese: 促されて、Uが廊下に足を踏み入れる。続いて林田が入り、廊下とデイルームを繋ぐ扉の鍵を閉める。
English: At her prompting, U entered the corridor. Hayashida followed and locked the door connecting the corridor to the dayroom.

Japanese: 保護室に入ると伝えてもUは別段騒ぐこともなく、素直だった。相変わらず目は金色ではあったが、先ほどのような興奮や緊張は見られず、かわりに理由のない笑いが顔に浮かんでいる。
English: Being told that she would enter a protective room had caused U no particular disturbance, and she remained compliant. Her eyes were still gold, but the excitement and tension from earlier had vanished. In their place, an unprompted smile lingered on her face.

Japanese: 「ここで靴と靴下を脱いで……。そうそう、あなたも慣れたもんだね」
English: “Take off your shoes and socks here... Yes, just like that. You know the routine by now.”

Japanese: そして美紗はUのズボンのポケットに手を突っ込んで、保護室持ち込み禁止のものがないかボディチェックをする。その間もUは身体を揺すり、クスクスと空笑している。
English: Misa put a hand into the pockets of U’s trousers and performed a body search for items forbidden in the protective room. Throughout it, U rocked her body and gave empty little laughs.

Japanese: 「よしOK。じゃあ、ヒロミちゃん、この部屋でゆっくり休んで心を落ち着けるんだよ」
English: “Good, all clear. Hiromi, rest quietly in this room and let your mind settle.”

Japanese: 美紗の言葉に、のっそりとした動作で従おうとするUの肩を林田が軽く叩いた。
English: U began to obey with sluggish movements. Hayashida lightly tapped her shoulder.

Japanese: 「ヒロミちゃん、さっき言ってたこと、直接伝えなよ」
English: “Hiromi, tell her directly what you said before.”

Japanese: すると、Uは笑いをやめる。
English: U stopped laughing.

Japanese: 林田はもう一度同じ言葉を繰り返す。すると、彼はしばらく林田の顔を見つめてから、美紗の方を振り返り、
English: Hayashida repeated himself. She watched his face for a time, then turned to Misa.

Japanese: 「ノウミさん。さっきは、ゴメンナサイ」
English: “Ms. Nomi. I’m... sorry about before.”

Japanese: ぺこりと頭を下げた。
English: She bowed her head.

Japanese: 「ヒロミちゃん……」
English: “Hiromi...”

Japanese: 美紗が目を丸くして絶句するのをよそに、Uは自分から部屋のなかに入り、マットレスの上にごろりと横になってそのやせ細った背を向ける。背中は時々小刻みに揺れる。笑っているのだ。
English: While Misa stood wide-eyed and speechless, U entered the room of her own accord, dropped onto the mattress, and turned her emaciated back. Her back shook faintly from time to time. She was laughing.

Japanese: 林田は扉を閉め、鍵をかけると、ガチャリと音がした。
English: Hayashida closed and locked the door with a metallic click.

Japanese: 「さあ、行こうか」
English: “Shall we go?”

Japanese: 美紗を振り返ると、その顔にちょっと驚き、それから笑顔を浮かべて、
English: He turned toward Misa, looked briefly startled by her face, then smiled.

Japanese: 「能見さん、感情失禁かい？」
English: “Ms. Nomi, is that emotional incontinence?”

Japanese: 美紗はその冗談に気の利いた返事が出来ない。慌てて首を横にブンブンと振ると、
English: Misa could find no clever reply to the joke. She hurriedly shook her head.

Japanese: 「違いますよぅ」
English: “Nooo, it isn’t.”

Japanese: と言い、ノーメイクの顔をゴシゴシと手で拭った。
English: Then she scrubbed at her unmade-up face with one hand.

Japanese: そして照れ隠しで笑うと、
English: She laughed to conceal her embarrassment.

Japanese: 「こういうのがあるから、患者さんって憎めないんですよね……」
English: “Moments like that make it impossible to dislike the patients...”

Japanese: 独り言のように呟いた。
English: She murmured it almost to herself.

Japanese: 美紗はY地区のすぐ側の住宅地にアパートを借りて一人暮らしをしている。
English: Misa lived alone in an apartment in a residential neighborhood just outside Y District.

Japanese: 友人からはそんな場所に住んで危なくないのかとよく訊かれるが、Y地区のなかならともかく、駅を越えた反対側は日本のどこにでもあるようなごく当たり前の住宅地である。
English: Friends often asked whether living in such a place was dangerous. That might have been true inside Y District, but beyond the station on its opposite side lay an entirely ordinary residential neighborhood like any other in Japan.

Japanese: 美紗には大胆不敵というか無頓着なところがあって、最初はもっと病院に近いY地区のなかのアパートを探したのだが、不動産屋に止められてこのアパートにしたのだ。その時は、言われるままに決めてしまったことを後悔したりもしたが、今となってはその提案に従って良かったと心底思う。
English: Misa possessed something of a fearless—or perhaps careless—streak. At first, she had searched for an apartment within Y District, closer to the hospital. A real-estate agent dissuaded her and found this apartment instead. At the time, she occasionally regretted letting herself be talked into it. Now, she was profoundly grateful that she had followed the advice.

Japanese: Y地区は遊ぶには良い場所で、そこで飲んだり買い物をしたりはしても、自分のような平凡な人間が住む場所ではないと実感している。滑走路通りなどの表通りを利用しているかぎり、よく語られる治安の悪さを体験することは少ないけれど、すれ違う人間が外国人ばかりで、街中に読むことの出来ない言語で書かれた文字があふれているというのは、顔見知りばかりが暮らす田舎町で育った美紗にはどうにも落ち着かない。
English: Y District was a fine place for entertainment. She drank and shopped there, but had come to feel that it was no place for an ordinary person like her to live. So long as she kept to the main roads, such as Runway Street, she seldom encountered the crime and danger people talked about. Yet nearly everyone she passed was foreign, and the city overflowed with writing in languages she could not read. For Misa, raised in a rural town where every face was familiar, it remained deeply unsettling.

Japanese: 夜勤明けの精神状態というのは不思議なものだ。病院にいた時はあれほど眠くて仕方がないのに、勤務時間が終わると妙に晴れ晴れとした気持になって睡魔などどこかへ消えてしまう。
English: The state of mind following a night shift was curious. At the hospital, she could scarcely endure her sleepiness. The moment her working hours ended, she felt strangely refreshed, and the drowsiness vanished.

Japanese: 同僚のなかには、そのまま遊びに行く者もいる。その気持は美紗にもわかるが、身体に残る疲労を考えると同じような行動は出来ない。
English: Some of her colleagues went directly out to enjoy themselves. Misa understood the impulse, but the fatigue remaining in her body prevented her from doing the same.

Japanese: シャワーを浴び、滑走路通りで買ったハンバーガーを食べながら勉強をする。そのハンバーガーの味付けは、美紗の好みからすると少し濃かったが、なかなかの美男子が販売しており、それが理由でしばしば購入している。
English: She showered, then studied while eating a hamburger she had bought on Runway Street. The seasoning was somewhat too strong for her taste, but the vendor was remarkably handsome, and for that reason she often bought one from him.

Japanese: 勉強と言っても、本を読むだけである。それは主任から勧められた出版されたばかりの新しい本で、タイプB患者の看護法について書かれた本であった。その冒頭には、タイプBについての基礎的な情報が書かれている。
English: By study, she meant only reading. The chief had recommended a newly published book about nursing care for Type B patients. Its opening chapters presented basic information about Type Bs.

Japanese: まずタイプBというのは、タイプAと同じ、ミュータントの一種である。
English: First, the book described Type B, like Type A, as a kind of mutant.

Japanese: ただ、そのありようはタイプAとは大分違う。
English: Its nature, however, differed considerably from Type A.

Japanese: タイプAは、いわゆるサイキックである。一般的な人間にはなかなか実現出来ない能力を持っている。
English: A Type A was what people commonly called a psychic: someone possessing abilities beyond what an ordinary human could readily achieve.

Japanese: それは、念動力や、発火、読心など、古典的なSFでよく目にするものから、例えば目隠しして指先で触れるだけでカップラーメンの銘柄を正確に当てるだけという、なぜ備わったのかよくわらない能力まで、数え切れないくらいの多様な能力が存在する。
English: Countless varieties of those abilities existed. They ranged from the familiar powers of classical science fiction—telekinesis, pyrokinesis, and mind reading—to the inexplicable gift of identifying the brand of instant noodles in a cup merely by touching it with a fingertip while blindfolded.

Japanese: その能力の強さも人それぞれで、例えば念動力なら、大の大人を宙高く飛ばしてしまうものから、何分も集中して一円玉を乗せた計りの数値がやっと一グラム軽くなるようなものまで幅広い。
English: Their strength varied just as greatly. A telekinetic might throw a grown man high into the air, or might concentrate for several minutes merely to reduce by one gram the reading on a scale holding a one-yen coin.

Japanese: 美紗が小学校の頃クラスに一人タイプAがいたが、集中してコップ一杯の水道水を見つめると五分で３℃上昇するというものだった。ミネラルウォーターや牛乳では出来ないし、手でさわって温度の上昇が確認出来るほど温度が上がるわけでもないので、そう語る本人の言葉を聞くだけで実際その能力を確認することは出来なかった。実際のところ、世間のタイプAというのはこの程度のささやかな能力者ばかりらしい。
English: When Misa was in elementary school, one child in her class had been Type A. He said that by concentrating on a glass of tap water for five minutes, he could raise its temperature by three degrees Celsius. It did not work with mineral water or milk, and the increase was not large enough to confirm by touch. Misa could therefore do nothing but listen to his claim and never verified the ability herself. Apparently, most Type As in society possessed only modest powers of this order.

Japanese: そして、タイプAのもう一つの特徴として『特質変異』がある。
English: The book identified another characteristic of Type A: ‘trait mutation.’

Japanese: タイプAとして生まれた人間の何割かは、とても考えられないような肉体の異常を持って生まれる。
English: A certain proportion of people born Type A also entered the world with physical abnormalities that seemed almost inconceivable.

Japanese: たとえば全身が毛むくじゃらで指の間に水かきがあるとか、目が一つしかなく顔の中央にあるとか、象のように長い牙が生えているとか。
English: One might be covered in hair and possess webbing between the fingers, have a single eye in the middle of the face, or grow long tusks like an elephant’s.

Japanese: 能力が強いほど人間離れした特質変異を持つ傾向があるというが、実際には大した能力がなくともとんでもない変形をしている人がいたり、絶大な能力がありながら全くノーマルと変わらない人もいる。
English: People said that stronger abilities tended to accompany more inhuman trait mutations. In practice, however, some people possessed extraordinary physical changes despite having no significant power, while others wielded immense power and looked no different from a Normal.

Japanese: こうしたタイプAは、ノーマルの延長線上に存在しているというのが最近の考え方だ。すべての人間はタイプAであり、現在ノーマルと認定されている人も、実際は測定が不可能な程度のなんらかの能力が備わっているのではないかと予測されている。この辺りが、タイプBとは特に違うところだ。
English: The current model, the book explained, placed Type As on a continuum with Normals. Some researchers predicted that every human being was Type A, and that even people presently certified as Normal actually possessed some ability too faint to measure. This was one of the principal differences between A and B.

Japanese: タイプBもかつてはタイプAの一種だと考えられていた。
English: Type Bs, too, had once been regarded as a variety of Type A.

Japanese: しかし、あまりにも同じ能力と、同じ肉体の変異を持つ者が多すぎたため、これは何か別の種類のミュータントなのではないかと考えられるようになり、独立して『タイプB』と呼ばれるようになった。
English: Yet far too many possessed the same abilities and the same physical changes. Researchers began to regard them as a separate kind of mutant, and they received the independent classification ‘Type B.’

Japanese: 『タイプB』と呼ばれる前は、『金目病』とか、『Berserkr』とか、世界各地で色々な名前をつけられていたようである。
English: Before the name ‘Type B’ was adopted, they had apparently been given various names around the world, including ‘Gold-Eye Disease’ and ‘Berserkr.’

Japanese: 古い人がタイプBのことを『金目』と呼んだりするのはその名残で、現在では差別用語とされて公的な場面では使われなくなったが、日常生活では未だに生きた言葉であった。魚のキンメダイと似たニュアンスになって、やはりちょっと馬鹿にしたような意味になるので一般的には使わない方が無難ではあるが。
English: The continued use of ‘Gold-Eye’ by older people was a remnant of that history. It was now considered discriminatory and had disappeared from official settings, but remained alive in everyday speech. The expression had something of the ring of a fish name and therefore carried a faintly contemptuous nuance. It was generally wiser not to use it.

Japanese: このタイプBは、普段はノーマルとほとんど変わらない。しかし、興奮したり発作を起こしたりしたときには、瞳の色が金色に変化する。これが『金眼』と呼ばれるタイプBを特徴付ける現象で、この目が現れたとき、患者は通常の人間より優れた肉体能力を発揮する。その結果、思わぬ怪力や俊敏性を見せる。それは、特別な訓練をしていないような人間でも、金眼時にはスポーツ選手顔負けの身体能力に達してしまうほど極端なものだ。それは筋肉だけでなく、視力、聴力といった部分にまで適用される。
English: According to the book, a Type B ordinarily differed very little from a Normal. During excitement or an episode, however, the irises turned gold. This phenomenon, called ‘golden eyes,’ was characteristic of Type B. When the eyes appeared, the patient displayed physical abilities superior to those of an ordinary person, resulting in unexpected strength and speed.
