The change was so extreme that even someone without special training could attain physical abilities rivaling a trained athlete’s. It extended beyond the muscles to vision, hearing, and the other senses.

Japanese: これだけならばノーマルよりも優れた人種ということになるが、しかし実際にはデメリットが存在する。
English: Taken alone, that would make Type Bs a race superior to Normals. In practice, the book continued, there were disadvantages.

Japanese: タイプBは一般的にノーマルよりも不安定な精神を持つ。泣いたり怒ったり、感情の変化が激しい。そして、もっとも悩ましいのが『タイプB発作』の存在だ。
English: It characterized Type Bs as generally possessing less stable minds than Normals, with frequent tears, anger, and violent changes of emotion. Most troubling of all was the existence of the ‘Type B episode.’

Japanese: この発作が起こると、タイプBは様々な精神症状に襲われる。それは麻薬や覚醒剤などの禁断症状と似ている。妄想、幻聴、幻視などが代表的である。
English: During an episode, the book said, a Type B suffered a variety of psychiatric symptoms resembling withdrawal from narcotics or stimulants. Delusions and auditory and visual hallucinations were typical.

Japanese: 発作を何度も繰り返すと、症状は次第に悪化してゆく。発作が起きてないときでも幻覚や幻聴に苛まれ、現実を認識する能力が失われる。知能が低下し、人格が荒廃する。意味もなく笑い続けるようになる。……こうなれば最早社会生活は営めない。
English: Repeated episodes gradually worsened the symptoms. Hallucinations and voices came even outside an episode, and the ability to recognize reality was lost. Intelligence declined. The personality deteriorated. A person might laugh endlessly for no reason. ...At that point, life in society was no longer possible.

Japanese: たとえ症状が人格を崩壊させるまで進行していなくとも、ひとたび発作が起きてしまえば、タイプBは妄想と幻覚で予想出来ぬ行動をとり、しかも優れた肉体能力を持つという、場合によっては非常に驚異的な存在となってしまうのだ。この状態で犯罪を起こしてしまうと、そのまま病院に収容され、多くの場合そのまま外に出ることは出来なくなる。現代社会はまだタイプBを受け入れることが出来ない。
English: Even before the symptoms progressed to the destruction of personality, a single episode could make a Type B act unpredictably under delusion and hallucination while possessing extraordinary physical ability. In some circumstances, that could make the person exceptionally dangerous. If she committed a crime in that condition, she would be confined to a hospital and, in many cases, never released. Modern society was not yet capable of accepting Type Bs.

Japanese: 向精神薬によってある程度幻聴や幻覚を抑制することは出来る。しかし、発作によって壊れてしまった人間性を取り戻すことは出来ないし、発作のリスクをゼロにする方法も現在は見付かっていない。どんなに穏やかに暮らしていても、ある日突然とんでもない発作に襲われて、自分でも予期せぬ行動をとって仕舞う可能性が、すべてのタイプBに常につきまとっている。
English: Psychotropic medication could suppress hallucinations and voices to some degree. It could not, the text said, restore the human character damaged by episodes, and no method had yet been found to eliminate the risk of another episode. However peaceful a Type B’s life might be, there always remained the possibility that a terrible episode would strike without warning and make the person act in a way even she had never imagined.

Japanese: つまり、タイプBとして生まれ、ノーマルと変わらない生活を送りたいのならば、ただ発作が起きないよう祈り続けるしかないのだ。
English: Thus, if someone born Type B wished to live no differently from a Normal, there was nothing to do but continue praying that an episode would never occur.

Japanese: こうした事情が、同じミュータントと言えども、タイプAが高い社会的地位を得たり指導者的な立場につくことが少なくないのに比べ、タイプBが差別的な境遇におかれたり、社会からドロップアウトして貧困に陥ったりする現状を作っている。
English: The book connected these circumstances to the difference in social position between the two mutant types. Type As not infrequently acquired high status or leadership, while Type Bs faced discrimination, exclusion from society, and poverty.

Japanese: ――本の冒頭に記述されたこれらの事柄は、美紗は今更言われなくともよく知っている話であり、看護学校の教科書にも記載されていた。
English: —Misa already knew everything described in the book’s opening. It had appeared in her nursing-school textbooks as well.

Japanese: ただ、学生の頃は文字としてしか受け取れなかったものが、今となっては言葉の一つ一つがすべて実体のある具体的なイメージとなる。例えば、幻聴や妄想によって善良なタイプBが犯罪を起こしてしまう例などを読むと、自分の病院にいる患者の何人かを思い浮かべる。そして、彼らの犯した犯罪と、症状の関係について考える。
English: As a student, she had received them only as words. Now every phrase possessed substance and called up a concrete image. When she read, for example, of a decent Type B committing a crime under the influence of hallucinations and delusions, several patients at her hospital came to mind. She found herself considering the relationship between their offenses and their symptoms.

Japanese: 自分は看護師としてその症状のケアがうまく出来ているだろうか？　そして、ケアした先に何があるのだろうか？　退院も出来ず、一生病院で暮らす患者ばかりなのに。十代から病院にいて、老境を迎えてしまったような患者の人生とは一体なんなのか？
English: Was she, as a nurse, caring for those symptoms well? And what lay at the end of that care? The patients could not be discharged and would live their entire lives in the hospital. What could one call the life of a person who entered the hospital as a teenager and reached old age there?

Japanese: その一方毎日幸福そうに楽しく生きている患者も少なくない。病院のなかは、社会とちがってタイプBだからといっていじめられないのが良いと言う。
English: On the other hand, not a few patients lived happily and with apparent enjoyment every day. They said that unlike in society outside, no one at the hospital bullied them for being Type B.

Japanese: それは確かに一理ある。この病院で長期入院をするような患者は、大体そとの世界で酷い目にあって、苦しい人生を過ごしていたものばかりだ。
English: There was certainly truth in that. The patients hospitalized here for the long term had generally suffered terribly in the outside world and lived painful lives.

Japanese: そういう人々と接すると、そもそも、人が幸福に生きて死ぬということは何なのかと考えさせる……。
English: Contact with people like these made Misa wonder what it really meant to live a happy life and die a happy death...

Japanese: でも、Uのようにまだほんの子供のうちから病院に入ってしまって、そしておそらく一生ここで暮らすような生き方は人生と呼べるのだろうか？　なんとか社会に戻してやりたいが、彼女のレベルまでADL（日常生活動作）が低下してしまうと、もうどんな手を尽くしても回復は難しいだろう。それに、たとえADLが改善されたとしても、受け入れる場所がないのかもしれない。彼女は外の世界で症状による大失敗を犯しており、真っ先に受け入れるべき家族達が、誰よりも社会復帰に反対している。
English: But could a way of living like U’s—entering the hospital while still little more than a child and probably remaining here for life—be called a life? Misa wanted somehow to return her to society. Yet with her ADLs, her activities of daily living, reduced to their present level, recovery would probably be difficult by any means. Even if those abilities improved, there might be nowhere prepared to accept her. Her symptoms had led to a disastrous failure in the outside world, and her own family, who ought to have welcomed her first, opposed her return to society more strongly than anyone.

Japanese: それはあまりにも悲惨な人生だ……。
English: It was far too wretched a life...

Japanese: 考えているうちに眠くなり、本題まで読み進める前に、机に突っ伏すように眠りについてしまった。
English: As she thought, sleep overtook her. Before reaching the book’s principal subject, she collapsed across the desk and fell asleep.

Japanese: そして、携帯電話の着信音で目が覚める。相手は、田舎の母親であった。
English: Her cell phone’s ringtone woke her. Her mother was calling from back home.

Japanese: 「美紗ちゃん、元気？」
English: “Misa, are you well?”

Japanese: 「うん、まあ……」
English: “Yes. More or less...”

Japanese: 美紗の声が我知らず暗くなるのは、母との仲が悪かったというわけではなく、むしろ良好な程なのであるが、母がこれから言い出そうとしていることがおおかた想像出来、しかもその話題があまり好ましくないということが想像出来てしまうからであった。
English: Misa’s voice darkened despite herself. This was not because relations with her mother were poor; they were quite good. She could simply anticipate what her mother was about to say and knew that she would dislike the subject.

Japanese: 母は実家から自転車で十分の銀行の事務員として働き、車で五分で到着する地元の役所に勤める公務員を夫にしたという、きわめて狭い世界で人生を送っており、看護師という美紗の仕事に対しても、タイプB、Y地区、という事柄に対しても、特別な知識を持たない。
English: Her mother had spent her life within an extremely small world. She worked as a clerk at a bank ten minutes from her family home by bicycle and had married a civil servant employed at the local government office five minutes away by car. She possessed no special knowledge of Misa’s work as a nurse, of Type Bs, or of Y District.

Japanese: メディアで取り上げられたり、知り合いの誰かが訳知り顔で偏見に満ちた言葉を語れば、そのまま信じてしまうような、あるいみ非常に純真な人物であった。
English: If the media discussed something, or an acquaintance offered a knowing opinion filled with prejudice, she took it at face value. In one sense, she was an exceptionally innocent person.

Japanese: ということはつまり、彼女は全く善良な親切心でもって、美紗の仕事に反対しているのである。今の職場に入職してから三年、常に辞めろ辞めろと言い続けている。
English: In other words, she opposed Misa’s work out of entirely sincere goodwill. During the three years since Misa started at her present job, her mother had never stopped telling her to leave.

Japanese: 「なんだか声が暗いわ。大丈夫？　身体の具合が悪いとか、仕事でいやなことがあるんじゃないの？」
English: “Your voice sounds so dark. Are you all right? Are you ill, or did something unpleasant happen at work?”

Japanese: 「そんなことないよ。仕事は毎日楽しいし、やりがいがあるもの」
English: “Nothing of the kind. I enjoy my work every day, and it gives me a sense of purpose.”

Japanese: 「本当？　お母さんにはとても信じられないわ……」
English: “Truly? I find that very difficult to believe...”

Japanese: 「お母さんにはわからないかもしれないけど、本当に楽しいのよ。患者さんと接していると、今まで考えなかったようなことも沢山考えるし、それに接する同僚からも色んな価値観を学べるわ。確かに特殊なところだとは思うけど、それがいろいろ考えさせてくれるの」
English: “You may not understand, Mother, but I truly enjoy it. Speaking with the patients makes me consider all kinds of things I had never thought about before, and I learn different ways of seeing the world from the colleagues who care for them. I agree it is an unusual place, but that is precisely why it gives me so much to think about.”

Japanese: 「そんなの、きっと他でも学べるわよ。そんなに良いところだって力説するのもなんだか不自然。毎日、ちょっと変になった患者さんと喋ってばかりで、それがうつってしまってるってこともあるんじゃない？」
English: “Surely you could learn those things somewhere else. The way you insist so forcefully that it is a wonderful place sounds unnatural. Could speaking every day with patients who are a little strange have made their strangeness rub off on you?”

Japanese: 「お母さんが、いっつもいっつも否定ばっかりするから、私は良いところを力説することになるんでしょ！」
English: “I have to insist on what is good because you do nothing but reject it, every single time!”

Japanese: つい語気が荒くなってしまう。
English: Her voice grew harsh despite herself.

Japanese: 母親の愛情や不安を想像は出来るが、しかしこちらの言葉を全く理解してくれずに何度も同じ話題を繰り返す母親には、美紗もさすがにストレスを感じている。
English: Misa could understand her mother’s love and anxiety. Even so, she could hardly help feeling stressed when her mother failed to understand a word she said and repeated the same subject again and again.

Japanese: 母親は受話器の向こうで溜息をついてから、
English: Her mother sighed on the other end of the line, then said,

Japanese: 「ごめんね。でも、本当に心配なのよ」
English: “I’m sorry. But I truly am worried.”

Japanese: 「それはわかってるよ。こっちこそ大きな声を出してごめん」
English: “I know. I’m sorry I raised my voice too.”

Japanese: 「もう美紗も大人だし、いちいち口を出すのはいけないって思うんだけど、この間電話を切ってからもずっと考えちゃってね。……ほら、患者さんのなかには、ひどい犯罪をした人もたくさんいるんでしょ？　美紗の職場は、そういう人を預かる場所なんでしょ？　いくら薬が効いて大人しくなってるって言っても、私からすると、とても危ない場所にいるようにしか思えないの」
English: “You are an adult now, Misa, and I know I shouldn’t interfere with everything you do. But I couldn’t stop thinking after our last telephone call. ...Some of the patients have committed terrible crimes, haven’t they? Your workplace is where they keep people like that, isn’t it? However well the medicine may be working, however quiet they may seem, from where I stand, you can only be in a terribly dangerous place.”

Japanese: なかなか理解をしてくれない母に、どうしても自分の気持ちを知って欲しかった。母の言うことはよく分かる。世間の人の多くはそんな偏見を持っているのだろう。その場を見なければ、なかなかわかりづらいことだ。言ってもわかるものではないのかもしれない。
English: Misa could not make her mother understand, and desperately wanted her to know how she felt. She understood her mother’s reasoning. Many people in society probably held the same prejudice. Without seeing the place, it was difficult to understand. Perhaps words could never make anyone understand it.

Japanese: それでも……それでも美紗は、自分がやりがいを持ってこの仕事に打ち込んでいることをこの母に伝えたかったのだ。自然と口調は熱を帯びる。
English: Even so... Even so, Misa wanted to tell her mother that this work gave her purpose and that she devoted herself to it. Her voice naturally grew impassioned.

Japanese: 「ごめんなさい、そんなことを話した私が悪かった。でも、本当にそんな場所じゃないの。私が新人のときにミスばっかりしてる時だって、助けてくれたのは患者さんだし、それに発作以外の部分は、みんな普通の人なのよ？　むしろ、普通の人よりも純粋で正直な人ばかりで……」
English: “I’m sorry. I was wrong to tell you such things. But it truly is not that sort of place. When I was new and did nothing but make mistakes, the patients were the people who helped me. And outside the episodes, every one of them is an ordinary person. If anything, they are purer and more honest than ordinary people...”

Japanese: 「美紗、あなたは仕事にのめりこみすぎよ。言えば言うほど、なにか、おかしな感じがするわ。昔とは違う」
English: “Misa, you are far too absorbed in your work. The more you say, the stranger it sounds. You are different from the girl you were.”

Japanese: 母の予想外に冷静な口調に、美紗は言葉を失う。
English: The unexpected calm of her mother’s voice left Misa without words.

Japanese: 「ねえ、看護師さんを辞めろとは言わないわ。でも、せめてもっと普通の病院に勤めて、普通の人と沢山関わって頂戴。お母さんね、何か美紗が知らない人になってゆくようでこわいの」
English: “Listen, I will not tell you to stop being a nurse. But at least work at a more ordinary hospital and spend time with plenty of ordinary people. Misa, I am frightened. I feel as though you are becoming someone I do not know.”

Japanese: 美紗は咄嗟に返事を口にすることが出来なかった。
English: Misa could not answer at once.

Japanese: 「私はやめないよ」
English: “I’m not quitting.”

Japanese: しばらく経ってから、どうにかそれだけを口にして、
English: After a long pause, she somehow managed to say only that.

Japanese: 「じゃあごめんね。今日は切るね。明日は明け日勤だから、今日はゆっくり休みたいの」
English: “I’m sorry. I’ll hang up for today. I am back on the day shift tomorrow, so I want to rest properly now.”

Japanese: 返事を待たずに一方的に通話を切った。
English: Without waiting for a reply, she simply hung up.

Japanese: そしてよろよろと椅子を経つと、ベッドの上に突っ伏す。
English: She rose unsteadily from the chair and collapsed facedown across the bed.

Japanese: この病院で、それまでは想像もしなかったような人たちとの出会いがあり、確かに変わった。自分ではそれを人間的な成長だと考えている。素晴らしいものを見つけたし、これまで考えられなかったことも考えられるようになった。有り体に言って、視野が広がったのだ。
English: At the hospital, she had met people she could never before have imagined, and she had certainly changed. She herself considered the change growth as a person. She had discovered something wonderful and learned to think about things that had never entered her mind before. Put plainly, her view of the world had broadened.

Japanese: しかし、母にはこの成長を、おかしくなったとしか受け止められないらしい。
English: Her mother, however, appeared able to interpret that growth only as Misa becoming strange.

Japanese: 毎日の努力のなかから手に入れたこの宝物を、もっとも自分を愛してくれているはずの母親が理解出来ないというのはどういうことだろう？
English: What did it mean that the mother who was supposed to love her more than anyone could not understand this treasure she had won through all her effort, day after day?

Japanese: それを思うと、声を出して泣きたいような、それとは逆にシンと醒めて心が鉄の塊になってしまったような、矛盾する二つの感情が一片に胸におしよせた。
English: At the thought, two contradictory emotions surged through her at once: the urge to sob aloud and, at the opposite extreme, a sudden cold clarity in which her heart became a lump of iron.

Japanese: その日美紗が出勤して看護室の隣にある休憩室に足を踏み入れると、すでに先輩ナースたちが出勤しており、長椅子に座って談笑をしていた。
English: When Misa arrived for work that day and entered the break room beside the nurses’ station, several senior nurses were already there, sitting on the couch and chatting.

Japanese: 「能見さん、もう聞いた？」
English: “Ms. Nomi, have you heard?”

Japanese: そのうちの、古川ナースが緑茶の入ったピンクのマグカップを片手に声をかけ来る。
English: Nurse Furukawa, holding a pink mug of green tea, called to her from among them.

Japanese: 「何をですか？」
English: “Heard what?”

Japanese: 「昨日、フクちゃんがステっちゃったんだって」
English: “Fuku died yesterday.”

Japanese: 「えっ？」
English: “What?”

Japanese: 「消灯後に転倒して頭打っちゃってね、洗面所の周りが血みどろだったらしいわよ」
English: “She fell after lights-out and struck her head. I hear there was blood all over the washroom.”

Japanese: 「そうなんですか。あんなに足腰しっかりしてたのに。なんで急に」
English: “Really? But she was so steady on her feet. Why would she suddenly fall?”

Japanese: 「眠剤を変えた影響かしらねえ。まあでも、あんた良かったわねえ。夜勤が一日ずれてたら、大変だったわよお。ねえ、箕田さん」
English: “Maybe it was the effect of changing her sleeping pills. Still, you were lucky, weren’t you? If your night shift had been one day later, you’d have been in for a terrible time. Isn’t that right, Ms. Minoda?”

Japanese: 古川ナースは、ちょうど休憩室に入ってきた箕田ナースを呼び止める。
English: Nurse Furukawa stopped Nurse Minoda, who had just entered the break room.

Japanese: 「そうなのよ。最近の夜勤帯はいつも平和だったから、余計忙しく感じちゃった。あ、お茶入れてくれてたの？　ありがとう。今日は仮眠もとれなかったから、眠くって眠くって」
English: “That’s right. Our night shifts have been peaceful lately, so it felt even busier than it was. Oh, did you make tea for me? Thank you. I couldn’t even take a nap today, so I’m just exhausted.”

Japanese: 箕田ナースは犬のキャラクターが描かれた可愛らしい自分のマグカップを手に取り、緑茶を一口すすると、
English: Nurse Minoda picked up her own charming mug, decorated with a cartoon dog, and took a sip of green tea before continuing.

Japanese: 「私も忍野さんもエンゼルケアやるの久しぶりで、いろいろ忘れちゃってたから、二階に電話してやり方聞きながらやったりね。まあとにかく大変だったけど、家族とすぐに連絡がついたから良かったわ。朝一で遺体を引き取りに来てくれたのよ。矢沢さんのときなんか、家族がごちゃごちゃしてて、結局二ヶ月も預かってたでしょ？　能見ちゃん、あの時の遺体見た？」
English: “It had been ages since either Ms. Oshino or I had done postmortem care, and we’d forgotten all sorts of things. We ended up calling the second floor and doing it while they talked us through the procedure. Anyway, it was a lot of work, but fortunately we reached the family right away. They came to collect the body first thing this morning. Remember Ms. Yazawa? Her family situation was such a mess that we ended up keeping her for two months. Misa, did you see the body that time?”

Japanese: 「いや、私は見てなかったですね」
English: “No, I never saw it.”

Japanese: 美紗は設置された電気ポットから自分のマグカップにお湯を注ぎ、インスタントコーヒーを作りながらそう答えた。
English: Misa answered as she poured hot water from the electric kettle into her mug and made instant coffee.

Japanese: 「私は見たよ。あれはかわいそうだったねえ。あ、そのおせんべい頂戴」
English: “I did. Poor thing. Oh, give me one of those rice crackers.”

Japanese: 古川ナースは、吉田主任が開封した醤油せんべいの袋に手を伸ばし、ポリポリと音を立てて咀嚼する。
English: Nurse Furukawa reached into the packet of soy-sauce rice crackers Chief Yoshida had opened and crunched noisily on one.

Japanese: 「まあでも、エンゼルケアくらいちゃんと覚えておいてもらわないと困るわ。おかげで、私は朝から二階の主任に小言言われちゃったのよ」
English: “Still, you need to remember how to perform postmortem care properly. Thanks to you, I had the chief from the second floor lecturing me first thing this morning.”

Japanese: 吉田主任は苦い顔をする。
English: Chief Yoshida grimaced.

Japanese: 「能見ちゃんも、ちゃんとやり方を確認しておきなさい。この階ではやる機会は少ないけど、いつ必要になるかわからないんだから」
English: “Misa, make sure you review the procedure as well. We don’t have many occasions to use it on this floor, but you never know when we’ll need it.”

Japanese: 「そうですね。わたしもあんまり当たってないから、いざという時自信がないです」
English: “You’re right. I haven’t had much experience with it either, so I’m not confident I could manage when the time came.”

Japanese: 美紗は言って、コーヒーを啜る。
English: Misa took a sip of coffee.

Japanese: Fの死はあまりにも唐突だった。しかし、この病棟では患者の死というものはいつも突然訪れる。
English: F’s death had been terribly sudden. But on this ward, a patient’s death always came suddenly.

Japanese: 内臓に腫瘍が出来たとか、癌が見つかったとか、そういった身体的な問題が発生して手厚い内科的看護が必要になった患者はC棟に移動してしまう。ここで暮らす患者は『タイプB症状が進んでいる』という以外は比較的健康である。
English: Patients who developed a physical problem—a tumor in an internal organ, for instance, or a cancer diagnosis—and consequently required intensive medical nursing were transferred to Ward C. The patients living here were comparatively healthy, apart from the fact that their Type B symptoms had progressed.

Japanese: だから、この病棟で死ぬケースと言えば、誤嚥で食べ物を喉に詰まらせるとか、Fのように転んで頭を打つとか、大量飲水をして水中毒になるというような前触れを発見しにくい事故ばかりだ。少なくとも、美紗が入職してから死んだ患者達はみなそうだった。何の前触れもなく突然死んだ。
English: As a result, the deaths that did occur on this ward were all accidents whose warning signs were difficult to detect: a patient aspirating and choking on food, falling and striking her head as F had done, or developing water intoxication after drinking an enormous quantity of water. At least, every patient who had died since Misa joined the staff had done so in that way. They had died suddenly, without warning.

Japanese: だから、それが突然であるということには美紗も慣れている。死そのものにも、激しく感情がゆさぶられたりもしない。
English: Misa was therefore accustomed to the suddenness. Death itself no longer shook her deeply.

Japanese: ただ、その死について思うところはある。
English: Even so, F’s death gave her something to think about.

Japanese: Fはいつもうるさい患者だった。昨日もUに突き飛ばされ、あんなに悪態をついていた。
English: F had always been a noisy patient. Only yesterday, U had pushed her down and she had been hurling abuse with such vigor.

Japanese: あの威勢のよかった人物が、今はもうこの世におらず、そしてその遺体さえも病院には存在しないと思うと不思議な気分だった。さらに、あんなに病院を出たがっていたFが、死体になった途端こんなに簡単に出て行けるというのも、何やら皮肉なものだと思った。
English: It felt strange to think that the person who had been so full of spirit no longer existed in the world, and that even her body was already gone from the hospital. Stranger still, and somehow ironic, was the fact that F—who had wanted so badly to leave—had been able to do so with such ease the moment she became a corpse.

Japanese: 美紗は看護師達の雑談を上の空で聞きながら、コーヒーを啜り続けた。
English: Misa continued sipping her coffee, only half listening to the nurses’ conversation.

Japanese: そうしているうちに時間になり、いつも通りの業務がはじまる。
English: Before long, it was time, and the day’s work began as usual.

Japanese: 満床だったのが、Fの死によりベッドが一つ空いた。しかし、その日の昼前には二階の患者が上がってきて、すぐに満床へと戻る。二階職員の言葉を聞き、サマリーを読む限り、新しく上がってきた患者はおとなしくてFよりも手がかからない人物のようだったので、職員達はみな安堵した。
English: F’s death had opened one bed on the full ward. Before noon that day, however, a patient was brought up from the second floor, and the ward immediately returned to capacity. From what the second-floor staff said and what the summary contained, the new arrival seemed quiet and likely to require less care than F, to the relief of the entire staff.

Japanese: 患者達は動揺しない。深夜に起きた事故とはいえ何人かの患者は目撃をしており、その死は認識されているはずだが、不穏になって大騒ぎをする患者はいなかった。ここの患者のほとんどは他人に無関心で、残りのうち何割かは死という概念そのものを理解出来ず、さらに残りの何割かは死に慣れて不感症になっている。いくらか悲しみはしても取り乱すようなものはいても、それだけだ。
English: The patients were not disturbed. Although the accident had occurred late at night, several of them had witnessed it and must have understood that F had died, yet none grew agitated or caused an uproar. Most patients here were indifferent to other people. Of those who remained, some could not understand the concept of death at all, while others had grown numb through familiarity with it. Some did grieve, and a few even lost their composure, but it went no further than that.

Japanese: 患者達は午前は作業療法で歌を歌い、午後は二日に一度のおやつである焼きプリンを食べて喜んでいた。
English: That morning, the patients sang during occupational therapy. That afternoon, they delighted in the baked custard served as their every-other-day snack.

Japanese: 美紗は明け日勤の眠い目をこすりながら業務をこなし、夕方に、昨日保護室にいれたばかりのUを解放する指示が出たので、水村ナースと二人で保護室に入ってその少女を連れ出した。
English: Misa rubbed the sleep from her eyes as she went about her duties on her first day shift after coming off nights. Toward evening, an order came to release U, the girl they had put in a protective room only the day before. Misa and Nurse Mizumura entered the room together and brought her out.

Japanese: Uは本来は黒く澄んだ瞳を持っているのだが、まだ金眼が治りきっていない。問いかけても反応が薄く、笑っている。
English: U’s eyes were normally a clear, deep black, but the gold had not yet entirely faded. She scarcely responded when spoken to and merely smiled.

Japanese: 「本当に出しても大丈夫なんですかねえ」
English: “Are you sure it’s safe to let her out?”

Japanese: 水村ナースは首をひねる。
English: Nurse Mizumura tilted her head doubtfully.

Japanese: 「まあ、先生の指示ですから」
English: “Well, those are the doctor’s orders.”

Japanese: 美紗はそう答えたが、彼女も半信半疑ではある。以前も保護室から出した後のお茶の時間に、他の患者のマグカップを片っ端からひっくり返すという事件があった。状態が安定していない状態でのUは、そういうことをする。
English: Misa answered, though she too had her doubts. Once before, after U had been released from a protective room, she had gone from mug to mug at tea time and overturned every one. U did such things when she was not yet stable.

Japanese: 金眼のまま不安定になると、強い薬を与えられて普段はふらふらしているような患者でも素早く動き、職員の静止が間に合わないケースがある。それが、他の病気とは違うタイプB患者のやっかいなところだった。
English: While unstable and golden-eyed, even patients who ordinarily staggered under heavy medication could move with such speed that the staff had no time to stop them. That was one of the ways Type B patients differed from patients with other illnesses—and one of the things that made them so difficult to manage.

Japanese: 実際二人の不安は的中したかのように見えた。
English: In fact, it soon appeared that the two nurses’ fears had been justified.

Japanese: ショートカンファの時間に、患者のKが看護室の小窓を叩く。
English: During the short conference, patient K tapped on the little window in the nurses’ station.

Japanese: 「どうしたの？」
English: “What is it?”

Japanese: 近くにいた水村ナースが尋ねると。
English: Nurse Mizumura, who was standing nearby, asked.

Japanese: 「看護師さん早くきて！　ヒロちゃんがまたやったの！」
English: “Nurse, hurry! Hiro did it again!”

Japanese: 「Kさん、わかったからそのキンキン声で叫ぶのやめて」
English: “K, I heard you. Stop shrieking in that piercing voice.”

Japanese: 水村ナースは苦い顔をして窓を閉めると、美紗を振り返る。
English: Nurse Mizumura closed the window with a sour look, then turned to Misa.

Japanese: 「らしいですよ」
English: “Sounds like it happened again.”

Japanese: 「行きます」
English: “I’ll go.”

Japanese: 美紗は立ち上がって看護室を出る。
English: Misa stood and left the nurses’ station.

Japanese: すると、すぐに廊下に全裸で座り込んでいるUの姿が目に入った。二人の女性助手が彼女を立たせようとするが、その手を振り払っていやいやをしている。
English: Immediately, she saw U sitting naked in the corridor. Two female assistants tried to lift her to her feet, but she batted their hands away and shook her head in refusal.

Japanese: 「どうしたんですか？」
English: “What happened?”

Japanese: 「尿失禁しちゃって。しかも、動こうとしないんです」
English: “She wet herself. And she refuses to move.”

Japanese: Uはヘラヘラと笑いながら、脱いだ自分の服の上に座っている。そして確かに、その服は湿っていた。
English: U sat on top of the clothes she had removed, grinning vacantly. The clothes were unmistakably wet.

Japanese: 随分大量の尿を失禁したようで、ピンクのトレーナーでは吸いきれず、廊下に尿が流れ出そうとする。助手の一人がそれを介護ペーパーで拭い、広がらないようにする。
English: She seemed to have passed an enormous quantity of urine, too much for the pink sweatshirt to absorb, and it threatened to spread across the corridor. One of the assistants wiped it up with an absorbent care sheet to keep it from spreading.

Japanese: 「立って」
English: “Stand up.”

Japanese: 美紗の促しは耳に入らないようで、中空をみつめて笑い、時折なにか呟いている。
English: U seemed not to hear Misa’s prompt. She stared into empty space and smiled, occasionally murmuring something.

Japanese: 「ほら、女の子なんだからこんな格好でおしっこしてたら恥ずかしいでしょ？　しっかりしないとダメよ」
English: “Come on. You’re a girl—you should be ashamed to sit here naked after wetting yourself. Pull yourself together.”

Japanese: 助手の一人が半透明のPVCグローブをつけた手でその肘の辺りを掴み、立たせようとしても、やはり動かない。
English: One assistant, her hand covered by a translucent PVC glove, gripped U around the elbow and tried to make her stand. Still she would not move.

Japanese: 「ダメなんですよぅ」
English: “I caaan’t.”

Japanese: Uは顔をしかめて、そう呟く。
English: U muttered the words with a grimace.

Japanese: 結局力ずくで立ち上がらせ、廊下の後始末は助手達に任せると美紗は自らシャワー室でUの体を洗った。洗っているさなかにもUは放尿をし、流れる水が黄色く濁った。
English: In the end, they forced her to her feet. Leaving the assistants to clean the corridor, Misa washed U herself in the shower room. U urinated again as Misa bathed her, clouding the running water yellow.

Japanese: しかし、問題はこれだけで、このあとすぐにUは金眼を脱していつもの状態に戻った。といっても、Uのいつもの状態というのは、年の近い患者のSにまとわりついて繰り返しグレートホールについて繰り返し同じ質問をしたり、部屋でノートに意味の分からない文言の日記を書き付けたりといった、正常な人間からすれば十分異常なものだが。こうした失禁も、彼女にとっては日常的な光景である。
English: That, however, was the end of the trouble. Soon afterward, the gold left U’s eyes and she returned to her usual condition. To a normal person, admittedly, U’s ‘usual condition’ was strange enough: she clung to S, a patient close to her own age, and asked her the same questions about the Great Hole over and over, or filled a notebook in her room with diary entries that made no sense. Incontinence like this was an ordinary occurrence for her as well.

Japanese: とにかく、夕食を取る様子も危なげがなく、夜に保護室に戻す必要もないと思われるほどであった。
English: In any event, she ate dinner without incident and seemed unlikely to require a return to the protective room that night.

Japanese: 「あぶなっかしかったけど、ちゃんと元に戻りましたね」
English: “She looked unstable for a while, but she really did get back to her usual self.”

Japanese: 一緒にUを保護室に戻した水村ナースが溜息をつく。
English: Nurse Mizumura, who had helped Misa bring U out of the protective room, sighed.

Japanese: 「保護室に入ると長引いちゃう子なのに、今回は早かったと思いません？　無理矢理外に出して刺激を与えたのがよかったんでしょうか。安田先生もたまには的確な指示を出すんですね」
English: “She usually takes so long to recover once she goes into seclusion. Don’t you think this was unusually fast? Maybe forcing her out of the room and giving her some stimulation did her good. I suppose Dr. Yasuda can give the right order every once in a while.”

Japanese: 「いえ、解放したのは主治医じゃなくて太刀川先生なのよ」
English: “Actually, it wasn’t her attending physician who released her. It was Dr. Tachikawa.”

Japanese: 美紗が伝えると、
English: At that,

Japanese: 「ああ、そうなんですか」
English: “Oh, I see.”

Japanese: 水村ナースは納得したように頷き、
English: Nurse Mizumura nodded as if everything now made sense.

Japanese: 「さすが名医ですね」
English: “That’s what you’d expect from a brilliant doctor.”

Japanese: と複雑な顔で言った。
English: Her expression remained complicated.

Japanese: 医者というものは個性がある。この病院の医者も、それぞれ個性、というか癖がある。他にいくらでも科があるだろうにわざわざタイプB専門医となるのだからよほど変わりものに決まっている、というのが看護師達の共通した認識だ。
English: Every doctor had a personality of their own. The doctors at this hospital certainly had theirs—or, rather, their own peculiarities. With so many other specialties available, anyone who deliberately became a Type B specialist had to be considerably eccentric. At least, that was the consensus among the nurses.

Japanese: 例えばUの主治医である安田医師は薬物療法よりも精神療法を重要視するタイプで、薬を最低限度しか処方しない、というよりも最低限度さえ処方しないときがある。
English: Dr. Yasuda, U’s attending physician, for instance, placed greater importance on psychotherapy than medication. He prescribed only the bare minimum of drugs—or, at times, less than the bare minimum.

Japanese: 「私はねえ、タイプBといえども、まずよく話を聞いてあげることが彼らの心にとって一番大切なんですよ。傾聴対応しながら観察をお願いします」
English: “You see, even with Type Bs, the most important thing for their mental well-being is that we begin by listening carefully to what they have to say. Please observe them while providing attentive listening.”

Japanese: この「傾聴対応しながら観察」というのが一種のキャッチフレーズで、患者が何か問題を起こして報告すると、大体この言葉を口にするだけで、よほどでなければ頓服薬などを出してくれない。
English: ‘Observe them while providing attentive listening’ was something of a catchphrase. Whenever the staff reported that a patient had caused a problem, he generally offered those words and nothing more. Unless matters were exceptionally serious, he would not even prescribe a PRN medication.

Japanese: が、いくら傾聴対応、つまりその話に耳を傾けたってタイプBはそう簡単に落ち着かない。この人手不足のなかで、看護師がまるまる一人とられてしまうのは現場にとっても苦しいし、妄想まみれで会話が成立しない相手に長時間対応するのは消耗が激しい。
English: But no amount of attentive listening—of lending an ear to what they said—would calm a Type B so easily. With the ward already understaffed, losing an entire nurse to a single patient put tremendous pressure on everyone else. Spending hours with someone so deep in delusion that no conversation could take place was also profoundly exhausting.

Japanese: それを言うと、
English: Whenever the staff raised those points, he answered,

Japanese: 「それは職員の都合でしょう？　患者さんのためじゃなくて、職員の手間の都合で薬なんか出せません。あなたたちが言っているのは、看護じゃなくて管理の話です」
English: “That is a matter of convenience for the staff, is it not? I cannot prescribe drugs for your convenience rather than the patient’s welfare. What you are discussing is control, not nursing.”

Japanese: よく言えば人道主義なのかもしれない。正論とも言えるのかもしれない。先生の言うこともわからないでもないよ？　しかし、現場からすればとてもたまったものじゃない。そりゃ一人一人にきめ細かい看護をしたいのはやまやまだが、人手不足の状態で事故を起こしてはいけないと思えばどうしても管理的になる時もある。
English: You might charitably call it humanism. You might even call his argument correct. The staff did not entirely fail to understand his position. But for those on the ward, it was intolerable. Of course they wanted nothing more than to give every patient attentive, individualized care. Yet when they had to prevent accidents while chronically understaffed, there were inevitably times when care became a matter of control.

Japanese: 理想を実現させたいならとりあえず人を増やせ。そもそも安田先生は電話で言うだけで滅多に実際の患者を見に来ないじゃないか。全くあの「ケイチョウシナガラカンサツ」は！　人に言うならまず自分が病棟に来て、四時間でも五時間でも傾聴して、現場がどういうものだか知った方が良い。眠らずに三日間でも平気で喋り続けるような患者だっているんだ！
English: If he wanted his ideal put into practice, he could start by hiring more staff. Besides, Dr. Yasuda only delivered these pronouncements over the telephone. He hardly ever came to see the patients himself. That damned “observe while listening” of his! If he was going to preach it to everyone else, he ought to come to the ward, listen for four or five hours himself, and learn what the work was actually like. Some patients could talk without sleeping for three days straight.

Japanese: というのが、看護室でよく聞かれる愚痴だ。
English: Such complaints were commonly heard in the nurses’ station.

Japanese: その正反対で、富川という年配の医師は何でもかんでも看護師の言う通りに処方してしまう。
English: At the opposite extreme was an older doctor named Tomikawa, who prescribed absolutely anything the nurses suggested.

Japanese: 「あのー、この人最近ちょっと眠れないんですけど……」
English: “Um, this patient has been having a little trouble sleeping lately...”

Japanese: 「あ、じゃあこの薬一錠増やしておくよ」
English: “Oh, then I’ll add another tablet of this.”

Japanese: 「こっちの患者さんは、最近便通が悪くて」
English: “And this patient has been constipated recently.”

Japanese: 「じゃあ夜の下剤を少し盛っておくね」
English: “Then I’ll increase her laxative a little tonight.”

Japanese: 職員だけでなく、患者からの訴えに対しても、ろくに話も聞かずにホイホイと薬を盛ってしまうので、看護師の方が心配になるときもある。
English: He did this not only in response to staff, but to patients as well, freely piling on medication without hearing the full complaint. At times, even the nurses grew concerned.

Japanese: 「私はみなさんを信頼しているから」
English: “I trust all of you.”

Japanese: 富川医師は笑顔でいつも言うのだが、単に面倒なのだろうというのが看護師たちの見解だ。
English: Dr. Tomikawa always said it with a smile. The nurses’ view was that he simply could not be bothered.

Japanese: それでもこの二人の医師は嫌われているわけではない。陰口を叩かれながらも愛されてはいるし、それなりの尊敬もされているだろう。大体医師である時点で看護師による愚痴や陰口の対象となってしまうことは絶対に避けられないのだ。
English: Even so, neither of those two doctors was disliked. For all the gossip behind their backs, the staff were fond of them and probably respected them in their own ways. Any doctor, by the very fact of being a doctor, would inevitably become a target of nurses’ complaints and gossip.

Japanese: ただ、たった一人だけ、きらわれている医師がいる。法条医師がそれである。
English: There was only one doctor they truly disliked: Dr. Hojo.

Japanese: 優れた論文を多数学会に発表し、世間での評価はすこぶる高い。業界のレジェンドとも言われている高名な医師の愛弟子で、格という意味ではこの病院の医師のなかで最上位だろう。それが、看護スタッフに評判が悪いというのは理由がある。
English: He had presented numerous highly regarded papers at medical conferences and enjoyed an exceptionally high reputation in the outside world. He was the favored pupil of a famous physician described as a legend in the field, and in prestige he probably ranked above every other doctor at the hospital. Nevertheless, he was deeply unpopular with the nursing staff—and not without reason.

Japanese: 病棟にはよくやって来る。というのは、看護スタッフを全く信用せず、自分の目で患者を観察しなければ気が済まないからで、看護師を介在させずに密室のなかで患者を診察し、それが終わると一方的に指示だけを下して帰ってゆく。それだけでも評判が悪いが、患者のためを思ってのことならまだ擁護するものもいるだろう。
English: He visited the ward frequently. That was because he had no trust whatsoever in the nursing staff and would not be satisfied until he had observed his patients with his own eyes. He examined them alone behind a closed door, without a nurse present, then emerged, issued his instructions unilaterally, and left. That alone did little for his popularity, but some might still have defended him if they believed he acted for the patients’ sake.

Japanese: しかし、実際法条医師のやっているのは、患者の症状を抑えて日々の苦痛を取り去ったり、生活のレベルを上げてやる、というようなものではないのだ。もちろん本人がそう宣言しているわけではないが、効果があるのかないのかわからない新療法を行い、患者が苦しんでも一般的な方法はほとんど使わずに続行し、そのすぐ後に新療法についての論文を発表するところを見れば、そうとしか解釈が出来ない。
English: In practice, however, Dr. Hojo’s work did not appear directed toward suppressing his patients’ symptoms, relieving their daily suffering, or improving their quality of life. He certainly made no such declaration himself. But the staff could find no other interpretation when he continued new therapies of uncertain benefit despite the patients’ suffering, almost never resorted to standard methods, and promptly published papers on those therapies afterward.

Japanese: つまり、彼は患者を実験台にしているというのが、看護師たちの理解であった。
English: In other words, the nurses understood him to be using his patients as test subjects.

Japanese: 法条医師の患者は例外なく問題児で、しかも症状は著しく悪化してゆく。間近でその苦しみを見て、後始末をさせられ、しかも厳密な指示によって他の患者にしているような当たり前の救済策を取ることが禁じられている看護師たちの苦痛というものは大変なものだ。
English: Every one of Dr. Hojo’s patients became a problem on the ward, and their symptoms grew markedly worse. The nurses watched that suffering at close range, cleaned up the consequences, and were forbidden by his strict instructions from offering the ordinary forms of relief available to other patients. Their own distress was considerable.

Japanese: 「あんなことをやりたいのなら、ここじゃなくて大学病院にでも行けば良いのに！」
English: “If he wants to do things like that, he should go to a university hospital instead of doing them here!”

Japanese: などという、大学病院への偏見と、医師への憤りの療法があわさった言葉が看護室ではよく聞かれる。
English: Words blending indignation at the doctor with prejudice against university hospitals were frequently heard in the nurses’ station.

Japanese: このように、多種多様な医師がいるなかで、さらに一風変わっているのが太刀川という医師であった。
English: Among this motley collection of doctors, one who was stranger still was Dr. Tachikawa.

Japanese: 名だたる大学を出たというわけでもなく、むしろこの病院のメンバーのなかでは劣った学歴であるらしいが、おそらく臨床医師としての能力は最も高い。処方も指示も的確で、はじめはどうかと思われるような常識外れの指示でも、投薬でも、実際行ってみるとぴたりと当たる。
English: He had not graduated from any celebrated university. In fact, his academic pedigree was apparently among the least distinguished at the hospital. Yet he was probably its finest clinician. His prescriptions and instructions were precise, and even an order or medication that at first seemed to defy common sense proved exactly right once put into practice.

Japanese: たまに失敗する時もあるが、けして評判を落とすような安易なものではない。名医と言ってまず間違いがない。主治医を差し置いて他の医者の患者の治療について指示を出すのは本来歓迎されないが、彼は頻繁にそれをやり、能力によってそれが許されている。
English: He did fail occasionally, but never through the kind of careless mistake that would diminish his reputation. He could safely be called a brilliant doctor. Ordinarily, a physician was not welcome to overrule the attending doctor and issue instructions for someone else’s patient. Tachikawa did so frequently, and his ability won him that license.

Japanese: が、とにかく変わっている。
English: But he was undeniably strange.

Japanese: まず風貌が変わっている。
English: His appearance was the first strange thing about him.

Japanese: まだそこまでの年齢ではないはずだが、前頭部から頭頂部にかけての髪がすっかり抜け落ちて、癖の強く黒々としたひじきのような髪が、その周囲に生え、肩のすぐ上あたりまで伸びていた。
English: He should not yet have been old enough for it, but all the hair from his forehead to the crown had fallen out. Around the bare expanse, thick black curls like tangles of hijiki seaweed grew down almost to his shoulders.

Japanese: そして身につけたものも特徴的だ。この病院の医師は、みな比較的自由な服を着ているのだけれど、それはあくまでも白衣の下に着る服の話で、太刀川のように四六時中サングラスをかけているものは他にいない。しかもそのサングラスはレンズが丸く、何の光も通さないほど黒いもので、これをこの太刀川がかけるといかにも異様だ。彼はタイプAで、このサングラスは目の辺りにあらわれた特質変異を隠すためだという説もあるが推測の域を出ない。誰もサングラスをとった素顔を見たことがないからである。
English: His accessories were equally distinctive. The doctors at this hospital all dressed relatively freely, but only in the choice of clothes they wore under their white coats. No one but Tachikawa wore sunglasses at every hour of the day. Their lenses were round and black enough to admit no light, and on Tachikawa they looked particularly bizarre. One theory held that he was Type A and wore them to conceal a mutation expressed around his eyes, but it remained pure speculation. No one had ever seen his face without them.

Japanese: そして彼は長身だった。いつもカツカツと杖をつきながら病棟へやって来るが、足が悪いらしく、一歩足を進めるたびに肩が妙な揺れかたをする。
English: He was also tall. He always arrived on the ward tapping a cane against the floor. Something appeared to be wrong with his leg, and his shoulders swayed oddly with each step.

Japanese: 白衣を肩に引っかけていなければどう見ても不審人物で、初めてこの医師の姿を見た者は誰でもぎょっとするに違いない。
English: Without the white coat draped over his shoulders, he would have looked like nothing but a suspicious character. Anyone seeing the doctor for the first time was sure to be startled.

Japanese: 変わっているのは外見だけではない。
English: His appearance was not the only strange thing about him.

Japanese: 人柄も変わっている。口調こそ丁寧で、患者のみならず看護師や助手、清掃員にまで敬語を使うが、愛想というものがない。いつも簡潔に用件だけを伝え、余計なことは全く言わない。挨拶さえもしない。無駄を省略するという一種の合理性なのだ。
English: His personality was strange as well. His speech was invariably polite—he used honorific language not only with patients, but even with nurses, assistants, and cleaners—yet he possessed no affability at all. He always conveyed only the immediate business, briefly, and said nothing extraneous. He did not even offer greetings. It was a kind of efficiency that eliminated anything unnecessary.

Japanese: 自分の担当外の患者を無断で診るのだって、普通の医者ならやりはしないが、自分の方がより適切な診断を下せるのだから診るという、ただそれだけの理由であろう。他の医者に対する面当てだとか、自分の能力を示すだとかいった様子はなく、ただただ患者第一主義で淡々としている。日中は医局にこもることなくあちこちの病棟を歩き回って多くの患者を診ている。当直をするときは、どんな時間に電話をかけても乱れのない身だしなみで病棟へやって来る。
English: An ordinary doctor would never examine another physician’s patient without permission. Tachikawa apparently did it for the simple reason that he believed he could make the more accurate diagnosis. There was no sign that he intended to spite the other doctors or advertise his own skill. He simply put the patient first, without fuss. By day, rather than seclude himself in the doctors’ office, he made the rounds of wards throughout the hospital and saw a great many patients. When he was on call, a telephone summons at any hour brought him to the ward impeccably dressed.

Japanese: 他の医者たちには相当嫌われているようだが、全く意に介することもない。彼自身も他の医者が嫌いなのかもしれない。いや医者だけではない。
English: The other doctors appeared to dislike him intensely, but he paid it no attention whatsoever. Perhaps he disliked them in return. Or perhaps his aversion was not limited to doctors.

Japanese: 職員に対しては、けして真正面から見ようとせず、会話をするときでもいつもそっぽを向いている。一説には視線を合わせるのを極度に嫌っているという話だ。そのくせ、患者に対してはいつだって真っ正面から見据えるのだから、職員より患者の方がよほど好きなのだろう。
English: He never faced members of staff directly; even in conversation, he always turned aside. According to one theory, he had an extreme aversion to meeting another person’s eyes. Yet he always looked his patients squarely in the face, so perhaps he simply preferred them to the staff.

Japanese: この太刀川を、業務を終えてロッカールームへ向かうところだった美紗はB棟の前で見かけた。
English: Misa encountered Tachikawa outside Ward B while she was on her way to the locker room at the end of her shift.

Japanese: 「お疲れ様です」
English: “Good work today.”

Japanese: 美紗は頭を下げたが、例によって太刀川は視線をやるそぶりも見せず、自分方向を向いた顔をチラとも動かさない。そして、挨拶を返すということもない。
English: Misa bowed. As usual, Tachikawa gave no sign of looking her way. Although his face was already turned in her direction, he did not move it so much as an inch. Nor did he return her greeting.

Japanese: 朝から病院にいた太刀川はもう勤務時間も終わって帰っても良さそうな時刻だが、まだ仕事をするつもりらしく、今美紗が出て来たB棟へ入ろうとしているようだった。
English: Tachikawa had been at the hospital since morning, and it was late enough for his working day to have ended. Nevertheless, he apparently intended to continue. He seemed about to enter the Ward B building from which Misa had just emerged.

Japanese: 「あの、Uさんのことですが」
English: “Um, about U...”

Japanese: 挨拶をしない太刀川だが、患者の名前を出すとぴたりと足を止める。が、美紗の方を見ようとはしない。
English: Tachikawa offered no greetings, but at the name of a patient his feet stopped at once. He still made no attempt to look at Misa.

Japanese: 「なんですか？」
English: “What about her?”

Japanese: そう問い返されると、呼び止めた美紗の方がどぎまぎしてしまう。風に吹かれて、側頭部から生えた太刀川のウェーブのかかった黒髪が揺れている。
English: The question left Misa—the one who had stopped him—flustered instead. The wind stirred the waves of black hair growing from the sides of Tachikawa’s head.

Japanese: 美紗はこの奇妙だが勤勉な医者に興味があった。
English: Misa was interested in this strange but diligent doctor.

Japanese: 「廊下で放尿などがありましたが、その後は落ち着かれて静穏経過で過ごされています」
English: “There was an episode of urination in the corridor, but she settled down afterward and has remained stable without incident.”

Japanese: 「そうですか」
English: “I see.”

Japanese: 太刀川は青白い顔に比べて紅すぎる唇を開いてそう答えた。
English: Tachikawa parted lips that looked remarkably red against his pallid face and gave his answer.

Japanese: 「あ、あの」
English: “Um—doctor...”

Japanese: 立ち去ってしまおうとする太刀川を、もう一度呼び止めた。
English: He began to leave, and Misa stopped him a second time.

Japanese: 「私、Uさんのプライマリーなんです。いつもUさんのことを観察しているのですが、その時の状態などがなかなかわかりません。太刀川先生は、どうやって一目で患者様の状態を的確に判断なさっているのでしょうか？　何か観察するポイントなどがあるのでしょうか？」
English: “I’m U’s primary nurse. I observe her all the time, but I still have great difficulty understanding her condition at any given moment. How are you able to assess a patient’s condition accurately at a glance, Dr. Tachikawa? Is there something in particular you look for?”

Japanese: 太刀川の洞察力に日頃から不思議なものを感じていたため、勢いでそう言ってしまったものの、言ってしまってからまっすぐ向かい合ってこのような質問をすることの不躾さに美紗は気付き、恥ずかしげに目をそらす。
English: She had long found his powers of observation mysterious, and the words had escaped her in a rush. Only after speaking did Misa realize how impertinent it was to ask him such a question straight to his face, and she averted her eyes in embarrassment.

Japanese: 「……あの、看護の参考にしたいんです」
English: “...I mean, I’d like to use it to improve my nursing.”

Japanese: 「それはですね」
English: “That is because...”

Japanese: 太刀川は美紗のとってつけたような言い訳を意に介さない。
English: Tachikawa paid no attention to Misa’s transparent afterthought.

Japanese: 「私だからわかるんです。あなたには同じことは出来ませんし、他のドクターにも不可能でしょう。あなたたちはあなたたちのやり方を見つけることです」
English: “I can tell because I am me. You cannot do the same, and neither can any other doctor. You must find your own way.”

Japanese: 「それは、先生がタイプAで、特別な能力があるからということですか？」
English: “Do you mean because you’re Type A and possess a special ability?”

Japanese: （つい、うっかり聞いちゃった！　みんな疑いながらも面と向かって聞けないことなのに、私はどうしてこんなに失礼なんだろう！）
English: (I went and asked him! Everyone wonders, but no one can bring themselves to ask him to his face. Why do I have to be so rude?)

Japanese: 美紗は自分でも予期しなかった言葉に動揺してしまったが、太刀川は態度に変化を見せない。
English: Misa was shaken by the words that had escaped her without warning. Tachikawa showed no change in manner.

Japanese: 「その通りです。私はタイプAです。しかし、その力については何も言えません。プライバシーに関することですのでね」
English: “That is correct. I am Type A. But I cannot tell you anything about my ability. It is a matter of privacy.”

Japanese: 看護師達の長年の疑問に、あまりにもあっさりと回答をした太刀川に、美紗は驚きを隠せない。おそらく秘密というわけでもなく、今まで誰も直接尋ねなかったから知られていなかっただけで、もし誰かが聞いていたら同じように説明していたのだろう。
English: Misa could not conceal her surprise at how readily Tachikawa had answered the nurses’ long-standing question. It was probably no secret. No one had known simply because no one had asked him directly before, and he would presumably have given the same explanation to anyone who had.

Japanese: 単に、美紗が最初の一人だったのだ。
English: Misa merely happened to be the first.

Japanese: が、美紗とすればさらに動揺を深めてしまう。
English: For her part, however, she only grew more flustered.
“Um... doctor...”

Japanese: 動揺のせいか、彼女は聞かなくて良いことまで聞いてしまった。
English: In her agitation, she asked something she had no need to ask at all.

Japanese: 「先生は、どうして職員と目を合わせようとしないのですか？」
English: “Why do you refuse to make eye contact with the staff?”

Japanese: こんな不躾な質問に対しても、太刀川はよどみなく言葉を返す。
English: Even to such an impertinent question, Tachikawa answered without hesitation.

Japanese: 「目を見れば、見たくないものまで見えてしまいますから」
English: “Because if I look into their eyes, I see things I do not wish to see.”

Japanese: 「そ、そうなんですか……」
English: “I-I see...”

Japanese: さすがに言い過ぎたと自覚した美紗は、その場に絶句してしまう。
English: Aware at last that she had said too much, Misa stood speechless.

Japanese: その様子を見て、これ以上の質問はないと悟ったのか、太刀川は無言でその場を去って行った。
English: Perhaps Tachikawa inferred from her silence that there would be no more questions. Without a word, he walked away.

Japanese: 「やっぱり、休日前の夜は最高ですね」
English: “There’s nothing better than the night before a day off.”

Japanese: 一杯目をあっという間にあけ、二杯目に手を付けた水村ナースはけろりとした顔でそう言った。
English: Nurse Mizumura had emptied her first drink almost at once and begun upon her second. She spoke with a perfectly composed expression.

Japanese: 大人しそうな見かけによらず大変な酒豪で、いくら飲んでも少し赤くなるくらいでほとんど行動が乱れない。
English: Contrary to her demure appearance, she was a formidable drinker. However much alcohol she consumed, she did little more than redden slightly and almost never lost control of herself.

Japanese: 年が近い美紗は彼女としょっちゅう飲みに出るが、最初は負けん気もあってその飲酒のペースについていこうとしていたが、今は完全に敗北を認めて彼女は彼女に任せ、自分はつき合わずにマイペースで飲んでいる。
English: Misa, who was close to her in age, frequently went drinking with her. At first, pride had driven her to keep pace, but she had now admitted total defeat. She let Mizumura drink as she pleased while she drank at her own pace.

Japanese: 二人はY地区の一角にある飲食店に来ていた。
English: The two had come to a restaurant in one corner of Y District.

Japanese: Y地区は世間ではとやかく言われるが、そこで働く利点の一つに、こうした仕事帰りなどに足を運ぶ飲食店に困らないという点がある。滑走路通りを含めた中心街は、そう広くない範囲に様々な国籍料理が密集して営業をしており、路上販売のワゴンなども含めれば、その日のどんな気分にも対応出来るだけのバラエティがある。
English: Whatever the rest of society might say about Y District, one advantage of working there was the inexhaustible supply of places to visit for food and drink after a shift. The central streets, including Runway Street, packed restaurants serving cuisines of every nationality into a relatively small area. With the street vendors’ carts included, there was enough variety to answer any appetite on any day.

Japanese: 今日彼女たちが訪れたのは、英国式のバーで、平日の夜にもかかわらず若者たちで賑わっていた。
English: Tonight they had chosen a British-style pub, bustling with young people despite the weekday hour.

Japanese: テーブルの上には、フィッシュアンドチップスと茹でたソーセージが乗せられ、二人はそれをつまみながらグラスのビールを飲んでいる。そして彼女たちが口にするのは、もっぱら職場の愚痴であった。
English: Fish and chips and boiled sausages lay on the table. The two nurses picked at them as they drank glasses of beer, and spoke almost exclusively of their grievances at work.

Japanese: 「私、今日またR野さんにしつこくつきまとわれちゃってえ」
English: “R—no kept following me around again today.”

Japanese: 水村ナースは油のついた指先を拭いながら言う。
English: Nurse Mizumura spoke as she wiped the grease from her fingertips.

Japanese: Ｒ野というのは、症状以前に人間性に問題を抱える患者で、その乱暴な言動でしばしば病棟の職員を困らせている人物であった。そして、水村ナースの担当患者でもある。
English: R—no was a patient with problems of character quite apart from her symptoms. Her violent words and behavior frequently troubled the ward staff. She was also one of the patients assigned to Nurse Mizumura.

Japanese: 「まーた、多訴的になってるんで、普段は適当に傾聴対応してるんですけど、今日は時間がなかったから、さっさと打ち切っちゃったんですよ。そしたら『お前らアタシを無理矢理閉じ込めやがって！　この病院は最低の場所だ！』がはじまっちゃって」
English: “She’s back to complaining about absolutely everything. Usually I just make a show of listening, but I had no time today, so I cut her off quickly. That set her off: ‘You people locked me up against my will! This hospital is the worst place on earth!’”

Japanese: 「ああ、いつもの」
English: “Oh, the usual.”

Japanese: 美紗が相づちをうつと、水村ナースが頷き、
English: Misa murmured her recognition, and Nurse Mizumura nodded.

Japanese: 「そう、いつものです。だからもう、私ムカっとしちゃって、言っちゃったんですよ。この病院よりあなたを大事に扱ってくれる場所はないって。あなたが退院出来るのなら、職員全員涙を流して大喜びするから、頑張って症状を克服してくださいねって」
English: “Exactly. The usual. I was so irritated that I finally told her there was nowhere in the world that would treat her better than this hospital. I said that if she could manage to be discharged, every member of staff would shed tears of joy, so she ought to work very hard at overcoming her symptoms.”

Japanese: 「それは、ムカっとしたわりには結構抑えたね」
English: “You were fairly restrained, considering how angry you were.”

Japanese: 「そうです！　全くその通りです！　出せるものなら出したいですよ！　でも、サマリーを書いて送っただけで門前払いでしょうね。まったく、どうしようもないやつだ！　あちこちの施設でブラックリストに入れられて、行き場がなくて、しょうがなくこの病院で引き取ったっていうのに、ここの他に行ける場所なんかあると思ってるのかしら……。出来るものなら、門を開いてどうぞご自由にって言いたいですよ。……固いものを食べればすぐ詰まらせて、おむつも自分で取り替えられないですぐ汚して、ふらふらしててすぐ転ぶからヘッドガードも外せないのに、なんで外で暮らしていけると思ってるのかしら？　家族全員にも嫌われてるし、外に出たら三日ももたないで死んじゃうでしょうね」
English: “Exactly! I was! Believe me, if I could put her out, I would. But the moment we wrote a summary and sent it anywhere, they’d turn her away at the door. She’s hopeless! Facility after facility put her on a blacklist, and when there was nowhere left for her to go, this hospital had no choice but to take her. Does she honestly imagine there’s somewhere else she can go? If it were possible, I’d love to open the gates and tell her she was free to leave. ...Anything solid immediately gets lodged in her throat, she can’t change her own diaper and soils it constantly, she staggers and falls so often we can’t even remove her protective helmet—and she thinks she can live outside? Her whole family hates her. Out there, she’d be dead in three days.”

Japanese: 水村ナースはジョッキのビールを飲み干すと、ドンとテーブルの上に置く。
English: Nurse Mizumura drained her mug of beer and brought it down heavily on the table.

Japanese: その顔には今風の化粧がなされている。仕事中はほとんどノーメイクだったのに、いつの間にほどこしたのだろう？　それに気がつくと美紗は、眉毛と目しか手を加えていない仕事時のままの自分の顔が恥ずかしくなった。
English: Her face bore stylish, contemporary makeup. At work she had worn almost none. When had she found the time to apply it? The moment Misa noticed, she grew ashamed of her own face, still exactly as it had been at work, with only the brows and eyes made up.

Japanese: 「でたらめなサマリー書いて遠くの病院に転院させちゃうとか、任意入院に切り換えて本人の言う通り退院させるとか、出来ないんですか？　あの人の生活がよくなるように一生懸命やってるのに、なんで顔を馬鹿にされたり、ちょっと考えられないような理不尽な悪意を持たれたりしなくちゃいけないのか……。受容的態度って言うけれど、なんでもかんでも受容しなくちゃいけないんですか？　我々は？」
English: “Couldn’t we write some nonsense in her summary and transfer her to a distant hospital? Or change her to voluntary admission and discharge her exactly as she demands? We work our hardest to make her life better, and in return she mocks my face and directs this incomprehensible, utterly unreasonable malice at me. They tell us to maintain an accepting attitude, but do we have to accept absolutely everything? Do we?”

Japanese: 「Ｒ野さんはあなたのことが好きで、構ってほしいからあれこれ言ってるだけよ」
English: “R—no likes you. She says all those things because she wants your attention.”

Japanese: 「そういう人格障害があるとはわかってるんですけど……」
English: “I know that’s part of her personality disorder, but...”

Japanese: 水村ナースは溜息をつく。
English: Nurse Mizumura sighed.

Japanese: 「あの人に限らず、患者さんの言う通りに全部やってみたらどうかしらって思うんですよ。出たいって人は出してあげて、食事制限に怒ってる糖尿病の人には好きなだけたべさせて……。あと、ここの患者さんはよくグレートホールに帰りたいっていう人が多いけど、一回穴までつれて行ってみたいと思ってるんです。本当にドンドン飛び込んじゃうのかしら？」
English: “Not just with her. Sometimes I think we should do exactly what every patient says. Let the people who want to leave walk out; let the diabetic patients who resent their dietary restrictions eat all they want... And so many patients here say they want to return to the Great Hole. I’d like to take them to the Pit once and see. Would they truly jump in one after another?”

Japanese: 「さあどうだろう。でも、なんだかみんな死んじゃいそうね。そうなったら、私たちの仕事が楽になりすぎちゃう」
English: “Who knows? Somehow, I think they might all die. Then our jobs would become much too easy.”

Japanese: 大分酒のまわりはじめた美紗が笑いながらそう答えると、
English: Misa, by now considerably affected by the alcohol, laughed as she answered.

Japanese: 「患者さんがいなくなったら、楽になるどころか失業しちゃいますよ」
English: “If the patients disappeared, our jobs wouldn’t get easier. We’d be unemployed.”

Japanese: 水村ナースは苦笑した。
English: Nurse Mizumura gave a wry smile.

Japanese: 「でも能見さん、いつまでここで働くつもりなんですか？」
English: “But Ms. Nomi, how long do you plan to keep working there?”

Japanese: 病院の職員が見ているわけでもないが、水村ナースは声をひそめて言う。
English: Although no one from the hospital was watching, Nurse Mizumura lowered her voice.

Japanese: 「特にやめることは考えていないけど、水ちゃんは何か考えてるの？」
English: “I haven’t particularly thought about leaving. Have you, Mizu?”

Japanese: 「どうしよっかなあって思ってて。私、タイプB相手の仕事向いてないような気がするんです」
English: “I’ve been wondering what to do. Sometimes I feel like I’m not suited to working with Type Bs.”

Japanese: 「そうかなあ？　そんなことないと思うけど。それに、ここより条件の良い職場なんかそうそうないわよ」
English: “Really? I don’t think that’s true. Besides, you won’t find many workplaces with better conditions.”

Japanese: 「そこ！　それが問題なんですよねえ」
English: “Exactly! That’s the problem.”

Japanese: 水村ナースは腕組みをすると、
English: Nurse Mizumura folded her arms.

Japanese: 「でも、ここにいると、普通の医療処置はたまにしかしないじゃないですか。いればいるほど、腕がなまって、看護師として潰しが効かなくなりそうな気がして……」
English: “Working here, we only perform ordinary medical procedures once in a while. The longer I stay, the rustier I’ll get. I’m afraid I’ll become useless anywhere else as a nurse...”

Japanese: 「それならC棟に行けば？　あそこなら一般科みたいな仕事も多いでしょ」
English: “Then why not transfer to Ward C? They do much more work like a general hospital there.”

Japanese: 「いやです！　いやです！　あんなとこ。あそこの業務、メチャクチャ大変じゃないですか。朝とか挨拶すると、職員みんな死にそうな顔してますよ。それに、能見さんは入職のとき見学させて貰いました？　あそこの上の方の階って、保護室みたいな個室が一杯あるんですよ。その一つ一つに患者さんが拘束されてて、ずーっと喚いてガチャガチャやってるんです。拘束帯も、見たことがないようなぶっとい奴なんですよ」
English: “No! Never! Not a place like that. The work is unbelievably hard. When I greet the staff in the morning, every one of them looks half dead. And did they let you tour it when you started, Ms. Nomi? The upper floors are full of private rooms like our protective rooms. There’s a patient restrained in every one of them, screaming and clanking away without end. Even the restraint belts are thicker than anything you’ve ever seen.”

Japanese: 水村ナースは目を丸くして、人差し指と親指でその太さを示してみせる。
English: Nurse Mizumura widened her eyes and used her thumb and forefinger to demonstrate their thickness.

Japanese: 「そこに入院してるのは薬が全然効かないような患者さんばっかりなんですって。力もすごくて、普通のやつだと引きちぎっちゃうから、そんなに太くて、しかも中に金属が入ってるんだそうです。暴れたら、みんなで押さえつけたり棒で殴ったりするんですって……。あんなところではとても仕事なんか出来ません」
English: “I hear every patient admitted there is someone medication has no effect on at all. Their strength is tremendous, too. They would tear an ordinary restraint apart, so the belts have to be that thick, with metal inside. And when someone starts thrashing, the staff all pin them down or beat them with rods... I could never work in a place like that.”

Japanese: 彼女は溜息をつく。
English: She sighed.

Japanese: 「それに知ってます？　C棟の最上階では、特に傾向値が高い患者さんを集めて、人体実験してるんだそうですよ？」
English: “And did you know? On the top floor of Ward C, they supposedly gather the patients with especially high tendency values and conduct experiments on them.”

Japanese: 「それは、ただの噂でしょう……」
English: “That’s only a rumor...”

Japanese: 「いやー、やっててもおかしくないですよ。だって、この病院はタイプBのなかでも極めつけの重症者ばっかりいるんですから。どこの国だってタイプBの研究は盛んでしょ？　きっと法条先生がここにいるのも、そこで実験して新しい論文を書くためなんだわ」
English: “Oh, it wouldn’t surprise me if it were true. This hospital has the most severe cases of all the Type Bs anywhere. Every country is actively researching them, isn’t it? I bet Dr. Hojo only stays here so he can perform experiments up there and write new papers.”

Japanese: 「それはさすがに人聞きが悪い……」
English: “That’s a terrible thing to suggest...”

Japanese: 美紗は苦笑する。
English: Misa gave a wry smile.

Japanese: 「C棟と言えば、知ってます？　最近幽霊がよく出るんですって！　黒い服を着た、女の人の幽霊が！　どこの病院でも、こういう噂ってすぐ出来るんですね。まったく笑っちゃいます」
English: “Speaking of Ward C, have you heard? A ghost has been appearing there lately—a woman’s ghost in black. Rumors like this spring up instantly at every hospital, don’t they? It’s ridiculous.”

Japanese: 「よっぽどストレスがたまってるのねえ」
English: “They must be under incredible stress.”

Japanese: 「そうなんですよ。そもそも、私、タイプBの人ってあんまり好きに慣れません。古い人はかわいいかわいいって言うけど、いつまで経ってもちっともそうは思えなくて……。能見さんはどうですか？」
English: “Exactly. To begin with, I can’t bring myself to like Type Bs very much. The nurses who have been here forever call them adorable, but however long I work, I never feel that way. What about you, Ms. Nomi?”

Japanese: 「わ、私はちょっと、かわいいかなって思う時もあるけど……ほらみんな、子供みたいで素直じゃない。病棟に行くと、能見さん能見さーんって、笑顔で寄って来るし……」
English: “I-I do think they’re rather sweet sometimes... You know, they’re all so straightforward, almost like children. The moment I enter the ward, they come running up with smiles, calling, ‘Ms. Nomi! Ms. Nomi!’”

Japanese: 「あー、能見さんも主任コースだ。きっと、患者さんに肩入れしすぎて一生この病院から出られなくなるんだわ」
English: “Oh, you’re already on the chief’s path. You’ll grow too attached to the patients and spend your entire life unable to escape this hospital.”

Japanese: 水村ナースは、さっきより深いため息をつく。
English: Nurse Mizumura sighed more deeply than before.

Japanese: 「入る前に、私友達に言われたんですよ。こういう病棟の患者さんは何十年も入院することになるから、必要以上に情がわいたら出られなくなるって。能見さん、危ないですよ？」
English: “Before I started, a friend warned me that patients on wards like this are hospitalized for decades. She said that if you get too attached, you can never leave. You’re in danger, Ms. Nomi.”

Japanese: 「あははは、わ、私はそんなことないよ？　きっと……」
English: “Ahahaha. Th-that won’t happen to me. I’m sure...”

Japanese: 「どうかしらねえ」
English: “Are you?”

Japanese: 水村ナースはくっくっと意地悪く笑う。こう見えても、多少は酔いがまわっているのだろう。
English: Nurse Mizumura chuckled wickedly. Despite appearances, perhaps the alcohol was reaching even her.

Japanese: 「でも、確かに辞めたくなる気持もわかるよ。普通の病院と違って、ここは元気になって退院してゆく人がいないし、なんだかやるせない感じもするもの。でも、発症してしまった人って、もうどうやっても回復することはないのかしら？」
English: “Still, I understand why you might want to leave. This isn’t an ordinary hospital. No one here gets well and goes home, and there’s something deeply dispiriting about that. But once someone’s symptoms manifest, is there truly no way for the person ever to recover?”

Japanese: 「能見さん、知らないんですか？」
English: “You don’t know, Ms. Nomi?”

Japanese: 「何を？」
English: “Know what?”

Japanese: 「一時的になら、回復させる方法はあるんですよ」
English: “There is a way to restore them temporarily.”

Japanese: 「ああ、もしかして、『ローズ』のこと？」
English: “Oh, do you mean Rose?”

Japanese: 「そう、それです」
English: “Exactly.”

Japanese: 「それなら、学校で習ったことあるけど、実際どれくらい回復するのかしら？　たとえばうちのヒロミちゃんみたいな子でも、発症する前に戻るの？」
English: “We learned about that at school. But how complete is the recovery in reality? Could even someone like our Hiromi return to the way she was before her symptoms appeared?”

Japanese: 「そうなるって話です。低下していた知能も元通りになるって話です。私も実際に見たことはないですけど」
English: “That’s what people say. They say even lost intelligence returns to its original level. I’ve never seen it myself, though.”

Japanese: 「とても信じられない。ある程度回復はしたとしても、そんなことが起こりうるなんて……」
English: “I can hardly believe it. Some degree of improvement, perhaps, but for that to be possible...”

Japanese: 美紗は首を横に振った。
English: Misa shook her head.

Japanese: 『ローズ』というのは、麻薬の名前である。強烈な快楽体験をもたらすその薬は、正体不明の誰かによって家庭用製薬機向けのレシピがネットに公開されることで、犯罪組織などが手軽に量産出来るようになり、世界中で大流行した。
English: Rose was the name of a narcotic. It produced an intensely pleasurable experience. After an unknown person published a recipe for home pharmaceutical synthesizers on the internet, criminal organizations and others were able to mass-produce it with ease, and its use surged throughout the world.

Japanese: これをタイプBに一定量以上投与すると、症状によって廃人同様になったような者でも発症前の人間性を取り戻すという意外な効果があるという。
English: It was said to have one unexpected effect: above a certain dose, it could restore a Type B’s former personality even after their symptoms had left them almost entirely incapacitated.

Japanese: タイプBの発症によって苦しむものたちにとっては夢のような話だが、そんなに簡単なものでもない。
English: For those suffering after the onset of Type B symptoms, the promise sounded miraculous. The reality, however, was not so simple.

Japanese: 『ローズ』は非常に強力な依存性を持っている。耐性もつきやすく、濫用すればすぐに使用量が増大して中毒死してしまう。死なずとも廃人になる。
English: Rose was powerfully addictive. Tolerance developed quickly, and abuse soon drove the necessary dose upward until the user died of an overdose. Those who survived could be left permanently incapacitated.

Japanese: 他の麻薬と比べても極めてデメリットが大きすぎるのだ。
English: Even compared with other narcotics, its drawbacks were overwhelming.

Japanese: その危険性が世間に知れ渡った現在では、頭のイカれたジャンキーでもこの薬を買い求めようとはしないほどなのである。
English: Now that the danger was widely known, even the most far-gone junkie would not seek it out.

Japanese: いくら快楽が強烈で、入手が容易でも、人をあまりにも簡単に廃人に変えてしまうようでは誰にも受け入れらない。家庭で簡単に作れることから、犯罪組織も商材として売り出すこともないし、現在ではたまに怖い物知らずのティーンエイジャーが製造、濫用して問題になるくらいで、世の中にはほとんど出回っていない。
English: No matter how intense the pleasure or how easy the drug was to obtain, no one could embrace something that destroyed a person so readily. Because anyone could produce it at home, criminal organizations no longer bothered to sell it. These days, a few reckless teenagers manufacturing and abusing it might occasionally cause an incident, but otherwise it had almost vanished from circulation.

Japanese: 医療現場でこの薬が使われることもない。モルヒネなどは、麻薬として有名だが、医療機関でも厳重に管理された上で限定的に使用されているのだけれど、ローズを認可している国はおそらく存在しないだろう。
English: Nor was the drug used in medicine. Morphine and similar substances were notorious as narcotics, but medical institutions administered them in limited circumstances under strict control. There was probably no country in the world that had approved Rose.

Japanese: こういう曰く付きのドラッグだが、これでタイプBを回復させるためには、娯楽に使うより大量に投与しなくてはならないのだ。これが何を意味するのかと言うと、たとえ薬効によって一時的に正気を取り戻したとしても、そのすぐ先に重い薬物依存が待っているということだ。
English: Despite the drug’s sinister history, restoring a Type B with Rose required a much larger dose than using it recreationally. Thus, even if the drug temporarily restored a patient’s sanity, severe dependence awaited immediately afterward.

Japanese: このような薬を、軽々しく使うことは出来ない。
English: A drug like this could not be administered lightly.

Japanese: 公的な機関で患者に投与したというデータも存在しないことになっている。だから、『ローズ』がタイプBに効くというのは、街の噂を前提とした、一種都市伝説のようなものだ。街の麻薬中毒者を調べてこの現象を調査した医療関係者の報告でも、報告する者によって結論が異なっている。
English: Officially, no public institution had ever administered it to patients, and no data existed. The claim that Rose affected Type Bs was therefore a kind of urban legend built upon rumors from the streets. Medical workers who investigated the phenomenon among drug users in the city had issued reports, but their conclusions differed.

Japanese: こうした事情を踏まえた上で、美紗は、『ローズ』を投与することである程度回復はしたとしても、完全に発症前の状態を取り戻すというようなことはないだろうと考えていた。タイプBについて医者が書いた本を何冊か読んだが、そこでも、発作を繰り返すごとにタイプBの脳は器質的に不可逆的な変化が起きているというような考え方が主流だったはずだ。つまり、発作を繰り返すごとに少しずつ壊れてゆくというのだ。
English: Given those circumstances, Misa believed that Rose might produce some recovery, but was unlikely to restore a patient completely to the condition before the symptoms appeared. She had read several doctors’ books on Type Bs. As she recalled, the prevailing view was that repeated episodes caused organic, irreversible changes in the Type B brain. In other words, each episode destroyed a little more of it.

Japanese: それが、麻薬などで回復するなんてあり得るのだろうか？
English: Could a narcotic truly reverse that destruction?

Japanese: 「でも、本当にそんなことが起こりうるなら、一回くらい患者さんみんながまともになったところを見てみたいですよね。私たちはおかしくなった彼らしか知らないじゃないですか？　だから、正常な頃があったということがうまく想像出来ない」
English: “But if such a thing is truly possible, I would like to see all our patients restored just once. We’ve only ever known them after they changed, haven’t we? I can’t really imagine that they were once normal.”

Japanese: 水村ナースは溜息をつき、
English: Nurse Mizumura sighed.

Japanese: 「それは確かに。私も患者さんのご家族と会った時とか考えるわ。患者さんのご家族はみんな少なからず正常な頃の思い出を持ってるから、どうしてもおかしいところしか知らない私たちとでは、患者さんの見え方も違うんだろうなって」
English: “That’s true. I think about it when I meet a patient’s family. Every family has at least some memories from when the person was normal. They must inevitably see the patient differently from those of us who have only known what is wrong with them.”

Japanese: 美紗もまた溜息をつく。
English: Misa sighed as well.

Japanese: 「もし私だったら、ローズを打って欲しいですね。耐性がついても、致死量をこえるまで打ち続けます。どんどん人間性を失いながら長く生きるよりは、たとえ薬物中毒ですぐに死ぬことになっても、正気のままでいたいです。能見さんもそう思いますよね？」
English: “If it were me, I’d want them to give me Rose. Even as I built a tolerance, I’d keep injecting it until the dose passed the lethal limit. I’d rather remain sane, even if addiction killed me almost immediately, than live for years while losing more and more of my humanity. You feel the same, don’t you, Ms. Nomi?”

Japanese: 「私は、なんとも言えないなあ。患者さんみてると、みんなニコニコしてて、それほど不幸そうにも見えないし……」
English: “I don’t know what to say. When I look at the patients, they’re all smiling, and they don’t seem particularly unhappy...”

Japanese: 「それは、ただの空笑で笑ってたり、認知能力が低下して悲劇が理解出来なくなったりしてるだけですよ」
English: “They’re only smiling emptily, or their cognitive ability has declined so far that they can’t understand the tragedy.”

Japanese: 「そうかなあ」
English: “Do you think so?”

Japanese: 美紗は首をひねる。彼女にはどうも、そうは思えないのだ。
English: Misa tilted her head. Somehow, she could not agree.

Japanese: 発症したばかりで症状が安定しない急性期のタイプBはみな苦しみそのものといった顔つきをしているが、発作を繰り返し慢性化し、ある程度まで人格が崩壊すると、幻覚や幻聴の氾濫した世界に生きながらも、ある種幸福な境地に達しているように感じる。
English: Type Bs in the acute phase, their symptoms newly manifested and unstable, all wore faces that seemed to embody suffering itself. But after repeated episodes made the condition chronic and the person’s character disintegrated beyond a certain point, Misa felt that some patients reached a kind of happiness, even while inhabiting a world flooded with hallucinations and voices.

Japanese: しかしそれを口にしたら、水村ナースにからかわれそうなので、口には出さなかった。
English: She did not say so aloud. Nurse Mizumura would only tease her.

Japanese: 「あー、もう、次の出勤したくないなあ。私、またリーダーなんですよねえ。指示受けしたくないなあ……」
English: “Ugh, I don’t want to go in for my next shift. I’m the leader again. I don’t want to take all the doctors’ orders...”

Japanese: 彼女は考え込む美紗をよそに、ブツブツと愚痴を続けている。
English: Oblivious to Misa’s thoughts, she continued muttering complaints.

Japanese: そう遅くならないうちに二人は店を出た。水村ナースはY地区外の実家から通っている。駅前で彼女と別れ、しかしまだ遊び足りなかった美紗は、またなんとなく滑走路通りに戻ってしまう。
English: The two left the pub before the night grew too late. Nurse Mizumura commuted from her family home outside Y District. Misa parted from her at the station, but was not yet ready to end the evening and drifted back toward Runway Street.

Japanese: ネオンの氾濫する街で服やアクセサリーを物色し、その間に少し酔いが醒め、そしてもう少し飲み直そうと考えた。そこで、普段とは少し違う場所の店を選んでみようと、一人歩きなのに思ってしまったあたり、酔いが正常な判断力を奪っていたのだと思われる。
English: She browsed clothes and accessories amid the flood of neon. By then she had sobered slightly and decided to have another drink. The fact that she chose, despite being alone, to try a bar somewhere a little different from her usual haunts suggested that the alcohol had already deprived her of sound judgment.

Japanese: 裏通りに足を踏み入れて、二つばかり角を曲がると、もうそこは滑走路通りとは別の世界だった。
English: She entered a back street and turned only two corners before finding herself in a world entirely different from Runway Street.

Japanese: 街灯もまばらな真っ暗で細い道。通りに出された立て看板は、どれも店名が書いてあるだけでどんな店なのかの説明など一切なく、ドアには窓一つなく中の様子をうかがえない。完全に、『知っている』客だけを相手にした店ばかりが並んでいる。
English: The road was narrow and almost completely dark, with only a scattering of streetlights. Every standing sign displayed a business’s name and nothing more; none explained what sort of establishment lay behind the windowless doors. These businesses existed entirely for customers already in the know.

Japanese: そして、所在なげに路上に立つ露出の多い服を着た女は、娼婦であろう。子供のように若い女も、シワの目立つ年頃の女も、白い肌も、黒い肌もいる。さらにもっと進むと、建物はまるきり普通のアパートだが、門のあたりに椅子を置いて老女が座っているような、建物ばかりが並んでいる地域に出る。
English: The women standing aimlessly in revealing clothes along the road were probably prostitutes. Some were young enough to look like children, others old enough for their wrinkles to show. Some had white skin, some black. Farther on, she entered an area lined with buildings that looked like perfectly ordinary apartment houses, except that an old woman sat on a chair near the gate of each one.

Japanese: 美紗は知らなかったが、これもやはり売春のための施設で、客は老女に話して交渉し、アパートの一室で待機している女とことをなすのだ。
English: Misa did not know it, but these too were places of prostitution. A customer negotiated with the old woman, then conducted his business with a woman waiting in one of the apartments.

Japanese: ここはちょっと違う。
English: This was a little too different.

Japanese: さすがに美紗も気がついて、引き返そうとしたところで声をかけられた。
English: Even Misa realized that much. Just as she turned back, someone called to her.

Japanese: 「あ、あの、お姉さん」
English: “E-excuse me, miss.”

Japanese: 振り返ると、髪の毛を金髪に染めたアジア系の少年が立っていた。街灯の下で笑顔を浮かべている。
English: She turned to find an Asian boy with dyed blond hair standing beneath a streetlight, smiling.

Japanese: 「さっきから見てたんですけど、このあたりをうろうろとして、何かお探しですか？」
English: “I’ve been watching you for a while. You keep wandering around here. Are you looking for something?”

Japanese: 「いえ、別に……」
English: “No, nothing...”

Japanese: 警戒しながら返事をしたその前で、少年の目から何かぽろりと落ちた。
English: As Misa answered warily, something dropped from the boy’s eye.

Japanese: どうやら落ちたものはカラーコンタクトらしい。何かが落ちた方の瞳の色が、先ほどとは変わっている。先ほどまで真っ黒に見えていた瞳が、暗くてわかりにくかったが、何か明るい色になった。
English: It appeared to be a colored contact lens. The eye from which it had fallen was now a different color. In the darkness it was difficult to tell exactly what she saw, but the iris that had appeared black a moment before had turned some brighter shade.

Japanese: （……この人、患者さんだ）
English: (...He’s a patient.)

Japanese: 街で暮らすタイプBは、金眼によってそうと知られないようにカラーコンタクトを装着して生活をするのが一般的だ。そして、相手の少年のもつ雰囲気は、明らかに病棟で毎日接している患者達が金眼状態になったときにもつものと同じだった。どこかふわふわしたような、浮き世離れした感じ。
English: Type Bs living in the city commonly wore colored contacts so that their golden eyes would not reveal what they were. And the atmosphere surrounding this boy unmistakably resembled the one Misa observed every day when a patient on her ward became golden-eyed: vaguely weightless and detached from the ordinary world.

Japanese: 「何かお困りだったら、お手伝いしますよ？　おれはそうしないといけないんです。誰かのお手伝いをするために、今日はずっとここを歩いていたんです」
English: “If you’re having trouble, I’ll help you. I have to. I’ve been walking around here all day so I could help someone.”

Japanese: 先ほど水村ナースに患者は可愛いと言ったが、病院の外で会うタイプBは思いの外に恐ろしかった。
English: Misa had told Nurse Mizumura that patients were sweet. Encountering a Type B outside the hospital was much more frightening than she had expected.

Japanese: 美紗は、タイプBの患者が思いも寄らぬ突発的な行動を起こすことを知っている。病院の患者達は薬でコントロールされている上に、危険物を持てないようになっている。さらに周りには頼りになる専門的なスタッフがいたが、しかし路上ではすべては違う。
English: She knew that Type B patients could act suddenly and without warning. In the hospital, medication kept the patients under control, and they were prevented from carrying anything dangerous. Reliable, trained staff were always close at hand as well. On the street, none of that was true.

Japanese: 目の前の人間がどんな症状を持ち、どんな道具を隠しているかわからない。
English: She had no idea what symptoms the person before her might have or what he might be hiding on him.

Japanese: それを思うと身が凍り付くような恐怖である。
English: The thought froze her with terror.

Japanese: （世間の人たちは、みんなこんな風に感じているんだわ）
English: (This must be how everyone outside the hospital feels.)

Japanese: 病院にいると、タイプBへの風当たりの強さはほとんど偏見によるものだと考えたくなる。実際根拠のない偏見も多いが、しかしこうして体験してみると、そう考えるのも仕方がないのだと実感する。
English: Within the hospital, it was tempting to regard the hostility toward Type Bs as almost entirely prejudice. Much of that prejudice truly had no foundation. But now that Misa experienced this fear herself, she understood why others might feel it.

Japanese: 後ずさりする美紗の肩を少年が掴むと、
English: Misa backed away. The boy caught her by the shoulder.

Japanese: 「きゃあっ！」
English: “Aah!”

Japanese: 自分でも信じられないくらい大きな声が出た。
English: The cry that escaped her was louder than she could believe.

Japanese: 相手が怪訝な顔をしたのを見た美紗は、大きな声を出して無用の刺激をしてしまったのではないかとおそれ、表情をひきつらせる。
English: The boy looked puzzled. Afraid that her shout had needlessly provoked him, Misa’s expression stiffened.

Japanese: そこに、もう一人別な人物が現れた。
English: Then another person appeared.

Japanese: 「何をしているんですか」
English: “What are you doing?”

Japanese: 背後から聞こえたその落ち着いた声には聞き覚えがある。そして振り返ると、やはり思った通りの、そして他の誰かと見間違いようのない人物が立っていた。
English: Misa recognized the calm voice behind her. When she turned, the person she expected stood there, as impossible to mistake for anyone else as ever.

Japanese: 「太刀川先生……」
English: “Dr. Tachikawa...”

Japanese: そう、そこに杖をついて立つ長身の人物は、医師の太刀川であった。
English: The tall figure standing there with a cane was indeed Dr. Tachikawa.

Japanese: 白衣のかわりに真っ黒なジャケットと真っ黒な帽子をかぶっている。そして目には、こんな暗い夜だというのにやはり黒いサングラスをかけている。
English: In place of his white coat, he wore a pitch-black jacket and hat. Black sunglasses still covered his eyes, even on a night this dark.

Japanese: （不便だろうに、一体、どんな特質変異なのかしら……）
English: (They must be terribly inconvenient. What kind of mutation could he possibly have...?)

Japanese: 美紗はふとそんなことを思った。
English: The thought occurred to Misa without warning.

Japanese: 「これは、フジワラ君じゃないですか。あまり調子がよくないみたいですね」
English: “Why, if it isn’t Fujiwara. You don’t seem to be doing very well.”

Japanese: 太刀川は美紗の方をチラとも見ずに、相手のタイプB少年の顔だけを見ながらそう言った。けして職員の顔は見ないのに、患者の顔はこんなにすんなりと見つめる。
English: Tachikawa did not glance at Misa. He spoke while looking only into the face of the Type B boy. He never looked at a member of staff, yet met a patient’s eyes with such ease.

Japanese: 「あ、先生！　こんばんは。今夜は本当に月が綺麗ですね！」
English: “Oh, doctor! Good evening. The moon is really beautiful tonight!”

Japanese: 少年はだらしのない笑顔を浮かべる。
English: The boy wore a slack smile.

Japanese: 美紗はつい空を見上げたが、どんよりと曇った漆黒の空があるだけだった。
English: Misa involuntarily looked up. There was only a black sky, heavy with cloud.

Japanese: 「ちょっと、腕を出してください」
English: “Please give me your arm.”

Japanese: 言うと、少年は素直に右腕を差し出す。
English: At the instruction, the boy obediently held out his right arm.

Japanese: 太刀川は手にした大きな黒い革の鞄をごそごそとあさって、中から注射器を取り出すと、その針を、熟練の手技で少年の静脈に突き刺した。
English: Tachikawa rummaged through the large black leather bag in his hand and removed a syringe. With practiced technique, he inserted the needle into the boy’s vein.

Japanese: 「もう家に帰りなさい。こういうときは外に出てはだめだと言ったでしょう？」
English: “Go home now. I told you that you must not go outside at times like this.”

Japanese: 「はい。すみませんでした」
English: “Yes. I’m sorry.”

Japanese: 少年は本当に驚くほど太刀川に対して素直で、ぺこりと頭を下げるとその場を辞した。
English: The boy’s obedience to Tachikawa was almost astonishing. He bowed and left at once.

Japanese: （一体どういうことなんだろう？）
English: (What in the world just happened?)

Japanese: 美紗が驚いて医師の顔を見つめると、
English: Misa stared at the doctor in amazement.

Japanese: 「彼は私の患者なんです」
English: “He is one of my patients.”

Japanese: 何も問うてはいないのに、その漆黒の衣で身を固めた名医はそっぽを向いたまま返答をする。
English: Although Misa had asked nothing, the brilliant doctor wrapped in garments of pure black supplied the answer without turning toward her.

Japanese: 「暇な時は、このあたりをブラブラしてね、診察なんかをしているんですよ」
English: “When I have spare time, I walk around this area and conduct examinations.”

Japanese: （暇な時なんか、とてもあるとは思えないけど……）
English: (I can’t imagine that he ever has spare time...)

Japanese: 太刀川は誰よりも早く病院に来て、誰よりも多くの患者を診て、誰よりも遅く帰る。暇な時間などあるようには思えない。それとも、独身だと時間を持てあますのだろうか？　そうだとしても、夜の街をうろうろしてタイプBを探し求めて診察するなど、酔狂と呼ぶにも程がある。正気の沙汰とは思えない。
English: Tachikawa arrived at the hospital before anyone else, saw more patients than anyone else, and left later than anyone else. It did not seem possible that he possessed spare time. Did a bachelor simply have that many empty hours to fill? Even if so, roaming the city at night to seek out Type Bs and examine them exceeded eccentricity. It was hardly the behavior of a sane man.

Japanese: （一体どれだけ仕事が、そしてタイプB患者が好きなのかしら。病棟の先輩ナースたちも相当だと思っていたけれど、この人はそれ以上だわ）
English: (How much can one person love work—and Type B patients? I thought the senior nurses on my ward were devoted, but he goes far beyond any of them.)

Japanese: 美紗はほとんど目の前がクラクラとするような思いだった。
English: Misa almost felt dizzy.

Japanese: 「能見さん」
English: “Ms. Nomi.”

Japanese: 「は、はい！」
English: “Y-yes?”

Japanese: 「これから一つ診察する場所があるのですが、見学しませんか？」
English: “I am about to examine someone nearby. Would you care to observe?”

Japanese: 「は、はい！」
English: “Y-yes!”

Japanese: （病院のなかの感覚でつい返事しちゃったけど、コレで良かったのかしら？）
English: (I answered automatically, as if we were in the hospital. Was that really the right thing to say?)

Japanese: 後ろも見ずに行く太刀川の後ろを歩きながら、美紗は未だに動揺を沈めることが出来ないでいた。
English: Tachikawa walked ahead without looking back. Following him, Misa still could not calm herself.

Japanese: （考えてみれば、助けて貰って「ありがとう」の言葉さえまだ言っていないんだよね。……でも、驚くに決まってるよ。急に名前なんか呼ばれちゃったし、こんな風に誘ってくるし……。病院ではそんな態度見たことがないもの）
English: (Come to think of it, I still haven’t even thanked him for helping me. ...Of course I’m surprised. He suddenly called me by name, and now he’s inviting me to come along... I’ve never seen him act this way at the hospital.)

Japanese: 病院ではどの職員に対しても冷淡と言えるほどにそっけなく、名前で誰かを呼んでいるのを聞いたこともない。
English: At the hospital he treated every member of staff with an indifference that approached coldness. Misa had never heard him call anyone by name.

Japanese: （私、もしかしてこの人に気にいられている？）
English: (Could he possibly like me?)

Japanese: そう考えると、ますます美紗の胸には動揺が広がった。
English: The thought only deepened Misa’s agitation.

Japanese: この不思議な医者が、自分に好感を持っているとしたらどうだろう？　それも、スタッフとしてではなく、異性としてだとしたら？
English: What if this mysterious doctor felt affection for her? And what if he liked her not as a member of staff, but as a woman?

Japanese: （ああ、どうしたらいいんだろう！　確かに先生は変な人だし、年も離れているけれど……。でも、独身だし、医者なんだよね）
English: (Oh, what would I do? He is certainly strange, and quite a bit older than I am... But he is single. And he is a doctor.)

Japanese: 収入に関して全く問題がない。医者という肩書きは、田舎の両親を喜ばせるだろう。
English: Money would certainly never be a problem. Her parents back home would be delighted that he was a doctor.

Japanese: （見た目はちょっと好みではないけど、だれもが認める名医だし、それに、仕事熱心なところとか、患者さんに優しいところはすごく尊敬出来るし……）
English: (His looks aren’t quite to my taste, but everyone agrees that he’s a brilliant physician. I can respect how hard he works, and how kind he is to his patients...)

Japanese: 改めて考えてみると意外と悪くない話で、そう気がつくと、より一層自分自身を動揺させる。
English: Upon consideration, the prospect was surprisingly far from terrible. The discovery threw her into still greater confusion.

Japanese: （私ってそんな人だったんだ！）
English: (I never knew I was that kind of woman!)

Japanese: 変な汗をかきながらグルグルと考えていると、前を行く太刀川が唐突に立ち止まり、振り返った。
English: She went round and round in her thoughts, breaking into a strange sweat. Then Tachikawa abruptly stopped and turned.

Japanese: そこで、はじめて美紗はこの医者と正面から向き合うことになる。
English: For the first time, Misa stood directly face-to-face with the doctor.

Japanese: 「ふむ」
English: “Hmm.”

Japanese: 彼は美紗を見て、妙な形に口を歪める。それは、いつも表情のないポーカーフェイスである太刀川にしては珍しい変化であった。
English: He looked at Misa and twisted his mouth into a peculiar shape. For Tachikawa, whose face was ordinarily an expressionless mask, it was a rare change.

Japanese: （私、こんな表情をされるほど変な顔をしていたのかしら！）
English: (Was I making a face strange enough to get that reaction?)

Japanese: 半分パニックになりながら、美紗は、
English: Half panicking, Misa said,

Japanese: 「さ、さっきは、助けてくれてありがとうございました」
English: “Th-thank you for helping me earlier.”

Japanese: と、完全にタイミングが遅れてしまった感謝の言葉を述べ、頭を下げた。
English: She delivered the badly belated thanks and bowed.

Japanese: 太刀川はそんな彼女を無言で見つめる。緊張しながら次の言葉を待つ美紗には、その沈黙はあまりにも長く感じられた。
English: Tachikawa stared at her in silence. To Misa, waiting nervously for whatever he might say next, that silence felt far too long.

Japanese: 太刀川は結局何も言わず、
