Japanese: 普段の父としての表情と、ボスとしての表情のいりまじった複雑な顔でそう言われると、トーマスも頷くしかなかった。
English: The look he gave Thomas held both the familiar father and the head of the family. Thomas could only nod.

Japanese: それを確認すると、廖は即座に立ち上がって自分の秘書を呼ぶよう従者に伝える。
English: Once Liao had confirmed his assent, he stood at once and ordered a servant to summon his secretary.

Japanese: 「よし、方針は決まったぞ！　さっきの少女は、我々の幸運の女神となるだろう！」
English: “Good. Our course is decided! That girl will become our goddess of fortune!”

Japanese: 一同にそう宣言すると、カツカツと靴音を立てて部屋を出て、エリオットが無言のままそれを追った。
English: After making the declaration to everyone present, he strode out of the room, his shoes striking sharply against the floor. Elliott followed in silence.

Japanese: 世界というものはどうしてこれほどにつまらなく、味気ないものだろうと、ずっと思っていた。
English: All my life, I had wondered why the world had to be so dull, so utterly devoid of flavor.

Japanese: 花や月などという自然の美しさも、賢そうな人たちが褒めそやす家よりも高い値がつくアートの価値もわからない。
English: I could see neither the natural beauty of flowers and the moon nor the value of art that clever-looking people heaped with praise and priced above a house.

Japanese: 食べ物は好きなものもあるけど、大体のものはまずくて口に出来ないようなものばっかりで、空腹だから仕方なく食べるけど食事の時間は基本的には苦痛だ。
English: There were foods I liked, but most things tasted so awful I could hardly put them in my mouth. Hunger left me no choice but to eat, yet mealtimes were, as a rule, an ordeal.

Japanese: 学校のテストでも、運動でも、悪い成績でもそんなものか、良い成績でもそんなものか。
English: On school tests or in sports, whether I did badly or well, my reaction was always the same: So that’s how it is.

Japanese: 小遣いを貰えばちょっと心弾むが、かといって大金持ちになって豪邸に住みたいとか、ブランド物の服を買いあさりたいとは思えない。
English: A little pocket money could make my heart leap. That did not mean I wanted to become fabulously wealthy, live in a mansion, or buy armloads of designer clothes.

Japanese: 人類にとって有益な何かを実現したいとも思えない。
English: Nor did I feel any urge to accomplish something useful to humanity.

Japanese: 何か名誉あることをなしとげて、人に賞賛されたり、尊敬されたりしたいとも思わない。そもそも、他人というものはみんな石の裏の湿った土に集まる虫のようにワサワサしていて、うごめいていて気持ち悪い。他人にはまるきり敬意がもてなくて、そういった争いで負けたらわりと悔しいのに、勝ってもさほど嬉しくない。
English: I had no desire to achieve some glorious feat and be praised or respected for it, either. To begin with, other people made me think of insects massing in the wet earth under a stone—all that swarming and writhing was revolting. I could not summon the slightest respect for them. Losing a contest with them could still be fairly galling, but winning one gave me no particular pleasure.

Japanese: 他人となんか関わりたくないし、話したくもないし、いい思い出なんか無邪気だった幼児のころまで遡らないと見つからないって言うのに、携帯電話に登録がないのを見ると死にたくなるし、一週間人と喋らず人に姿を見られることもない生活を送るとこの若くて人生で一番美しい時期を見られずにしわくちゃになってしまうのかと思って死にたくなるし、誰にも愛されていないということは世の中にとって必要のない人間なのだなと死にたくなる。矛盾していると思う。
English: I wanted nothing to do with other people, did not even want to speak to them, and had to go all the way back to my innocent early childhood to find a pleasant memory—yet an empty contact list on my phone made me want to die. A week in which I spoke to no one and no one even saw me made me think I would grow old and wrinkled without anyone ever looking upon me in this young and most beautiful season of my life, and that made me want to die. The fact that no one loved me meant the world had no need for me, and that made me want to die. I thought I was a contradiction.

Japanese: 実際私はありとあらゆるところで、矛盾し、破綻し、混乱している。
English: The truth was that I contradicted myself, came apart, and lost my way in every conceivable respect.

Japanese: 死にたい死にたいとすぐ心の中で呟くわりには、自殺をしようなんてちっとも思わないし、むしろ醜くもがいて世界にしがみついてでも生きて行きたいと思っている。
English: For someone so quick to mutter I want to die, I want to die inside my head, I did not want to attempt suicide in the least. Quite the opposite: I wanted to live, even if I had to cling to the world in an ugly, desperate struggle.

Japanese: 幸福になりたいと思う反面、みんなに愛されて欲しいものを全部手に入れていい気になって笑っている自分を想像すると吐き気がして、気持ち悪くて、死ねばいいと思ってしまう。
English: Part of me wanted happiness. But when I imagined myself loved by everyone, possessed of everything I wanted, laughing in smug satisfaction, the image nauseated me. It was repulsive. I thought that version of me ought to die.

Japanese: 他人をすべて見下しているくせに、全人類の誰よりも自分の方が劣っているクズだと感じている。
English: I looked down on every other person alive, yet felt that I was garbage, inferior to every last one of them.

Japanese: ひとりぼっちでじゅくじゅくとねちねちと色んなことを考えている自分のあり方は自分らしい生き方だと思うけど、その価値観が欺瞞にしか思えず耐えられない時もある。
English: Brooding alone, letting one thought after another fester and ooze inside me—that seemed like an honest way for me to live. At times, though, that entire system of values felt like nothing but hypocrisy, and I could not bear it.

Japanese: 他人と自分でやりとりをすると、あるいは他人同士のやりとりを見ると、世間の人の多くは、目の前の人間を人間だと思っていないように感じる。心があり人生があり生まれた背景があり、自分と同じだけのものを持った存在が目の前にいるってことをちっとも想像出来ていないように感じる。そして表面だけを撫で合って、本当の意味ではかみ合っていない言葉をなげあって、何か人間関係をやっている気になっている。そういうのを見るのがつらい。
English: Whenever I dealt with another person, or watched two other people deal with each other, I felt that most people in society did not regard the human being before them as human at all. They seemed wholly incapable of imagining that this person had a heart and a life and a history that had brought them into being, that the person standing there possessed as much within them as they themselves did. Instead, they stroked one another’s surfaces and tossed back and forth words that never truly met, then congratulated themselves on having some sort of human relationship. It hurt to watch.

Japanese: 私にとって世の中は、寒いし暑いし痛いし眠たいのに眠れないしくさいし哀しいし寂しいし、寂しい。寂しい。
English: To me, the world was cold, hot, painful; it made me sleepy yet would not let me sleep; it stank; it was sad; and it was lonely, lonely. Lonely.

Japanese: 私はファウスト博士の前にあらわれた、すべてを否定する霊なのだ。時間よ止まれ、汝は美しい！　死ぬまでにそんなことを言えるような体験をしたいのだ。しかし、どこにもそんなものはありえないというような気もしていた。
English: I was the spirit who appeared before Doctor Faust, the spirit that negates all things. Time, stand still—you are beautiful! Before I died, I wanted to experience something that would let me say those words. But part of me suspected that no such thing could exist anywhere.

Japanese: 私はいわゆるタイプAというやつだ。サイキックとも言う。ミュータントとも言う。
English: I was what they called a Type A. Also known as a psychic. Also known as a mutant.

Japanese: 同じミュータントに分類されるタイプBは心がおかしくなってしまうことがあるが、タイプAは身体がおかしくなる。おかしくならない人もいるらしい。残念ながら私はおかしな身体を持った人間だ。
English: Type Bs, who were classified as mutants too, sometimes went wrong in the mind; with Type As, it was the body that went wrong. Some people apparently escaped without anything going wrong at all. Unfortunately, I was someone with a body that had gone wrong.

Japanese: どう見ても人間とは思えない姿になってしまう人もいるのだ。人間だとはわかるが、一目でそうとわかる明らかに異常な特徴を与えられる人もいるのだ。そういう人たちと比べれば、私は一見すると普通の人間と区別がつかないだけ恵まれた特質変異だと言えるのかもしれない。
English: Some people acquired an appearance no one could possibly take for human. Others remained recognizably human but were given some obvious abnormality visible at a glance. Compared with them, perhaps I could call myself fortunate: my trait mutation at least left me indistinguishable from an ordinary person at first sight.

Japanese: だけれどまあ、より酷い誰かをみて自分はあの人よりマシだって安堵するのは、人間性のくさった反吐の出るような人間がやるおぞましい満足の仕方だよね。
English: But then, looking at someone worse off and comforting yourself that at least you are better than them is a hideous pleasure reserved for rotten, vomit-inducing specimens of humanity, isn’t it?

Japanese: 比較のなかでしか喜びを見いだせない人間の魂は比較の泥沼で死ぬ。私は誰がなんと言おうと、何と比べようと、絶対に揺るがない心の根底から確信が持てる黄金の価値観を持ちたいんだ。それが本当の人生だと思うから。
English: A soul capable of finding joy only through comparison will drown and die in comparison’s mire. No matter what anyone said, no matter what anyone compared it with, I wanted a golden system of values—something absolute and unshakable, something I could believe from the very bottom of my heart. Because that, I thought, would be a real life.

Japanese: 私の特質変異はとめどもなく流れる体液だ。
English: My trait mutation was a ceaseless flow of bodily fluid.

Japanese: 普通の人でも汗をかく体質の人とそうでもない人に別れるだろうが、その中でもとびっきりの汗っかきを十人くらい集めて、その流れ出る汗にゆるゆるの鼻水みたいな若干の粘りけをもたせたら私の特質変異になると考えてもらっていいだろう。
English: Even among ordinary people, some sweat more than others. Imagine gathering ten of the very sweatiest, then giving all the sweat pouring off them the slight viscosity of runny mucus, and you will have a fair idea of my trait mutation.

Japanese: 精神や体調の調子で多少の変動はあるものの、肌はいつもしっとりと濡れ、半日も服を着替えず拭いもせずにいるならば何もかもぐっしょりと濡れて、池にはまりでもしたのかと思われる。髪の毛もすぐにべっとりとしてみっともなくなってしまうので、タオルが手放せない。
English: The volume varied somewhat with my physical and mental condition, but my skin was always damp. If I went half a day without changing my clothes or wiping myself down, everything would be soaked through as though I had fallen into a pond. My hair quickly became slick and disgraceful too, so I could never be without a towel.

English: And wherever I walked, my bodily fluid left behind a glittering Rainbow Road. The sight resembled Moses parting the sea to show his people a path—or a slug.

Japanese: そしてこのナメクジの身体と引き替えに手に入れた能力は、飛行。私の何の力を借りなくても空を飛ぶことが出来る。しかも、ふんわりではなく、割と速い速度でぴゅんぴゅんと飛べる。能力強度だとかいうやつが相当すぐれているらしく、歩いたり走ったりするよりも飛んでるほうが全然疲れなくて、人の目がなければもう一生歩かずに移動は飛行と乗り物だけにしたいくらい快適である。
English: In exchange for this slug’s body, I had received the ability of flight. I could fly without drawing upon any strength of my own. Not merely drift gently, either: I could zip around at a fairly high speed. Apparently my ability was exceptionally powerful, and flying tired me far less than walking or running. If not for other people’s eyes, it was so comfortable that I would gladly have spent the rest of my life traveling solely by air or vehicle, never taking another step.

Japanese: まさしく私は空飛ぶナメクジ女である。
English: I was, in the most literal sense, the Flying Slug Woman.

Japanese: 一口にタイプAといっても、しょうもない能力を与えられるのが大多数だが、これはとても素晴らしい能力だ。使い方によっては就職にも役に立つだろうし、実際親や親戚もそうすべきだと言う。
English: The great majority of Type As were given worthless abilities, but mine was superb. Employed properly, it could even help me find work. My parents and relatives certainly said I should put it to use that way.

Japanese: しかし私は働きたくなかった。
English: But I did not want to work.

Japanese: いや、家にいながらのんびりとできる仕事ならやってもいい。でも、飛行能力を活かした仕事となると、大抵肉体労働なわけでしょ？　しかも屋外で。そんな仕事をやりたいわけがない。
English: Well, I might have accepted some leisurely job I could do from home. But work that made use of flight would usually mean manual labor, wouldn’t it? Outdoors, no less. Why would I want a job like that?

Japanese: そもそも私だって最初から働きたくなかったわけじゃない。
English: It wasn’t as if I had never wanted to work at all.

Japanese: 学校を中退して家に引きこもる日々を続けるなかで、いくらなんでもこのまま一生を追えてはいけないと、社会復帰をしなければいけないと、一度だけアルバイトに挑戦したことがある。
English: After dropping out of school and spending my days shut away at home, I told myself I could not go on like this for the rest of my life, that I had to rejoin society, and once—exactly once—I attempted a part-time job.

Japanese: 明るいオシャレな仕事や人と会話する仕事や複雑な動きをする仕事は絶対に出来ないと思ったので、工場でライン上に流れる物品を検査するという私の性格にぴったりな職場だった。
English: I knew I could never handle a bright, stylish workplace, a job where I had to converse with people, or one involving any complicated motions. So I found a position perfectly suited to my nature: inspecting goods as they traveled down a factory line.

Japanese: まわりも外国人ばかりでみんな顔をマスクで隠して髪の毛も帽子で隠して、私はタイプAであることを隠して、ああ、これなら出来ると思ったのだけど、いくらタオルを取り替えてもびしょびしょ床を塗らしてしまうし、そんな場所にも同僚間での派閥があってどこにも入れずに孤立して昼休みはご飯を食べる場所がないので敷地外に出ようとしたら課長に怒られるし、仕事はくそつまんないし、タイプAであることが完全にばれるとなんだかいじめられるようになって、もう、休憩のたびにトイレでゲロを吐くし。
English: Everyone around me was a foreigner, and everyone concealed their face behind a mask and their hair beneath a cap. I hid the fact that I was a Type A and thought, Ah, I can do this. Except however often I changed my towels, I still soaked the floor; even a place like that had factions among the workers, and I belonged to none of them, so I was isolated; at lunch I had nowhere to eat, and when I tried to leave the premises, the section chief yelled at me; the work was fucking boring; and once everyone realized I was a Type A, somehow they started bullying me, and by then I was vomiting in the bathroom at every break.

English: That broke my spirit completely and renewed my conviction that I would never, ever work again.

Japanese: 今では労働を具体的に考えるだけでも、わけのわからぬ緊張で心臓がバクバクし、目眩がしてしまう。これはかつて学校に対して私が持っていた感情そのものである。どうして自分はこんなにメンタルが弱いのか、本当に嫌になってしまう。
English: Now, merely thinking about the concrete realities of employment brings on an anxiety I cannot explain: my heart pounds and I grow dizzy. It is precisely what I once felt toward school. I truly hate how mentally weak I am.

Japanese: バイトにめげて家で号泣している私を母親が慰めに来た時も「お母さんがこんな変な身体に生んだせいでつらいことばっかりだ！」と、叫んでしまった。
English: When my mother came to comfort me as I sobbed at home, crushed by the job, I screamed at her, “It’s because you gave birth to me with this freakish body that my whole life is misery!”

Japanese: 両親が自分をタイプAとして産んでしまったことで負い目を感じているのを私は知っている。
English: I knew my parents felt guilty for having brought me into the world as a Type A.

Japanese: その一方で、私がタイプAとして生まれたのに、両親の責任は全くないのも知っている。
English: At the same time, I knew that my being born a Type A was not their fault in the slightest.

Japanese: なのに私はさらにこうも叫んでしまった。
English: And despite that, I went on to scream this as well:

Japanese: 「なんで私なんか産んだんだ！　タイプAだと分かった時点でしめ殺してくれれば良かったのに！」
English: “Why did you ever have me? Once you knew I was a Type A, you should have strangled me to death!”

Japanese: 痛い、痛い。思い出しても心が痛い。
English: It hurts. It hurts. Even the memory makes my heart hurt.

Japanese: 中学生なら許されるその台詞。だけど私はもう十八才。
English: A line one might forgive from a middle schooler. But I was already eighteen.

Japanese: 両親だけが世界で私を気にかけてくれる人間なのだ。だから甘えているだけなんだ。
English: My parents were the only people in the world who cared about me. That was precisely why I let myself take advantage of them.

Japanese: でも親の愛だって無限とは限らない。両親は、私の人格などを評価してのものではなく、ただ産んだ子だったからという立場的なもので愛してくれているのだけれど、その立場が本当に盤石とは思えない。ひどいことをする親は世の中に沢山いるわけで。そういう親だったら、私なんかとっくに見放されていてもおかしくない。
English: But even a parent’s love was not necessarily infinite. My parents loved me not because they had weighed the merits of my personality, but simply because I was the child they had produced—and I could not believe that status was truly secure. The world contained plenty of parents who did terrible things. With parents like those, it would hardly have been surprising if someone like me had been abandoned long ago.

Japanese: 私の両親は本当に心が強く、すごいと思う。感謝もしている。
English: My parents were both astonishingly strong at heart. I truly admired them. I was grateful to them too.

Japanese: 出来れば私の関与によってあの人達を幸福に出来ることがあればいいが、残念だ。無理だ。それは私の能力の限界というものを越えているのです。悪く言わんから消えてなくなれば良いのにね。
English: I would be pleased if there were some manner in which my involvement might contribute to their happiness, but alas. Impossible. Such a feat lies beyond the limits of my capabilities. Best to take the hint and disappear, then, isn’t it?

Japanese: 「どこでも働けないのなら、うちの手伝いでもしたらどう？」と両親は安易に言う。我が屋はわりと歴史の古い蕎麦屋で、出前などもやっている。「空を飛んで届けたら、きっと評判になって売り上げもあがるから沢山お給料をあげるよ」と言う。
English: “If you can’t work anywhere else, why not help us?” my parents proposed with blithe simplicity. Our family ran a soba shop with a fairly long history, delivery service included. “If you flew the orders out, people would talk, and sales would rise. We could pay you lots of money.”

Japanese: でも私はあの岡持を持っておおっぴらに街を飛ぶのはいやだ！　そんなの絶対にいやだ！　私は誰にも見られずにこそこそ飛びたいんだ。それに私は全然蕎麦が好きじゃない。ラーメンは大好きだ。むしろ食べ物のなかではっきり胸を張って好きだと言えるのはラーメンくらいだよ。なんだよ蕎麦って。つゆは甘塩っぱいだけで、麺はなんだか貧乏くさい味がする。
English: But I did not want to fly openly through the city carrying that soba delivery case! Absolutely not! I wanted to fly furtively, where nobody could see me. Besides, I did not like soba in the least. I adored ramen. In fact, ramen was about the only food I could plant my feet and proudly proclaim that I loved. What the hell was soba? Its broth was nothing but sugary salt, and its noodles tasted vaguely of poverty.

Japanese: だから百歩譲ってラーメン屋にするならやってもいいけど、蕎麦なんか絶対に運びたくない。売りたくない。そもそも、そんな風に能力を使ったら、サイキック探知機がギャンギャンなって、警察がやって来てしまうじゃないか！
English: I might have considered it if I bent over backward and they converted the place into a ramen shop, but I would never carry soba. Never sell it. And to begin with, using my ability that openly would set every psychic detector wailing and bring the police down on me!

Japanese: そんなわけで私はせっかくの飛行能力を全く有意義に使ってはいない。社会のために使ってはいない。そうして何に使っているのかと言うと、自分の性癖を満足させるためにのみ使っているのである。
English: Thus I made no meaningful use whatsoever of my precious power of flight. I did not use it for society. What did I use it for, then? Exclusively to satisfy my own sexual proclivities.

Japanese: 私の趣味というのはひたすら家に引きこもって自慰をしながらネットゲームをしたり、自慰をしながら本を読んだり、とにかく性器を弄りながら何かをするのだが、貴重なタイプA能力ももちろんそのために使われる。
English: My preferred pastime was to barricade myself at home and masturbate while playing online games, or masturbate while reading a book—to do something, anything, with my hand on my genitals. Naturally, my precious Type A ability was put to the same purpose.

English: I never flew on clear days. I could not stop worrying that the fluid of my trait mutation would drip to the ground and make people notice me. So I flew only on rainy days, and at the darkest hour I could manage.

Japanese: そうすると、他人の人生の様々なシーンを盗み見ることが出来てしまう。人は頭上からの視線に対して無警戒で、特に背の高い建物に住む人はなおさらだ。大事な異性との愛の営みをカーテンも閉めずに行ってしまう人もいる。
English: That let me steal glimpses of all manner of scenes from other people’s lives. People were heedless of eyes above them—especially those who lived in tall buildings. Some even made love to the person most precious to them without bothering to close the curtains.

Japanese: 私はそういうシーンを空に留まりつつ、いつも持ち歩いている双眼鏡で観察する。時には空中に留まったまま自慰を行った。
English: I would hover in the sky and observe such scenes through the binoculars I always carried. Sometimes I masturbated while suspended in midair.

English: Not The Stalker in the Attic, but The Flier in the Air.

Japanese: 働きもせず、養ってくれる親を傷つけ、貴重なタイプA能力を無駄にしているという罪悪感も、そうしている間だけは薄れるような気がするのである。相手が自分を見ない、自分だけが相手を見ているというのは、なんだか自分が無生物になったような、大気の一部になったような、なんとも言えない存在の軽さを感じさせてくれる。
English: Only while I was doing that did the guilt of refusing to work, wounding the parents who supported me, and squandering a precious Type A ability seem to recede. To watch someone who could not watch me in return—to be the sole observer—made me feel somehow inanimate, part of the atmosphere, possessed of an indescribable lightness of being.

Japanese: そうして私はだらだらと毎日を過ごしていた。何もしないでいると苦痛で塗りつぶされてしまう時間を、いろいろな気休めで無理矢理埋めながら、無為に生きていた。
English: And so I let one day after another dribble away. I lived in idleness, filling by brute force and with one empty distraction after another the hours that pain would otherwise have blotted out completely.

Japanese: それが変わったのは、彼女と出会ってからだ。
English: That changed when I met her.

Japanese: 私の家から最も近い駅を越えた向こう側はY地区という、非常に治安の悪い地域となっている。親や学校の教師たちは口を酸っぱくして近づくなと言うけれども、他では手に入らない服やアクセサリーが手に入ったり、最近はオシャレな食べ物屋も出来たり、雑誌でもよく取り上げられたりでこのあたりの学生はよく遊びに行く。
English: Across the station nearest my home lay Y District, a notoriously dangerous neighborhood. Parents and teachers warned students until they were hoarse never to go near it. But it offered clothes and accessories unavailable elsewhere, fashionable restaurants had opened there lately, and magazines covered it often enough that local students regularly visited for fun.

Japanese: 私は学生ではないけれども、やはりこの地域の空をふわふわと飛ぶのが好きだった。
English: I was no longer a student, but I too loved drifting through the sky above the district.

Japanese: Y地区には外国人やミュータントが多く、日本の法律とは別のルールで生きている世界もあり、空から見える景色も随分とスリリングで楽しい。売春地域なども多く、男女の営みに関しても独特のものがある。下から鉄砲で狙い撃ちでもされたらどうしようというドキドキ感とあいまって、刺激の少ない私にとっては格好の遊び場だった。
English: Y District was home to many foreigners and mutants. Some communities within it lived by rules separate from Japanese law, and even the views from above were thrilling and entertaining. Prostitution districts abounded, along with their own unusual practices surrounding sex. Combined with the excitement of wondering whether someone below might shoot me out of the sky, it made a perfect playground for a person as starved of stimulation as I was.

Japanese: 雨の日に、この街のネオンの上を飛ぶだけで、私は何か世界のどこかにうまった大事な宝物を探しているような気持に浸れるのだった。
English: Simply flying above the city’s neon on a rainy day could immerse me in the feeling that I was hunting for some precious treasure buried somewhere in the world.

Japanese: 実際はただのオナネタを探してるだけにしても、である。
English: Even if what I was really hunting was nothing but masturbation material.

English: It was on one such rainy night that I met her.

Japanese: Y地区で他人の性交を覗くのは楽しい。それは性欲だけの話ではない。そこには金持ちがいて、貧乏人がいて、売春婦がいて、ギャングがいて、肌の違う様々な人々がいて、ミュータント達がいる。色んな立場と、色んな姿形を持った人々が、思い思いの性交をしている。
English: Watching other people have sex in Y District was fun, and not merely because it aroused me. There were wealthy people and poor people, prostitutes and gangsters, people of every color, and mutants. People of every station and every conceivable shape had sex in their own fashion.

Japanese: そこには文化があり、個性がある。私はそうして、人々が全裸になってお互いの個人的嗜好と、文化的背景をぶつかり合わせるのを見ながら、人間の奥深さを日々学ぶのであった。最近はもう、よほどきわどいものを見ても性欲などが起こることもない。窃視を続けていると、段々自分が人間でなく風景の一部になったような気になるとさっき言ったが、しばらくするとその感覚がさらに進んで、普段あれだけごちゃごちゃとくだらないことばかり考えてしまう私なのに、なぜかアタマが空っぽになって妙に冷静で落ち着いた気持になるようになった。
English: There was culture in it. Individuality. By watching people strip naked and bring their private tastes and cultural backgrounds into collision, I deepened my understanding of humanity day by day. Lately, even the most extreme sight rarely stirred any sexual desire in me. I said before that continued voyeurism gradually made me feel less like a human being and more like part of the scenery. After a while the sensation went further still. Despite all the pointless, tangled thoughts that ordinarily crowded my head, it would somehow empty completely, leaving me in a strangely cool and tranquil state.

Japanese: これはもう性欲を満たすよりも良い感覚で、このまま窃視を続けていたら仏教で言う悟りの境地に達してしまうんじゃないかと心配になるほどだ。
English: The feeling was better than satisfying my lust. I began to fear that if I persisted in my voyeurism, I might attain what Buddhism called enlightenment.

Japanese: だから、私は雨の夜には休まず他人の生活の一部を盗み見る。そこには誰かに知られたくない秘密もあるだろうし、重要な弱点もあるだろう。そうした情報を利用すれば、私は自分に利益をもたらすことが出来るのを理解していたが、それは絶対にしてはならないと自分で決めていた。
English: So on rainy nights, without fail, I stole pieces of other people’s lives. They must have contained secrets the subjects wanted no one to know, and weaknesses of great importance. I understood that exploiting this information could bring me profit, but I had made an absolute rule against doing so.

Japanese: ただ観察するだけで、そこで見た者は誰にもけして話さないし、観察対象とは接触しない。それがもっとも純粋でいいやり方だ。
English: I would only observe. I would never tell anyone what I had seen, and I would not make contact with the subject of my observation. That was the purest and best method.

Japanese: 私は、私の存在になど全く気づかない他人の大事な生活を見る。それは性欲だけを満たすわけではない。自分を意識しない相手の動きを見るということは、それだけでもう相手と充分な繋がりを得ることができるのだ。
English: I watched the private life of another person who remained wholly unaware that I existed. It did more than satisfy lust. Simply watching the movements of someone who had no awareness of me felt, in itself, like connection enough.

Japanese: そして、見たことに最後まで気づかれず、私が完全に黙っていれば、誰も何も失わない。誰も何も失わないのに、私の心はしっかりと充足感を得ているのだから、これはもう幸福というものを無からクリエイトしていると言っていいんじゃないだろうか？
English: And if I was never discovered and kept perfectly silent until the end, no one lost anything. No one lost a thing, while my heart found genuine fulfillment. Surely one could say that I had created happiness out of nothing?

Japanese: もし、見たものを前提に相手を脅すなどしてしまえばそれはただの暴力でしょう？　私は暴力は嫌いだし、そんな風に誰かを貶めて手に入れる充足感というのも不純な気がする。だから、なるべく対象には接触しない、ばれそうになったら絶対に逃げるというようなつもりでいたんだけど……しかし人間というのは、力をもつと最終的に暴力に流されてしまうものだ。
English: If I threatened someone on the basis of what I had seen, that would simply be violence, wouldn’t it? I hated violence, and any satisfaction acquired by degrading another person that way seemed impure. I therefore meant to avoid contact with my subjects whenever possible and flee without fail if they looked likely to discover me... But human beings, once given power, ultimately drift toward violence.

Japanese: 私にも、ついにそのルールを破ってしまう時が来た。
English: At last, the day came when I too broke my rule.

Japanese: Y地区には大きなビルは少ないが、そのうちの一つにグランドタワーという建物がある。
English: Y District had few large buildings. One of them was a structure called Grand Tower.

Japanese: なんでもY地区で最も強いギャングが根城にして、部下と一緒に住んでいるとかで、私もその評判を聞いて普段は近寄らないようにしていた。いくら飛行能力があるとはいえ、相手に補足され、狙撃でもされてしまえばひとたまりもないからだ。
English: According to rumor, the strongest gang in Y District used it as a headquarters and lived there with its subordinates. After hearing its reputation, even I ordinarily kept my distance. Flight or no flight, if someone caught sight of me and took a shot, I would not stand a chance.

Japanese: その日も、サイキック探知機の効力が及ばない高さまで飛んでふらふらと飛び回っていたのだけれども、面白そうなものがなにも見つからず、退屈だった。だから魔が差した。
English: That night too, I had risen beyond the reach of psychic detectors and drifted aimlessly about. But I could find nothing interesting and had grown bored. Temptation seized me.

Japanese: ギャングの本拠地って普段どんな生活をしているのかしら？　と、ふと芽生えた余計な好奇心に勝つことができなかったのである。
English: How did people live inside a gang headquarters? A seed of unnecessary curiosity sprouted within me, and I could not resist it.

Japanese: といっても私は臆病なので、出来うる限り慎重なやりかたでの観察である。
English: Coward that I was, however, I observed as cautiously as I possibly could.

Japanese: ビルの最上階よりも少し高い場所から、見下ろすようなポジションを取った。空は黒く曇っていたし、そうすれば暗灰色でかためた全身の服がカモフラージュの役割を果たす。
English: I positioned myself a little above the top floor of the building and looked down. Against a sky black with clouds, the dark-gray clothing I wore from head to toe would camouflage me.

Japanese: その上で充分な距離をとり、双眼鏡の焦点距離を最も遠くにして、ビルの窓の一つ一つを観察したのだ。
English: Then, keeping a generous distance and setting my binoculars to their most distant focus, I examined each of the building’s windows in turn.

Japanese: もう日が暮れている。
English: The sun had already set.

Japanese: 昼は日光を反射して鏡みたいに見える窓も、内側の方が明るくなれば中を見通すのは容易い。
English: Windows that reflected the daylight like mirrors became easy to see through once the room within was brighter than the world outside.

Japanese: 大体の窓にはカーテンやらブラインドやらが掛かって内部が見えなくなっていたり、真っ暗で使っていなそうな感じだったのだけれども、灯りが点ってカーテンも開き、無防備に内部を見通せる部屋もいくつかある。
English: Most were covered with curtains or blinds that hid their interiors, or else dark and apparently unused. But a handful of lighted rooms had their curtains open, leaving the interiors exposed and plainly visible.

Japanese: サイキックの能力というのは体力を使うものだけど、私の場合は速度に応じて疲労度が等比級数的に増えていくけれども、浮いているだけならばほとんど疲れない。
English: Psychic abilities consumed physical energy. In my case, fatigue rose geometrically with speed, but simply floating in place required almost no effort.

Japanese: 私は空中にふわふわと浮かびながら、双眼鏡をのぞき込んでそうした部屋の一つ一つを覗くのである。
English: I hovered softly in the air, peering through the binoculars into each of the exposed rooms.

Japanese: 窓が開いているのは、大体ビルの中層辺りだった。窓越しにリビングなどが見えるのだけれど、当たり前と言えば当たり前なのかもしれないが、ギャングといっても部屋の中は普通の家庭とさほどかわらない。
English: Most of the uncovered windows were around the middle floors. I could see living rooms through the glass, but obvious as the point might have been, their interiors differed little from ordinary homes despite belonging to gangsters.

Japanese: 鹿の頭の剥製とか、熊の頭がついた毛皮の絨毯とか、神棚に日本刀とか、そういうのを期待していたのだけれども、そんなものは見つからない。どこにでもあるマンションみたいな白い壁紙の部屋に、システムキッチンがあったり、量販店の家具屋で買ったようなありふれた家具が並び、エプロンをした女の人が料理を作ったり、ジャージやスウェットを着た人たちが集まって麻雀をしたりしている。
English: I had expected mounted deer heads, bearskin rugs with the heads still attached, or a Japanese sword on the household shrine. Nothing of the kind appeared. The rooms had the plain white wallpaper of any apartment, fitted kitchens, and commonplace furniture that looked as if it had come from a mass-market store. Women in aprons cooked, while people in tracksuits and sweats gathered to play mahjong.

Japanese: いやらしいことをしている場面も見つからないし、薬を打ったり銃の手入れをして居る場面も見られない。なんて健全なのだろう！　それとも、そういうことをする人たちはさすがにカーテンを閉めているのかな。
English: I found no one engaged in anything indecent, shooting drugs, or cleaning a gun. How wholesome! Or perhaps the people doing those things had, sensibly enough, closed the curtains.

Japanese: よく分からないけれども、思ったより面白くない。
English: I could not tell. In any case, it was less interesting than expected.

Japanese: その辺の階の住人は下っ端だから平凡な生活をしているのかな？　上の方には幹部などが住んでいるのかもしれない。
English: Perhaps the residents on those floors were rank-and-file and led ordinary lives. The officers might live higher up.

Japanese: しかし、さすがに上の階に住む幹部達は用心深いのか、灯りがついている部屋はあれども、カーテンを開けっ放しにしている部屋はない。
English: The officers on the upper floors did appear more cautious. Some rooms had their lights on, but not one had left its curtains open.

Japanese: 思ったよりドキドキワクワクがない。……もうちょっと、近づいてみようかな？
English: This was nowhere near as heart-poundingly exciting as I had expected. ...Maybe I could go a little closer.

Japanese: この暗い夜でカーテンが閉まっているということは、向こうからこちらも見えないはずだ。上の方から近づけば、誰にも気づかれないかもしれない。
English: If the curtains were closed on a night this dark, no one inside should be able to see out, either. If I approached from above, I might escape everyone’s notice.

Japanese: ここまで来ると、もう窃視に対する欲望よりも、誰も近づけないギャングの本拠地に接近してみたいという変な欲求の方が強かった。
English: By that point, the bizarre desire to approach a gang headquarters no one was permitted near had become stronger than any appetite for voyeurism.

Japanese: 辺りを警戒しながら近づく。
English: I advanced, keeping a wary eye on my surroundings.

Japanese: 地上には高い塀があって、外部の人間を寄せ付けないようになっているが、私には全くの無力だ。
English: A high wall on the ground kept outsiders at bay, but it was utterly powerless against me.

Japanese: ふわふわと上空を通り抜けると、塀の内側の光景なども見られるが、特にめぼしいものもなく、関係者以外見られないものを見ているという喜び以外のものはない。
English: Drifting above it let me see the grounds within, but I found nothing of note and felt no pleasure beyond the illicit thrill of seeing what outsiders were never meant to see.

Japanese: さて、そうしてビルの窓ガラスに触れるほど近づいた。
English: And so I drew near enough to touch the building’s windows.

Japanese: 一つ一つ窓をチェックして、カーテンやブラインドの隙間を探しながらゆっくりと飛ぶ。
English: I flew slowly along, checking each one and hunting for gaps in the curtains and blinds.

Japanese: まず、灯りのついていない部屋を点検する。それらは、何の面白みもない白いカーテンやブラインドが使われており、隙間を覗いても、何もない空き部屋か、棚が並ぶ倉庫みたいな部屋、椅子と机が並べられた企業の会議室みたいな部屋だったりする。
English: First I inspected the dark rooms. Their wholly uninteresting white curtains and blinds concealed either empty rooms with nothing in them, storage spaces lined with shelves, or corporate-looking conference rooms furnished with rows of chairs and tables.

Japanese: やはり灯りがついている部屋を調べるしかないようだ。さすがに緊張するけれども、まさか、この高さにある部屋の窓から人が覗いているとは思わないはずだ。
English: It seemed I would have to examine the lighted rooms after all. That certainly made me nervous, but no one would imagine a person peering through a window at this height.

Japanese: そんな風に、心臓をときめかせながら灯りのついた窓を巡っても、しかし思ったような面白さはない。
English: Yet even as I made the rounds of the lighted windows with a fluttering heart, I found none of the excitement I had imagined.

Japanese: YSの幹部の顔とか知っていたら少しは楽しめるのか、なんなのか。私が聞いているのは、YSのボスが謝だかなんだかという若い人で、とても危険な人だというくらいで、しかもその顔は知らない。
English: Perhaps I could have enjoyed it if I knew the faces of the YS officers. All I had heard was that the boss of YS was some dangerous young man named Tse or something, and I did not even know what he looked like.

Japanese: さて、最初の興奮もさめて開き始めてきたころ、私はその窓に出くわしていた。ピンク色の地に、花のついた可愛らしいカーテン。
English: Just as my initial excitement had faded and boredom begun to set in, I came upon that window. The curtains were pink, patterned with darling little flowers.

Japanese: こんなビルに女の子の部屋でもあるのかな、と、迂闊に窓の目の前に浮かんでしまうと、急にカーテンが開いた。
English: Wondering whether there might be a girl’s room in a building like this, I carelessly floated directly in front of the window. The curtains abruptly opened.

Japanese: 「うわっ！」
English: “Whoa!”

Japanese: びっくりして、反射的にぴゅんと後ろに逃げてしまう。
English: I started and instinctively zipped backward.

Japanese: けれども、もっと驚いたのは、カーテンが開いたことよりも、開けた人物だった。
English: What astonished me more than the opening curtains, though, was the person who had opened them.

Japanese: ワンピースを着た女の子が、そこに立ち、驚いた顔でこちらを見ているのである。
English: A girl in a dress stood there, staring at me with surprise.

Japanese: 年は私と同じくらいだろうか？　私と同じくらいの身長だけれど、私よりすらっとしていて、私より足が細くて、私より色が白くて、そして私より遥かに美人だった。
English: Was she about my age? She stood about as tall as I did, but she was more slender, with finer legs and fairer skin—and she was incomparably more beautiful.

Japanese: 観察対象に近づかないという私のポリシーからすれば、ここで飛び去るべきだった。でも私はそれが出来なかった。
English: My policy against approaching the subject of my observation required me to fly away. But I could not.

Japanese: 「うわあ、きれい……」
English: “Oh, wow. You’re beautiful...”

Japanese: うっとりして近づいてしまうと、相手は何か口を動かして言っている。
English: As I drifted toward her in a daze, she moved her lips and seemed to say something.

Japanese: ガラスは分厚いらしく、私のグレーのレインコートを叩く雨音と相まって、彼女の声を通さない。窓ははめ殺しになっていて開かない。
English: The thick glass, together with the rain beating down on my gray raincoat, refused to let her voice through. The window was fixed and could not be opened.

Japanese: 「なに？　聞こえない！」
English: “What? I can’t hear you!”

Japanese: 私はフードをとって耳に手を当て、首を横に振り、全力で聞こえないというジェスチャーを行う。
English: I pulled down my hood, cupped a hand to my ear, shook my head, and gave the most emphatic I-can’t-hear-you pantomime of which I was capable.

Japanese: すると意図が伝わったらしく、ガラスの向こうで彼女は右手の方を指さした。そちらを見ると、ベランダがある。
English: Apparently my meaning reached her. From behind the glass, she pointed to her right. I looked that way and saw a balcony.

Japanese: 私は頷いた。すると彼女も頷きを返した。
English: I nodded. She nodded back.

Japanese: ベランダは割と広く、一脚の机と、二脚の椅子が設えられ、隅には柄のついた器に観葉植物が飾られている。晴れた昼下がりに紅茶でも飲んだら似合いそうな空間で、多分さっきの女の子もそうしているんだろう。
English: The balcony was fairly spacious, furnished with a table and two chairs. In one corner, a leafy plant stood in a decorated pot. It was the sort of space that would suit afternoon tea on a clear day, and the girl had probably used it for precisely that.

Japanese: 部屋とは大きなガラスがはめ込まれたドアで仕切られており、その向こうにはさっき窓から覗いた部屋が見えた。けれど、少女の姿がない。
English: A door inset with a great pane of glass separated it from the room I had seen through the window. But the girl was no longer there.

Japanese: どこへ行ったんだろう？
English: Where had she gone?

Japanese: 風はさほどなく、雨は奥の方まで吹き込んでいなかった。私は乾いたところを濡らすのをきらい、ベランダに腰掛けた。後から考えると不用心だったと思う。こんな建物の住人と接触しようだなんて、無思慮にもほどがある。
English: There was little wind, and the rain had not reached the inner part of the balcony. Hating to wet a dry area, I sat down on the balcony. In hindsight, I had been terribly careless. Attempting contact with a resident of that building was thoughtless beyond belief.

Japanese: そもそも私は観察対象と接しないというポリシーがあったはずだ。しかし、もうこの時点で、私のアタマからポリシーは消え去っていた。まあ、私が自分に要求するルールなんか、いつもこのようにして簡単に破られてしまうのだけど。
English: I was, after all, supposed to have a policy against contact with the people I observed. By then, however, the policy had already vanished from my head. Well, every rule I imposed on myself was always broken just this easily.

Japanese: その時の私は女の子のことばかりで頭がいっぱいになっていて、他のことなどすっかり抜け落ちていた。
English: My mind was filled entirely with the girl, to the exclusion of everything else.

Japanese: すると、すぐに女の子が駆け足でやって来て、ガラス戸を開く。
English: A moment later, she came running back and opened the glass door.

Japanese: 彼女はショールのようなものを羽織っていて、それを取りに一旦奥へ引っ込んでいたのかもしれない。
English: She now had something like a shawl around her shoulders. Perhaps she had gone deeper into the room to fetch it.

Japanese: 女の子はくっきりとした二重まぶたの目を驚きに見開いて、私に呼びかける。
English: She called to me, her sharply double-lidded eyes wide with astonishment.

Japanese: 「空を飛べるの？」
English: “You can fly?”

Japanese: 「そうだよ」
English: “That’s right.”

Japanese: 女の子は美しすぎてコンプレックスを感じてしまう。私はフードで自分の顔を隠しながらそう答えた。
English: She was so beautiful that merely looking at her gave me an inferiority complex. I answered while hiding my face beneath my hood.

Japanese: 夢中になって飛びついてしまったけれど、ろくに髪の毛もとかしていないし、化粧もしていないし、なんなら風呂に入って身体を洗ったのはいつだったろうか？　こんな状態でかわいい子の前に出るのはあまりにも恥ずかしい。
English: I had thrown myself into the encounter without thinking. I had barely combed my hair, I wore no makeup, and when had I last taken a bath and washed my body? Appearing before a pretty girl in this state was mortifying.

Japanese: 「雨の日はよくここらへんを飛んでる」
English: “I fly around here a lot when it rains.”

Japanese: どうしようどうしようどうしよう！
English: What do I do what do I do what do I do!

Japanese: 内心はどぎまぎしていて心臓はバクバクしていたけれど、声も態度も自分でもびっくりするくらい落ち着いている。
English: Inside, I was in a panic and my heart was pounding. My voice and manner, however, remained so composed that even I found it astonishing.

Japanese: 「タイプAなの？」
English: “Are you a Type A?”

Japanese: 「うん」
English: “Yes.”

Japanese: 「空を飛べるなんて、いいなあ……」
English: “It must be so wonderful to fly...”

Japanese: 彼女は目を輝かせている。
English: Her eyes shone.

Japanese: あきらかに不審人物な私に対して、警戒心というものがないのだろうか？
English: Did she have no caution whatsoever around someone as obviously suspicious as I was?

Japanese: 「私も空が飛べれば良かったのに」
English: “I wish I could fly too.”

Japanese: そう言って、溜息をつく。
English: She sighed.

Japanese: 「ねえ、そんな端っこにいるから、雨がかかってるよ？　もっとなかにおいでよ？」
English: “You’re sitting so close to the edge that the rain is hitting you. Why don’t you come farther in?”

Japanese: 「いいんだ、ここで」
English: “I’m fine here.”

Japanese: 「でも、風邪ひいちゃうよ？」
English: “But you’ll catch a cold.”

Japanese: 「大丈夫、私、能力の副産物なのか、なんなのか自分でもわからないんだけど、寒さに異常に強いんだ。雨の中、服を湿らせて空を飛んでても、冷え込まないで全然平気。やったことないけど、多分真冬に氷水に飛び込んでも普通に泳げる。雪のなかで眠っても死なないんじゃないかと思う」
English: “It’s fine. I don’t know whether it’s a side effect of my ability or what, but I’m abnormally resistant to cold. I can fly through the rain with my clothes soaked and never get chilled. I’ve never tried it, but I could probably jump into ice water in midwinter and swim normally. I might even survive sleeping in the snow.”

Japanese: 「すごーい」
English: “Amazing!”

Japanese: 彼女は素直に感情を顔に出してそう言うと、
English: She said it with her delight plain on her face. Then—

Japanese: 「でも、そんな雨に打たれてる姿、かわいそうで見てられないから、もっと近くに来て」
English: “But I can’t stand watching you sit there in the rain. Come closer.”

Japanese: 有無を言わせぬ調子だった。
English: Her tone allowed no argument.

Japanese: 「仕方ないな」
English: “If you insist.”

Japanese: 近づくと、彼女の身体のいいにおいさえかげそうで、もう内心とても平静じゃいられない。可愛いその肉体が、こんなに近づいてしまうなんて！　きめ細かい肌の艶さえはっきりと見える！
English: Once I drew nearer, I felt I could almost catch her lovely scent, and there was no hope of keeping calm inside. That lovely body was so close! I could see the luster of her fine-grained skin!

Japanese: それにしても、なんて豊かな睫毛をもっているんだろう？　つけまつげをして増やしたり、変にカールさせたりする必要なんかないくらい、ちょうどいい長さと密度だ。瞬きするたびに目の間から音符が転がり出てきそうだ。
English: And what extraordinary eyelashes she had. They possessed exactly the right length and fullness, with no need for false lashes or unnatural curling. Every blink seemed ready to send musical notes tumbling from between her eyes.

Japanese: 「あなたはここに住んでるの？」
English: “Do you live here?”

Japanese: 訊ねると、彼女はうんと頷き、
English: When I asked, she gave a firm nod.

Japanese: 「もう何年くらいになるのかな……。お母さんと街に住んでたんだけど、お母さんが亡くなってから、ずっとここに暮らしてる。ほとんど外に出してもらえない」
English: “I wonder how many years it’s been... I used to live in the city with my mother, but I’ve lived here ever since she died. I’m hardly ever allowed outside.”

Japanese: 表情を曇らせる。
English: Her expression clouded.

Japanese: どうも、悪いことを聞いちゃったんだろか？
English: Had I asked something I shouldn’t have?

Japanese: 黙っていると、彼女は言葉を続ける。
English: When I said nothing, she continued.

Japanese: 「私タイプBなの。お母さんもタイプBだった。お父さんは私たち華族のことは愛しているけど、タイプBは苦手なんだと思う。だから、お母さんと私を家から離したところで暮らさせて、今は私をほとんど部屋から出さないでいるような気がする。私のところにもあまり会いに来ない。私のためだ、お母さんのためだってずっと言ってるけど……身内がタイプBだってことを、直視したくないんだよ。哀しいし、仕方がないことだけど」
English: “I’m a Type B. My mother was a Type B too. I think Father loves our family, but Type Bs make him uncomfortable. That’s why he had Mother and me live away from the family home—and I feel as if that’s why he hardly ever lets me out of this room now. He rarely comes to see me himself. He always says it’s for my sake, and it was for Mother’s... But he doesn’t want to face the fact that someone in his family is a Type B. It’s sad, but I suppose it can’t be helped.”

Japanese: 急に打ち明け話をするなんて、よほど話し相手がいないんだろうか？
English: Why had she suddenly confided all of that? Was she so starved for someone to talk to?

Japanese: 私はちょっと戸惑いながら、
English: A little bewildered, I asked—

Japanese: 「いいの？　こんな、空からやって来た不審者にそんなことを話して」
English: “Are you sure you should tell all that to a suspicious stranger who just dropped out of the sky?”

Japanese: すると彼女は頷いて、笑顔を作る。
English: She nodded and smiled.

Japanese: 「顔見たらわかるもの。あなたはきっといい人だから、大丈夫」
English: “I can tell from your face. I’m sure you’re a good person, so it’s all right.”

Japanese: その言葉と表情で私はすっかりやられてしまった。
English: That answer, paired with that expression, did me in completely.

Japanese: 世間知らずというのか、純粋培養というのか、ちょっと痴呆みたいな感じがするけど、その汚れのなさがまた可愛い。汚れに塗れた私の目には笑顔がまぶしいくらいだ。
English: Call it ignorance of the world or a hothouse upbringing—she seemed almost half-witted, but that very lack of corruption made her lovelier still. To my eyes, steeped in filth, her smile was dazzling.

Japanese: 私のことをいい人だなんて、外に出したらあっというまに悪い奴に騙されて散々暴行された上にどっかに売り飛ばされそうなくらい無防備だけど、そういう危ういところもまたたまらない。
English: Calling me a good person left her so defenseless that, if released outside, she seemed liable to be deceived by the first villain she met, brutally assaulted, and sold off somewhere. Even that dangerous vulnerability was irresistible.

Japanese: 「この噂のビルにどんな人が住んでるんだか気になってきたんだけど、あなたみたいな子がいるなんて想像もしてなかったよ」
English: “I was starting to wonder what sort of people lived in this infamous building, but I never imagined I’d find a girl like you.”

Japanese: 「そう？」
English: “Really?”

Japanese: 「うん、YSってギャングの本拠地なんでしょ。怖い人ばかりいるんだと思ってた」
English: “Yeah. It’s the headquarters of a gang called YS, isn’t it? I thought everyone here would be frightening.”

Japanese: 「そんなことないよ。下の方にはYSに入ってない人も一杯住んでるし、この階とかに住んでる人も、小さい子とか女の人も多いし」
English: “That’s not true. Lots of people on the lower floors aren’t even in YS. And on floors like this one, there are plenty of little children and women.”

Japanese: 「そうなんだ」
English: “I see.”

Japanese: 「でも、なんで今日が大丈夫な日ってわかったの？」
English: “But how did you know today was safe?”

Japanese: 「大丈夫って？」
English: “Safe?”

Japanese: 「だって、今日はお父さん達が出かけてて、見張ってる人がいないのわかってたんでしょ？」
English: “Father and the others are out today, so no one is watching. You knew that, didn’t you?”

Japanese: 「え、どういうこと？」
English: “What do you mean?”

Japanese: 「知らなかったの？」
English: “You didn’t know?”

Japanese: 彼女は目を丸くする。
English: Her eyes widened.

Japanese: 「う、うん……ただちょっとふらっと好奇心が出て……」
English: “N-no... I just happened to wander over when curiosity got the better of me...”

Japanese: 「じゃあ、すごくラッキーだったんだね」
English: “Then you were incredibly lucky.”

Japanese: 彼女の説明によると、彼女の父親はタイプAで、透視能力を持っているのだと言う。そして父親のボディガードもタイプAで、これはレーダーのように周囲の生命を感知することが出来るのだそうだ。つまり、ボディーガードが不審者を発見し、父親がどこに隠れていてもその正体を見極める。これによって、近づく侵入者はほぼ完全に把握されてしまうのだという。
English: According to her, her father was a Type A gifted with clairvoyance. His bodyguard was another Type A, supposedly able to detect life in the surrounding area like radar. In other words, the bodyguard found an intruder and her father identified them wherever they might be hiding. By this means, she said, they obtained an almost complete picture of anyone approaching the building.

Japanese: 「それは……」
English: “That...”

Japanese: 私は絶句してしまう。
English: Words failed me.

Japanese: もしそんな能力者がいて、ギャングに空から近づくのを察知されていたとしたらと考えると背筋が冷たくなる。
English: A chill ran up my spine at the thought that people with such abilities might have detected me approaching a gang from the air.

Japanese: サイキック探知機には多少の警戒はしていたけれども、そんなタイプA能力者がいるとは想像していなかった。そんなのが居るときにうっかり空からふわふわ近づいていたら、銃で撃ち落とされてもおかしくないし、そうなったら私の死体はこのY地区のカオスの狭間にひっそり飲み込まれてゆくだけだったろう。お母さんとお父さんは娘が帰ってこないからと、おかしくなってしまうかもしれない。
English: I had been somewhat wary of psychic detectors, but had never imagined Type As like those. If I had casually drifted down from the sky while they were present, they might well have shot me down. My corpse would simply have vanished in silence into the folds of Y District’s chaos. My mother and father might have lost their minds when their daughter failed to come home.

Japanese: 「でも、それってすごい偶然だよね！」
English: “But that’s an incredible coincidence!”

Japanese: 彼女はまた笑顔になって言う。
English: She smiled again.

Japanese: 「たまたま見張りが居ない時にビルの近くに来て、たまたま私の部屋の前に来たところで私がカーテンを開けたってことでしょ？　こんなの偶然ってあると思う？」
English: “You happened to come close to the building while no guards were here, and just as you happened to reach my room, I opened the curtains. Do you think a coincidence like that can really happen?”

Japanese: 「まあ、あるんじゃないかな……」
English: “Well, I suppose it could...”

Japanese: 少なくとも、前から知っていてストーカーのように窓の側で見張っていたんではないよ。そんな変質者ではないよ。別の意味では変質者だろうけど、そこはちがうんだ。という意味を込めて私はそう言った。
English: What I meant was: At least I wasn’t a stalker who already knew about you and waited outside your window. I am not that kind of deviant. A different kind of deviant, perhaps, but not that kind.

Japanese: 「いいや、これ偶然じゃないよ」
English: “No, this wasn’t a coincidence.”
“What...?”

Japanese: 「きっと、何かの運命なんだよ。私たちが会うの」
English: “It must have been some sort of fate that brought us together.”

Japanese: 彼女はきっぱりとそう言った。
English: She said it with finality.

Japanese: 「そう思うよね？」
English: “Don’t you think so?”
“Oh, sure...”

Japanese: 私は運命とか幽霊とか奇跡とか神とか占いとかジンクスとかマーフィーの法則とかそういうものは全然信じない。全くもって非科学的だからだ。まあ、その存在が確認されたとき有名な科学者が自殺したほど非科学的であるタイプAという人種の一人である私が言うのもなんだが。
English: I did not believe in fate, ghosts, miracles, gods, fortune-telling, jinxes, Murphy’s law, or anything of the sort. They were entirely unscientific. Admittedly, that was a strange complaint from a Type A like me, when the very confirmation of our existence had supposedly driven famous scientists to suicide.

Japanese: しかし、彼女が私に好感を抱いてくれる方に運ぶのなら認めるのにやぶさかではない。私は欲望のためならいつでも主義主張と相反する行動をとれる、融通が効き過ぎるくらい効く人間である。
English: But I had no objection to accepting fate if it would make her like me. I was an exceedingly flexible person, always capable of acting against my principles and convictions in the service of desire.

Japanese: 「そうだね。きっとこれは運命だ。私たちはきっと出会うべきして出会ったんだよ」
English: “You’re right. This must be fate. We met because we were meant to meet.”

Japanese: いけしゃあしゃあとそう言った。
English: I said it without the slightest shame.

Japanese: すると、彼女はうんと満足げに頷き。
English: She gave an emphatic, thoroughly satisfied nod.

Japanese: 「私、筱喬。シウってよく呼ばれる。あなたは？」
English: “I’m Siu-kiu. People usually call me Siu. And you?”

Japanese: 「さくらっていうんだ。よろしく」
English: “My name’s Sakura. Nice to meet you.”

Japanese: 私が調子に乗って濡れた手を出すと、彼女は躊躇なく握る。
English: Getting carried away, I offered her my wet hand. She took it without hesitation.

Japanese: ああ、私の、普段あんなことやこんなことをしている手が、こんな可憐な美少女の手を握っている！
English: Ah! This hand of mine—the hand I usually used to do this and that—was clasping the hand of such a delicate young beauty!

Japanese: その場で倒れたくなるけれども、見せかけ上はあくまでも冷静でいなければならない。
English: I could have collapsed on the spot, but appearances required me to remain perfectly composed.

Japanese: 名残惜しく手を離すと、
English: When at last I reluctantly released her hand—

Japanese: 「ねえ、そのフードをとって、顔をよく見せて」
English: “Take off that hood and let me see your face properly.”

Japanese: 「ああ、うん、でもびしょびしょだから……」
English: “Oh, sure, but I’m soaked...”

Japanese: ただでさえたいしたことがない顔を、ノーメイクで見せるというのは気が進まない。
English: I was reluctant to display a face that was nothing special to begin with, particularly without makeup.

Japanese: 「さっき、窓越しのときちょっと見せてくれたじゃない。いいでしょ？　ねえ」
English: “You let me see a little through the window. So it’s all right, isn’t it? Please?”

Japanese: しかし、こんな子にまっすぐな視線で懇願されては、従わないわけにはいかなかった。
English: But when a girl like her looked straight at me and pleaded, how could I refuse?

Japanese: 「わあ、かわいい」
English: “Wow, you’re pretty.”

Japanese: お世辞だろうけれど、そんなことを言ってくれる。
English: She even said that to me, though it was probably flattery.

Japanese: 私は照れくさくて相手の顔を直視出来ない。
English: I was too embarrassed to look her directly in the face.

Japanese: 「目がきりっとしてて、なんだかりりしい顔してるんだね」
English: “Your eyes look so sharp. You have such a dashing face.”

Japanese: 「そ、そういえばさ……」
English: “S-speaking of which...”

Japanese: 私は自分の顔の話題が苦手なので、顔だけでなく話題もそらしにかかる。
English: I did not handle conversations about my face well, so I worked to turn away both my face and the conversation.

Japanese: 「あなたのお父さん、ボディガードがいるとか言ってたけどさ、YSでも偉い人なの？」
English: “You said your father has a bodyguard. Is he important in YS?”

Japanese: 「そうみたいだね。お父さんの仕事のことはよく知らないけど」
English: “I suppose so. I don’t know much about Father’s work.”

Japanese: 私のあからさまな話題転換に、彼女は屈託なくそう答えてくれる。
English: She took my blatant change of subject in stride and answered without a care.

Japanese: 「なんて人？」
English: “What’s his name?”

Japanese: 軽い気持でそう訊ねたのだけれど、彼女の答えは驚くべきものだった。
English: I asked casually, but her answer was astonishing.

Japanese: 「クリス・ツェーって言うんだ」
English: “Chris Tse.”

Japanese: 「えっ？」
English: “What?”

Japanese: びっくりして彼女の顔を振り返る。
English: Startled, I turned to stare at her.

Japanese: 彼女は、自分の言葉が私のような一般人に対して、どんんあふうに聞こえているのか理解していないらしく、相変わらずの笑顔を浮かべていた。
English: She apparently had no idea how those words sounded to an ordinary person like me. The same smile remained on her face.

Japanese: こんないたいけな子が、私でも知っている最強ギャングの娘だっていうの？　じゃあ、変に手を出したら、ものすごく大変なことにならない？　でも相手は、どうも私と仲良くしたがってるみたい！
English: This innocent little girl was the daughter of the strongest gang leader even I knew? Wouldn’t making any kind of move on her land me in a truly catastrophic mess? But she seemed to want to be my friend!

Japanese: ……実にいいじゃないか。
English: ...Excellent.

Japanese: 「知ってる？」
English: “Have you heard of him?”

Japanese: 不安げに小首をかしげる彼女に対し、私はうんと頷き、
English: She tipped her head anxiously. I gave an emphatic nod.

Japanese: 「うん、知ってる。すごい有名人だね」
English: “Yes, I have. He’s incredibly famous.”

Japanese: なんでもないような声色を作る。
English: I made my voice perfectly casual.

Japanese: 「そんな有名人の子で、こんなに可愛い子と友達になれるなんて幸せ」
English: “I’m so happy I get to be friends with the cute daughter of someone so famous.”

Japanese: 「えへへ」
English: “Hee hee.”

Japanese: 私の言葉に彼女は照れくさそうに笑い、
English: She laughed shyly at my words.

Japanese: 「私も、空を飛べる友達が出来るなんて最高」
English: “It’s wonderful to have a friend who can fly.”

Japanese: 控えめにそう言ったのだった。
English: That was her modest way of putting it.

Japanese: これが、私と謝筱喬の出会いである。
English: That was how Siu-kiu Tse and I met.

Japanese: もう三ヶ月は前のことだ。このとき携帯電話の番号を交換し、クリス・ツェーが外出して例のボディガードがいないという連絡を受けて、私は彼女の窓へ忍び、親しくなっていった。
English: It was more than three months ago. We exchanged phone numbers that night, and afterward, whenever I heard that Chris Tse had gone out and taken the bodyguard with him, I stole up to her window. In that fashion, we became close.

Japanese: クリス・ツェーの娘がどんな人間で、どんな生活をして居るのか、世間の人はほとんど知らないだろう。
English: Virtually no one in the outside world could have known what kind of person Chris Tse’s daughter was, or how she lived.

Japanese: 彼女はほとんどグランド・タワーから出ることがない。どころか、自分の住む階の他に行くこともまれだ。ビルの下の方には映画館や飲食店などが入り、それなりに楽しむ施設もあるそうなのだが、そこに降りることが出来るのは月に一度か二度だと言う。
English: She almost never left Grand Tower. For that matter, it was rare for her to visit any floor but her own. The lower levels apparently contained a movie theater, restaurants, and a respectable assortment of other entertainment, but she said she was allowed down only once or twice a month.

Japanese: 同じ階には他の幹部の家族などが住んでいて、そこの子供や夫人と話したり遊んだりするのが、彼女のごく少ない他人との接点なのだそうだる。夫人達は、ボスの娘である筱喬に気を遣い、子供と遊んでいる時が一番癒やされると彼女は言う。
English: The families of other officers lived on her floor. Speaking and playing with the women and children there provided some of her very few points of contact with other people. The wives treated Siu-kiu with great care because she was the boss’s daughter, and she said she felt most at ease when playing with the children.

Japanese: ましてや、ビルの外に行くことは、ほとんどありえない。
English: Going outside the building was all but inconceivable.

Japanese: タイプBは精神の動揺やストレスによって発作が引き起こされる、ということで、極力刺激を遠ざけて暮らすよう父のクリス・ツェーがはからっているらしい。
English: Type B episodes were said to be triggered by emotional disturbance and stress, so her father, Chris Tse, had apparently arranged her life to keep all stimulation at the greatest possible distance.

Japanese: 「昔お母さんと街に住んでいるときは、シウは外がこわくってあんまり出たいと思わなかったけど、ここに住むようになってから、妙に出たくなっちゃった。このビルのなかにも、なんでもあるんだけどね」
English: “When I lived in the city with Mother, the outside frightened Siu, and I hardly ever wanted to go out. But since I started living here, I’ve developed this strange longing to leave. There’s everything you could want inside this building, too.”

Japanese: 筱喬はよくそう言って苦笑する。親しくなってから、時々彼女は自分を呼ぶときに「私」ではなく「シウ」と名前で呼ぶことが混じるようになって来た。本人は気づいていないようだ。信頼してくれている証拠のように思えて嬉しい。
English: Siu-kiu often said that with a rueful smile. After we became close, she sometimes began to refer to herself as ‘Siu’ instead of ‘I.’ She did not seem aware of it. I was happy, taking it as proof that she trusted me.

Japanese: 彼女が今言った気持は私もよくわかる。私だって、人から禁止されたり、駄目だと言われると何が何でもやりたくなる。その逆に、やれと言われたり、最善の方法だとしたり顔で教えられたりすると、何が何でもやりたくなくなる。
English: I understood the feeling she described perfectly. Tell me something was forbidden or that I must not do it, and I would want to do it at any cost. Conversely, tell me to do something, or smugly explain that it was the best course available, and I would do anything not to.

Japanese: 人間の心というものはそのように出来ているのだと教えてあげたが、彼女はあまり納得がいかないようだった。まだ私の域には達していないのだろう。
English: I explained that the human heart was built that way, but she did not seem entirely convinced. Evidently, she had not yet reached my level.

Japanese: それはともかく、あんまりにもしょっちゅう外の世界を見たいというので、私は、それならひとっ飛びで街まで連れてってあげようかと提案したのだ。
English: In any case, she talked so constantly about wanting to see the outside world that I finally offered to fly her into the city.

Japanese: 「えっ、本当？」
English: “What? Really?”

Japanese: 彼女は大きな目を見開いて希望に輝かせるが、すぐに困ったような顔になってしまう。
English: Her great eyes widened and shone with hope, only for her face to grow troubled a moment later.

Japanese: 「でも、勝手にそんなことしたらお父さんが悲しまないかな……」
English: “But if I did that without asking, wouldn’t Father be sad?”

Japanese: 筱喬はしょっちゅう父親について愚痴をこぼすが、それでも非常に父親のことを気にかけているらしく、いつもそんな言葉が口から出て来る。
English: Siu-kiu complained about her father often, yet she appeared extremely concerned for him all the same. Something like that was always slipping out.

Japanese: 彼女の語る言葉だけでクリス・ツェーという人間を想像すると、なんだか、健康や品性については口やかましいけれども、他の面ではだだ甘な、どこにでもいる平凡な娘大好きお父さんになってしまう。
English: If I imagined Chris Tse from nothing but her accounts, he became an ordinary father who adored his daughter, strict about her health and morals but utterly indulgent in every other respect.

Japanese: 筱喬とつき合うようになってから、私もクリス・ツェーについて調べた。そうして実際に行われたと思われる情報をもとにすると、かなり非道なこともやっている、恐ろしい人物である。この無茶苦茶な街で帝王と呼ばれているのは伊達ではない。どう考えても、彼女が言うような人物ではない。
English: I had researched Chris Tse myself after becoming involved with Siu-kiu. According to reports of acts he appeared genuinely to have committed, he was a terrifying man capable of considerable cruelty. They did not call him emperor of this lawless city for nothing. There was no possible way he could be the person she described.

Japanese: それからもう一人、よく話題に出て来るのは街を出て一人暮らしをしている大学生の兄の話だ。
English: The other family member who frequently entered her stories was her elder brother, a university student who had left the city and lived alone.

Japanese: 彼女の言葉だけで想像すると、どうも頭が良くてルックスも良くて服のセンスも良くて人望もあって優しく、そして妹のことを愛しているという、まるで完全無欠のような人間が出来上がってしまう。
English: Constructed solely from her words, his image became that of a flawless human being: intelligent, handsome, well dressed, respected, kind, and devoted to his sister.

Japanese: その兄のことは何の情報もないけれど、多分彼女がそう思っているだけでそのような人物ではないのだろう。
English: I possessed no information whatsoever about the brother, but he was probably nothing like that in reality. Perhaps that was simply how she saw him.

Japanese: 死んだ母親のことも、よく会話には出て来る。そして話ながらいつも涙ぐんでしまうのだ。
English: Her dead mother often appeared in our conversations too, and Siu-kiu’s eyes invariably filled with tears as she spoke.

Japanese: 私は、そんな風に家族のことを溺愛している筱喬が好きだった。
English: I loved Siu-kiu for the way she adored her family.

Japanese: 「じゃあやめとく？」
English: “Should we forget it, then?”

Japanese: 父への罪悪感で苦しむような無理にとは思わない。純粋にそう思って、私は撤回しようとした。
English: I had no wish to force her into anything that would make her suffer with guilt toward her father. I tried to withdraw the offer, and I meant it.

Japanese: 「……ねえさくらだったら、どうする？」
English: “...What would you do, Sakura?”

Japanese: 「私だったら悩みもしない。だって、こっそり出かけて、何事もなくこっそり帰ってくれば、私はやりたいことが出来て満足。親も自分の言う通り部屋に閉じこもってると信じて満足。お互い満足でまるくおさまる」
English: “I wouldn’t even agonize over it. If I slipped out in secret and came back without incident, I would be satisfied because I’d done what I wanted. My parents would be satisfied because they’d believe I was obeying them and staying in my room. Everyone would be satisfied, and the whole thing would end happily.”

Japanese: 彼女は私のこの考え方には全然共感しなかったようだけれども、しかし、よくよく考えて、外界を見ることを選んだ。
English: She seemed incapable of sympathizing with that philosophy in the least. But after a great deal of thought, she chose to see the outside world.

Japanese: 「だって、じっとしてたって発症する人はするんだよ。私もいつ発症して頭がおかしくなっちゃうかわかんないもの。それまでに、一杯いろんなものを見て、いろんなことを感じて、いろんなことを考えておかないと、私、なんのために生まれてきたのかわかんない！　このまま、世の中の何もかもが嫌いなまま死んでしまうなんてあんまりだよ。……無から有は生まれないけど、有から有は作り出せるでしょ？　この世界にも素晴らしい意味があるってわかれば、私の人生にも意味があるって信じられるかもしれない」
English: “Some people develop symptoms even if they sit perfectly still. I might develop them and lose my mind at any time. Before that happens, I have to see all sorts of things, feel all sorts of things, and think about all sorts of things—or I’ll never know why I was born! It would be too cruel to die while I still hate everything in the world. ...You can’t make something out of nothing, but you can make something out of something, can’t you? If I discover that this world has some wonderful meaning, perhaps I’ll be able to believe that my life has meaning too.”

Japanese: なんのために生まれてきたのか？　人生に意味はあるのか？
English: Why had she been born? Did life have meaning?

Japanese: そんなの私だって全然わからない。というか、なんの理由もないんだろう。人間はただ親がセックスした結果によってのみ生まれるのであって理由も意味もない。
English: I had no idea either. Rather, there probably was no reason. Human beings were born solely because their parents had sex. There was neither reason nor meaning in it.

Japanese: はっきり言ってそう思ってるんだけど、自分の決意に対して目をきらきらさせている筱喬にそう言う勇気はなかったし、もしかしたら私にはまったく存在を想像も出来ないそれを、彼女は見つけ出すことが出来るのかもしれない。そうだったら、それは素晴らしいことだ。
English: That was honestly what I believed. But I lacked the courage to say it to Siu-kiu when her eyes shone with determination. And perhaps she could find something I could not even imagine existed. If she did, it would be wonderful.

Japanese: そりゃ、彼女を連れ出すのは危険だ。YSの本拠地から、ボスの娘をさらうというのは、いくら本人の手引きがあるとしても危険この上ない。ことによっちゃ死ぬなんてこともあるが、どうせ大した価値もない命。それでも彼女に出来ることをしてやりたかった。そういう風に思える自分に驚きだ。なんだか、生きてるっぽい。いや生きてるのだろう私は。
English: Taking her out was dangerous, of course. Abducting the boss’s daughter from YS headquarters was as dangerous as anything could be, even with the girl’s cooperation. It might get me killed. But my life was worth little anyway, and I wanted to do what I could for her. I was astonished to find myself capable of feeling that way. It made me seem alive. No—presumably, I was alive.

Japanese: さっそく次の機会に連れ出した。
English: At the very next opportunity, I took her out.

Japanese: クリス・ツェーは仕事の用事でY地区を一週間ほど離れるという。これほど良い機会はないだろう。もちろん、途中で気が変わってUターンするなんていう可能性はないわけでもないが、そんなの歩道を歩いていたら突然車道から暴走した車が突っ込んで来てそれに直撃して死ぬくらいのものだ。そんなにアンラッキーならどうせ何をしたって死ぬだろう。
English: Chris Tse was leaving Y District on business for about a week. There could be no better chance. Of course, it was not impossible that he might change his mind midway and turn back, but the likelihood seemed comparable to a car suddenly careening off the roadway while I walked down the sidewalk, striking and killing me. If I was that unlucky, I would die no matter what I did.

Japanese: いつものようにベランダで彼女と出会い、用意した大人用のおんぶひもを取り出して見せた。母親が赤ん坊を背中にくくりつけるアレの大人版で、本来は防災用で、ぐったりした要救護者を運ぶための道具らしい。
English: I met her on the balcony as usual and produced an adult rescue harness I had prepared. It was an adult-sized version of the carriers mothers used to secure babies to their backs, apparently intended for disaster response and transporting people in need of rescue who could not move under their own power.

Japanese: それを使って彼女を背中にくくりつけ、いざ飛ぼうとしたその時、
English: I strapped her to my back with it. Just as I prepared to fly—

Japanese: 「ちょ、ちょちょっと待って！」
English: “W-w-wait!”

Japanese: 筱喬は急にストップをかける。
English: Siu-kiu abruptly stopped me.

Japanese: 「なに？」
English: “What?”

Japanese: 「なんかこれ、想像以上に恥ずかしい……」
English: “This is much more embarrassing than I imagined...”

Japanese: 「赤ちゃんみたいだから？」
English: “Because you look like a baby?”

Japanese: 首をねじって背後の筱喬に尋ねると、すぐ至近距離に頬を赤らめて頷く顔が視界の端に入った。
English: When I twisted my neck to ask her, the edge of my vision caught her blushing, nodding face only inches from mine.

Japanese: あまりにも顔が近いので、私はどぎまぎしてしまう。
English: The closeness of her face flustered me.

Japanese: ああ、そうか、今私はこの美少女と密着しているのだ。とめどなくあふれる体液を吸い取るために、上着の下に分厚い衣服を着込んでしまったのを後悔した。正直いってこれほど後悔したことはかつてない。これがなければ、彼女の胸の柔らかみなどを背中に感じることが出来たというのに。そして青春のときめき以上の何かを感じることが出来たというのに。
English: Oh. Of course. At that moment, this beautiful girl was pressed against me. I bitterly regretted the thick clothing I had put on beneath my jacket to absorb the endless flow of fluid. Frankly, I had never regretted anything so much in all my life. Without it, I could have felt the softness of her breasts against my back. I could have felt something beyond the tender stirrings of youth.

Japanese: でも、それは出来ない。この気持ちの悪い粘液のことは、彼女に知られたくない。絶対に知られたくない。
English: But that was impossible. I did not want her to learn about this revolting slime. Absolutely not.

Japanese: 彼女の前ではクールな態度を気取っている私は、そんな本音をおくびにも出さずに、
English: I affected a cool manner in her presence, and gave no sign of my true feelings.

Japanese: 「気にしない、気にしない」
English: “Don’t worry about it.”

Japanese: 一方的に言うと、ベランダから飛び出した。
English: Having settled the matter for both of us, I launched myself from the balcony.

Japanese: 「こわい？」
English: “Are you scared?”

Japanese: 「こわくない。とっても気持ちいい」
English: “No. It feels wonderful.”

Japanese: 降りる地点を探してゆっくり飛びながら、背中の筱喬と話すと、首筋に彼女の温かい吐息がかかって幸せな気分だ。
English: We talked as I flew slowly in search of a place to land. Siu-kiu’s warm breath brushed the nape of my neck, filling me with happiness.

Japanese: 「さくらはいつもこんな気分なんだね。うらやましいな。こんな能力があるなんて、とっても恵まれてるよ」
English: “This is how you feel all the time. I envy you, Sakura. You’re so fortunate to have a power like this.”

Japanese: それは確かにそうかもしれない。
English: She might have been right.

Japanese: いろいろなことが嫌いな私だけれども、この力で空を飛び回ることは、正直好きだ。
English: I hated many things, but I honestly loved using this power to fly through the air.

Japanese: 何故私のような性格の人間に、こんなあまりにも自由な翼が授かっているのか、どうにも似つかわしくないような気がして、考え込みたくなってしまうくらいだ。
English: It was enough to make me brood over why someone like me had been granted such impossibly free wings, and how completely they failed to suit me.

Japanese: 「降りたら何をしたい？」
English: “What do you want to do once we land?”

Japanese: 何か食べ物屋に行きたいとか、洋服を見たいとか、そういった返答を予想していたのだが答えは違った。
English: I expected an answer like visiting a restaurant or looking at clothes. Her reply was something else.

Japanese: 「何をしたいって言うか……どこか、ミュータントの人がたくさんいるところを知らない？」
English: “It’s not exactly something I want to do... Do you know anywhere with lots of mutants?”

Japanese: 「たくさんって……Y地区は他の地域に比べて明らかに多いけど」
English: “Lots? Y District clearly has more than other parts of the city...”

Japanese: 「そのなかでも多いところってない？」
English: “Is there anywhere with especially many?”

Japanese: 「……私はあんまり詳しくなからなあ。でも、滑走路通りを歩いているだけでも、働いているタイプAやBの人とか、よく見かけるよ」
English: “...I don’t know that much about it. But even walking down Runway Street, you see Type As and Type Bs working all over the place.”

Japanese: 「じゃあ、ぷらっとお散歩したいな。……それでもいい？　さくらはどこか遊びに行きたい？」
English: “Then I’d like to take a little walk. ...Is that all right? Was there somewhere you wanted to go, Sakura?”

Japanese: 「私はシウの行きたいところならどこでもいいよ」
English: “Wherever you want to go is fine with me, Siu.”

Japanese: 「ありがとう」
English: “Thank you.”

Japanese: 筱喬は上機嫌だ。
English: Siu-kiu was in high spirits.

Japanese: 彼女がミュータントとしての自分にこだわりがあるのは知っている。だけど、こんな時くらいは同年代の普通の若者らしいことをした方がいいんじゃないかと、それをしたかったんじゃないかと、私は思っていたのである。彼女はどうも、タイプBのことばっかり考えているせいか、最近疲れが見える。
English: I knew how deeply she was preoccupied with being a mutant. But I had thought that, at a moment like this, she ought to do something ordinary for a person her age—perhaps that was what she wanted too. Lately, perhaps because she thought of nothing but Type Bs, she had begun to look tired.

Japanese: 「ねえさくら」
English: “Sakura.”

Japanese: 筱喬は黙っている私の耳元に独り言のようにささやきかける。
English: As I remained silent, Siu-kiu whispered into my ear as though talking to herself.

Japanese: 「あなたは、死ぬまでに絶対にしたいこととかある？」
English: “Is there something you absolutely want to do before you die?”

Japanese: 「急に何を……」
English: “Where did that come from...?”

Japanese: 「生まれたからにはこれをしないと死ねないもの、でもいいよ。……なんていうかなあ、京都に行ったら絶対これを見たい、とか、フランスに行ったらこれを体験したい、みたいなノリで、命があって現世にいるならこれだけはしたいってことない？」
English: “It could be something you can’t die without doing, now that you’ve been born. ...How can I put it? The way you might say, I have to see this if I go to Kyoto, or, I have to experience this if I go to France. Is there anything you absolutely want to do, given that you’re alive and here in this world?”

Japanese: 「突然言われても困るなあ……」
English: “That’s a difficult question to spring on me...”

Japanese: 私は首をひねって考える。
English: I tilted my head and thought.

Japanese: 「そんなの、思いつかない。ないような気がするなあ……あ、そうだ、私、ガンジス川をこの目で見てみたいかも」
English: “Nothing comes to mind. I don’t think I have anything like that... Oh, wait. I might want to see the Ganges with my own eyes.”

Japanese: 「ガンジス川ってインドの？」
English: “The Ganges in India?”

Japanese: 「そうそう。ガンジス川ってインドの人にとってはとても聖なるものだそうでね、人間が死んだら火葬した灰を流したり、燃やしもせずに死体をそのまま流したり、その水につかって沐浴したり、洗濯したり、飲んだり、食べる物を煮たり、工業廃水も垂れ流してるし、とにかく何にでも使う、世界で一番汚い川なんだってー。すごいよねー？　なんかそこに人間のすべてがあるような気がする。それを肉眼で見てみないと、人間ってどういうものかなんて、絶対にわからないような気がするよ」
English: “Right. They say the Ganges is extremely sacred to the people of India. When someone dies, they put the ashes from the cremation in it—or don’t even burn the corpse and send it down whole. They immerse themselves in the water for ritual bathing, wash their clothes in it, drink it, boil their food in it, dump industrial wastewater into it—use it for absolutely everything. Supposedly, it’s the filthiest river in the world. Isn’t that incredible? I feel as if everything human is contained there. As if I could never understand what human beings are until I’d seen it with my own naked eyes.”

Japanese: 「……それはインド旅行すればすぐに叶いそうだね」
English: “...You could make that happen easily enough by traveling to India.”

Japanese: 「いやだよめんどくさい」
English: “No way. Too much trouble.”

Japanese: 「うーん」
English: “Hmm.”

Japanese: 筱喬は納得いかなそうな顔をする。私の答えはなにか間違っていたのだろうか？
English: Siu-kiu looked unconvinced. Had I answered incorrectly somehow?

Japanese: 「筱喬はそういうの、あるの？」
English: “Do you have something like that, Siu?”

Japanese: 沈黙に気まずくなって私がそう尋ねると、
English: The silence grew awkward, so I put the same question to her.

Japanese: 「うん」
English: “Yes.”

Japanese: 彼女は子供のようにこくんと頷き、
English: She gave a little nod like a child.

Japanese: 「シウはね、答えが欲しいの」
English: “Siu wants an answer.”

Japanese: 「答え？」
English: “An answer?”

Japanese: 「そう。生まれてから死ぬまで……それか、正気をうしなうまでの間に、自分の人生の答えを見つけておきたい。自分の人生とはなんだったのかという、総論？　意味のあるものだったって、納得出来る何か。……他のみんなみたいに遊びたいとも思うけど、それよりもっと大事なことなんだ」
English: “Yes. Between my birth and my death... or until I lose my sanity, I want to find the answer to my life. An overall conclusion about what my life was, perhaps? Something that will convince me it meant something. ...I want to have fun like everyone else, but this matters much more.”

Japanese: 私は考えを見透かされたようなその説明に、どきりとして何も言うことが出来なかった。
English: Her answer seemed to see straight through my thoughts. My heart gave a start, and I could find no reply.

Japanese: 「最近特にそう思う。……ねえさくら、私のお父さん、病気みたいなの」
English: “I’ve felt it especially strongly lately. ...Sakura, I think my father is ill.”

Japanese: 「お父さんが？」
English: “Your father?”

Japanese: 「そう。教えて貰ったわけじゃないけど、なんとなくわかる。今回の出張も検査か何かだと思う。きっと、とても悪い病気……。父さんに何かあったら、私もどうなるかわからない。今のうちに、少しでも出来ることはしておかなくちゃ」
English: “Yes. No one told me, but I can somehow tell. I think this business trip is really for tests or something. It must be a very serious illness... If anything happens to Father, I don’t know what will happen to me. I have to do whatever little I can while there’s still time.”

Japanese: YSの龍頭クリス・ツェーに何かあったら、その無力な一人娘はどうなるか。
English: If something happened to Chris Tse, the Longtou of YS, what would become of his powerless only daughter?

Japanese: ちょっとお金のある家庭でも、家長が死ねばそれなりの混乱が生まれるものだ。YSともなれば、私の想像もつかない事情もあるのかもしれない。少なくとも筱喬はそう予測している。
English: Even a moderately wealthy household falls into some disorder when the head of the family dies. YS might involve circumstances beyond anything I could imagine. Siu-kiu, at least, seemed to expect as much.

Japanese: 「その時は、私がなんとかするよ」
English: “When that happens, I’ll do something about it.”

Japanese: そう言いたかったが、口に出すかどうか、迷った。
English: That was what I wanted to say. I hesitated to let the words out.

Japanese: だって、私はサイキックだけど、それ以外はどうってことのない人間だし、言ったって何の説得力もない。
English: I might have been a psychic, but in every other respect I was nothing special. Anything I said would carry no conviction.

Japanese: ……いや、それでも口にするのが人として正しいありかたなんじゃない？
English: ...But wasn’t speaking it anyway the proper human thing to do?

Japanese: 「その時は……」
English: “When that happens...”

Japanese: 私がうっかり真剣になって言葉を出しかけたとき、
English: I had let myself grow serious and was just beginning to speak when—

Japanese: 「ねえさくら」
English: “Sakura.”

Japanese: 筱喬が同時に口を開いて、彼女の言葉によって遮られるようなかたちになる。
English: Siu-kiu opened her mouth at the same instant, and her words cut across mine.

Japanese: 「あっ、ごめん」
English: “Oh, I’m sorry.”

Japanese: 「いいよ。シウが言って」
English: “It’s fine. You go ahead, Siu.”

Japanese: 私が促すと、筱喬はもう一度やり直す。
English: At my prompting, Siu-kiu began again.

Japanese: 「うん。……あのね、さくら」
English: “All right. ...Sakura?”

Japanese: 「なに？」
English: “What?”

Japanese: 「髪の毛、今度伸ばして見なよ。短いのもかっこよくて似合ってるけど、長くしたところも見てみたいな？」
English: “You should try growing your hair out sometime. It looks good short—it makes you look dashing—but I’d like to see it long too.”

Japanese: 「……アハハ」
English: “...Ha ha.”

Japanese: 「なに？」
English: “What?”

Japanese: 何か真剣な話をされるのかと思って身構えていた私は、拍子抜けして苦笑してしまったのだ。
English: I had braced myself for some grave pronouncement. The anticlimax drew a wry laugh from me.

Japanese: 「なんでもない。……伸ばす気はないかな」
English: “Nothing. ...I don’t think I want to grow it out.”

Japanese: 「なんで？」
English: “Why not?”

Japanese: 「私はなんだっていいんだ。シウみたいに可愛いわけじゃないし。長くしたってめんどくさいだけだよ」
English: “It doesn’t matter what I look like. I’m not cute like you, Siu. Long hair would only be a nuisance.”

Japanese: 「そんなことないんだけどなあ」
English: “That isn’t true...”

Japanese: 筱喬は不満げに溜息をついた。
English: Siu-kiu sighed unhappily.

Japanese: このときは二人で滑走路通りをぷらぷらと歩き、彼女は特質変異の強いタイプAの店員などと会話をしたり、タイプBのストリートチルドレンに声をかけたりしていた。私は人見知りなのでそれを黙って隣で見ているだけだった。
English: That day, the two of us wandered down Runway Street. She spoke to shop employees with pronounced trait mutations and called out to Type B street children. Being shy with strangers, I merely watched in silence beside her.

Japanese: これは彼女にとって感慨深い体験だったようで、帰ってからもよくこのときのことを話題にしたがった。そして、もう一度、外に遊びに行こうという話が出て来た頃だ。
English: The experience appeared to affect her deeply, and afterward she often wanted to talk about it. Just as we had begun to discuss going out again—

Japanese: 彼女の父、クリス・ツェーが死んだ。
English: Her father, Chris Tse, died.

Japanese: 私はその葬儀の列を、滑走路通り沿いの建物のてっぺんに座り込んで、双眼鏡で眺めていた。黒塗りの高級車や、コワモテの男達が多数列を成して往来をゆっくりと練り歩く様はなかなかの壮観で、全く何も知らない頃の私だったら、馬鹿みたいに口をぼんやり開けて見守っていただろうけれど、筱喬と知り合った今では胸中複雑だった。
English: I sat on the roof of a building along Runway Street and watched his funeral procession through my binoculars. A great number of black luxury cars and hard-faced men formed ranks and made their stately way down the street. It was an impressive spectacle. Before I knew anything, I would have watched slack-jawed like an idiot. Now that I knew Siu-kiu, my feelings were not so simple.

Japanese: そして、行列が通り過ぎると、部屋に閉じこもる筱喬を訊ねた。
English: Once the procession had passed, I visited Siu-kiu in her room.

Japanese: 彼女はベッドの上で泣きじゃくっていた。私が入ると一瞬泣き止んで顔を上げたが、
English: She was sobbing on the bed. When I entered, she stopped for an instant and raised her face.

Japanese: 「う、う、うあぁぁぁああん……」
English: “U-uh—uwaaaaaah...”

Japanese: すぐにまた子供のような声をあげて泣き出した。
English: Then she immediately began crying aloud again like a child.

Japanese: 私はそのすぐ隣に座って、震える細い肩を眺めた。
English: I sat directly beside her and watched her slender shoulders tremble.

Japanese: 彼女の最大の庇護者である父親が死んだら、これから先誰が彼女を守るのだろう？　母親はもういない。兄が唯一の肉親になるけれど、行列で見たそれらしい人物は、あまりにも若すぎて頼りなかった。しかも学生だと言う。
English: Now that her father, her greatest protector, had died, who would keep her safe? Her mother was already gone. Her elder brother would be her only remaining blood relative, but the figure who appeared to be him in the procession looked far too young and unreliable. He was supposedly a student, no less.

Japanese: クリス・ツェーにはたくさんの部下がいたが、そうした人々は本当にアテになるのだろうか？　本当の家族のようには信じられないだろう。
English: Chris Tse had many subordinates, but could she truly rely upon those people? She could hardly trust them the way she would real family.

Japanese: そのことを考えると、私の方が心細くなってしまいそうだった。
English: Thinking about it threatened to make me feel helpless myself.

Japanese: 一方、おそらく筱喬自身はそんな自分の将来の心配などはしていないだろう。
English: Siu-kiu herself, on the other hand, was probably not worrying about her own future at all.

Japanese: ただただ、父親の死を悲しみ、泣き続けている。
English: She did nothing but grieve her father and cry.

Japanese: 私は慰めの言葉を探したが見つからなかった。大好きな身内を失った悲しみというのは、絶望的で、個人的で、どうしようもないものだ。他人がどんな言葉をくれても、何をしてくれても、その行為と自分の心の間に透明の壁が出来てしまって、何も届かなくしてしまう。
English: I searched for words of comfort and found none. The grief of losing a beloved family member was hopeless, personal, beyond repair. Whatever another person said, whatever they did, a transparent wall rose between the act and your heart and kept it from reaching you.

Japanese: 私がいまここで何を言っても説得力のない的はずれの言葉になってしまうのだ。
English: Whatever I said now would miss the point and ring hollow.

Japanese: 私はそっと手を伸ばし、彼女の背中をさすった。
English: I quietly reached out and stroked her back.

Japanese: それは、まだ幼い頃、夜中に目が覚めて眠れないと泣きじゃくった私に、死んだ祖母がしてくれた行為だった。その手のひらの温かみには途轍もない安心感があり、それをなんとか再現出来ないだろうかと考えたのだ。
English: When I was still small and woke crying in the middle of the night because I could not fall asleep again, my late grandmother had done that for me. The warmth of her palm carried a tremendous sense of safety. I wondered if I could reproduce it somehow.

Japanese: 実際はそれほどわかっているわけでもないが、何でもわかっているような穏やかな表情をして、静かに撫で続ける。
English: In truth, I understood very little. But I arranged my face into the tranquil expression of someone who understood everything and continued stroking her in silence.

Japanese: 「うっ、うっ、うううぅ……」
English: “Uh... uh... uuuuh...”

Japanese: 私のなでなで大作戦は、少しは効果を示したのか、彼女の泣き声は段々小さくなってゆく。
English: My grand back-rubbing strategy appeared to have some effect. Little by little, her sobs grew quieter.

Japanese: やがて、歯を食いしばり、ときおりしゃくり上げるという程度にまで収まってきたが、しかし泣き止むというところまではいかなかった。その姿を見ていると、祖母が死んだときの幼い自分の姿が思い出された。
English: At length, her crying subsided until she merely clenched her teeth and occasionally hiccuped, though it had not stopped altogether. Looking at her brought back my younger self when my grandmother died.

Japanese: 祖母が死んだとき、もし祖母が側にいてくれたならば、こんなふうに背中を撫でてくれて慰めてくれたのだろうか？　矛盾した想像だけど。
English: When my grandmother died, if my grandmother had been there beside me, would she have stroked my back and comforted me like this? A contradiction, of course.

Japanese: 「哀しいね」
English: “It’s sad.”

Japanese: 私は初めて同情の言葉を口にした。
English: For the first time, I put my sympathy into words.

Japanese: 彼女は私の顔を振り返ると、引きつった顔を見せて、そして両手で私の身体にしがみつくようにして、また声をあげて泣き始める。
English: She turned to my face, her features contorted, then clung to me with both arms and began wailing once more.

English: Perhaps there were reasons for killing them the way he had. Still, the incident was more than enough to make me feel that we inhabited different worlds.

English: It would hardly have been unnatural to reject everything—to say, I can’t follow you any farther, I don’t want anything more to do with you, don’t contact me don’t don’t don’t. Nor was it actually impossible.

Japanese: 筱喬に言った言葉は嘘じゃない。だけど、そのときに補足したように、あくまでもその瞬間の真実だ。
English: The words I had spoken to Siu-kiu were not lies. But as I had added then, they were true only at that moment.

Japanese: 私は意志が強い人間ではないし、情に厚い人間でもないし、誠実な人間でもない。むしろその逆ばかり行っているような気がする。認めたくないけれども、冷静に自己分析を試みると結論はそうなる。その時その時のことがいつも一番大事で、そのためだけに生きている。……正直言って、それらにどんな価値があるのかがわからない。強い意志とかいって、自分にやりたくもないことを自分に強制するのはいやだし、情だとかいって義務みたいにいつもかわらず誰かにやさしくするなんて馬鹿みたいだし、誠実とかいって善人でもないのにいつでも善良に振る舞いたくもない。自分に嘘をついているような気がする。誰かのふりをして生きるなんていやだ。
English: I was neither strong-willed, warmhearted, nor sincere. If anything, I seemed to head unfailingly in the opposite direction. I did not want to admit it, but a sober attempt at self-analysis could reach no other conclusion. Whatever belonged to the immediate moment was always most important to me, and I lived solely for that. ...Frankly, I had no idea what value those qualities held. I did not want to use something called a strong will to force myself to do what I did not want to do. I thought it absurd to call something warmheartedness and turn unchanging kindness toward another person into an obligation. I was no good person, and did not want something called sincerity to make me behave well at all times. It felt like lying to myself. I refused to spend my life pretending to be somebody else.

Japanese: 私はやりたいときにやりたいことをやり、優しくしたい時と相手にだけ優しくして、嘘をつきたいときは嘘をついて、素直に話したいときは話す。
English: I did what I wanted when I wanted to do it, showed kindness only when and to whom I wished, lied when I wanted to lie, and spoke honestly when I wanted to speak.

Japanese: それ以外にこの人生をすこしでもマシに生きる方法がわからない。
English: I knew no other way to make this life even slightly more bearable.

Japanese: だから、その時になったら筱喬を見捨ててしまうかもしれないし、こわくなってしまうかもしれないし、気持が醒めているかもしれない。……まあ傍観者として考えると、未来の私にもっとまっとうな人間として振る舞ってほしいという気持はあるし、出来ればみなの期待に確実にこたえる立派な人であってほしいのだけど、過去の実績を考えると、まあ難しいだろう。悲しい。
English: So when the moment came, I might abandon Siu-kiu. I might grow afraid. My feelings might have cooled. ...As a detached observer, I did want the future me to behave like a more decent human being. Ideally, that future me would become an admirable person who unfailingly lived up to everyone’s expectations. Judging from my past performance, however, the prospect seemed poor. How sad.

Japanese: 私は携帯電話を手にとって、電話帳から筱喬の名前を探し出す。
English: I picked up my phone and found Siu-kiu’s name in the contacts.

Japanese: それを見ているだけで、なんだかうっとりとするような良い気持ちになれる。今のその感情に嘘偽りはないのだけれども、今度この相手から電話がかかってきた瞬間、私は、どんな気持で居るだろうか？
English: Merely looking at it gave me a dreamy, wonderful feeling. There was no lie or deception in what I felt now. But the next time that person called me, what would I feel at the very instant the phone began to ring?

Japanese: 何もしたくないし、しなければいけないことについて考えたくもなかったので、ゲームをはじめた。
English: I did not want to do anything, or even think about the things I had to do, so I started a game.

Japanese: 銃を持った兵士を操作して、戦争に参加するゲームだ。味方の兵士たちも、敵の兵士たちも、ネットワークで繋がれた世界の誰かが操作している。どこの国の、どんな年齢の、男か女かもわからない。お互いに銃弾を飛ばして殺し合っている。
English: It was a game in which you controlled a soldier with a gun and took part in a war. Every soldier on both sides was controlled by someone elsewhere in the networked world. You knew neither their country nor their age, not even whether they were male or female. You fired bullets at one another and killed one another.

Japanese: 昔は外国の人とネットでゲームをすると通信の遅れが出てすぐにそうとわかったらしいが、現代ではアパートの隣の部屋のケンちゃんと遊ぶのも、世界の裏側のブラジルのなんちゃらと遊ぶのも、ほとんど区別がつかない。
English: Apparently, playing online with foreigners once produced enough lag to make their location immediately obvious. In the present day, there was virtually no difference between playing with Kenny in the apartment next door and playing with somebody-or-other in Brazil on the other side of the world.

Japanese: ちなみに、この素晴らしい高速回線の費用を払っているのは両親だ。私は学校へも行かず、働きもせず、ひたすら好き勝手にふるまっている毎日なのである。
English: Incidentally, my parents paid for this splendid high-speed connection. I did not attend school or work, and spent every day doing precisely as I pleased.

Japanese: 私はこのゲームが結構得意で、お互い正面から撃ち合うような場面ならまず負けない。相手が有利な地形に陣取った時などに、侵入して崩すのが得意だ。チームの状況にもよるけれど、自分が一回殺されるまでの間に、平均２．８人くらいは殺すことが出来る。上位のクラン戦ならともかく、野良なら大体私のいる方のチームが勝つんじゃないかしら。
English: I was fairly good at the game and almost never lost in a frontal firefight. My specialty was infiltrating and breaking up enemy positions when they had entrenched themselves on favorable terrain. It depended on the team, but on average I could kill about 2.8 people for every time I was killed. At the highest level of clan play, things might be different, but in random matches, the team with me on it generally won.

Japanese: だけれど今日はどうも調子が悪くて、殺したり殺されたり、勝ったり負けたりを繰り返してしまう。
