Japanese: そしてもう動かない、完全に冷たくなったその身体にすがりつき、声を立てて泣いたのである。
English: She clung to the unmoving body, now completely cold, and wept aloud.

Japanese: ひとしきり泣き、そしてまたバットを握って立ち上がったところで彼女は背後に物音を聞いた。
English: After weeping for some time, she gripped the bat and stood again. Then she heard a sound behind her.

Japanese: さっきの大男が戻ってきたのかと思い、彼女は全身を固くする。
English: Believing the large man had returned, she stiffened throughout her body.

Japanese: しかし今は恐怖よりも怒りの方が上回っていた。
English: But now her anger outweighed her fear.

Japanese: バットを振りかぶりながら振り返ると、そこには想像と違った人物がいた。
English: She raised the bat and turned. Someone entirely different stood there.

Japanese: 姿形が全く同じ二人の美しい少女が入り口のそばに立っている。
English: Two beautiful girls, identical in every detail, stood near the entrance.

Japanese: 「何もする気はないわ」
English: “We have no intention of doing anything to you.”

Japanese: 「その死体を見せて」
English: “Show us the body.”

Japanese: 二人は交互にそう言った。
English: They spoke in turn.

Japanese: 彼女たちは張り詰めた表情をしているが、敵意は感じられない。タナベはその静かな口調に促されて、彼女たちのために道を空けた。
English: Their faces were taut, but Tanabe sensed no hostility. Prompted by their quiet voices, she moved aside for them.

Japanese: 「ありがとう」
English: “Thank you.”

Japanese: 「ありがとう」
English: “Thank you.”

Japanese: 二人は軽く頭を下げると、松子に近づく。
English: The two bowed their heads slightly and approached Matsuko.

Japanese: そして二人は両腕が折れ、顔は腫れ上がり、身体のあちこちはガラスが突き刺さって血みどろになり、下半身の衣服は脱がされている無惨なその遺体を見た。
English: They looked upon the mutilated body: both arms broken, the face swollen, glass embedded throughout the blood-soaked flesh, and the clothing removed from the lower body.

Japanese: そして手を伸ばし、その首のあたりに触れる。
English: They reached out and touched her neck.

Japanese: 「冷たいね」
English: “She’s cold.”

Japanese: 「冷たい」
English: “Cold.”

Japanese: 彼女は小さな声で囁きあう。
English: They exchanged the words in whispers.

Japanese: そして、二人の目からは同時に大粒の涙がぽろぽろと落ち、彼女たちはそれを袖で拭った。
English: Large tears fell from both pairs of eyes at once, and the girls wiped them away with their sleeves.

Japanese: 「あなたたち、なんなの？」
English: “Who are you?”

Japanese: タナベはまだバットを構えたまま二人にそう尋ねる。
English: Still holding the bat ready, Tanabe addressed the pair.

Japanese: 二人はゆっくりとタナベを振り返った。
English: The two slowly turned toward her.

Japanese: 「私たちは何者でもないわ」
English: “We are no one.”

Japanese: 一人がそう言い、
English: One of them spoke.

Japanese: 「汐松子とは昔友達だったの」
English: “We used to be friends with Matsuko Shio.”

Japanese: もう一人がそう言った。
English: The other spoke.

Japanese: 良い天気ってわけじゃないが、雨が降ってるわけでもない。
English: It was not what anyone would call fine weather, but at least it was not raining.

Japanese: こう低い雲が垂れ込めていては気持ち晴れやかにとはいかないが、これくらいの空模様ならばまあよしとしなければいけないのは、天気も人生も同じだ。
English: Low clouds like these did little to brighten the heart. Still, with weather as with life, one sometimes had to accept things when they were no worse than this.

Japanese: おれは朝早く起きると自転車に乗って、その日出来たばかりの饅頭を店に届けに行く。ついに完成したグレートホール饅頭はなかなか好評で、知り合いのいくつかの店が棚においてくれることになった。店頭でもそこそこ売れてくれているらしい。
English: I rose early that morning, got on my bicycle, and delivered the day’s freshly made buns to the shops. At last, the finished Great Hole Buns were proving quite popular. Several stores run by people I knew had agreed to give them shelf space, and apparently they were selling reasonably well.

Japanese: まだ大ヒット商品というわけにはいかないけれど、なかなか順調だと思わないか？　このまま売り上げが伸びれば、もっと従業員も雇えるようになるし、生産体制も強化出来る。人を増やすときは、なるべく他で雇ってはもらえなさそうなタイプBを選んで雇うって決めてるんだ。そしたらおれは念願の『社長』を名乗れるだろう。
English: They were not a smash hit yet, but don’t you think things were going well? If sales kept growing, I could hire more employees and strengthen our production system. I had already decided that when I expanded the staff, I would give preference to Type Bs who were unlikely to find work anywhere else. Then at last I could claim my long-coveted title of ‘president.’

Japanese: 『見土社長』……ああ、なんて甘美な響きだ！
English: ‘President Mido’... Ah, what a delicious sound!

Japanese: といっても、今はやっと売り上げだけで従業員の給料が払えるようになって来たって段階なんだけれどね。でもそれでも、最低限遊びじゃなくて仕事だと言えるスタートラインには立てた気がするよ。
English: Admittedly, we had only just reached the point where sales alone could cover our employees’ wages. Even so, I felt we had at least reached the starting line, where I could call this work rather than play.

Japanese: 少しずつでもいいから、とにかくこのままだ。このまま売り上げを伸ばし続けないと。
English: A little at a time was fine. We simply had to keep going like this. We had to keep raising our sales.

Japanese: さて、そうして一通りの配達が終わって工場、と呼ぶにはちょっと大げさな気がするようなこぢんまりとしたおれたちのアジトに帰って来ると、ちょうどコンタが出て来たところで、路上で出くわすこととなった。
English: Once I finished my rounds, I returned to our little hideout—calling it a factory still felt somewhat grandiose—and happened to meet Konta just as he came out into the street.

Japanese: 「道夫君」
English: “Michio.”

Japanese: おやと思ったのは、なんだか切迫した顔つきで、喋り方も焦っている感じだったからだ。
English: I knew something was wrong because his face looked desperate and there was a hurried edge to his voice.

Japanese: 仲間がこういう顔をしているとドキッとする。
English: Seeing one of my companions with a face like that always made my heart skip.

Japanese: 我々タイプBにはいつ何時どんなトラブルが発生するかわからないし、しかも現在は爺さんたちが何か陰謀を張り巡らしている。おれたちの店の人間は全員タイプBで、そして八龍会の所属だ。それこそ、考え得る限りどんな最低のアクシデントが発生してもおかしくない。
English: For us Type Bs, trouble of any kind could strike at any time. Worse, the Elders were presently spinning some sort of plot. Every person at our shop was Type B, and every one of us belonged to Hachiryukai. Quite literally, the worst accident I could imagine could happen at any moment.

Japanese: 「どうしたんだい？　血相なんか変えて」
English: “What happened? You look frantic.”

Japanese: こういうときは落ち着かせるのがおれの役目だ。
English: At moments like this, it was my job to calm him down.

Japanese: ゆったりと微笑してみせて、彼の肩をぽんと叩く。
English: I gave him an easy smile and clapped him on the shoulder.

Japanese: 「レナちゃんが、キちゃったみたいなんだ」
English: “Looks like Rena’s been Hit.”

Japanese: 「レナが？」
English: “Rena?”

Japanese: それは我々の仲間である十九才のシングルマザーで、飲食店のウェイトレスとかけもちで働いてくれている。
English: She was one of our companions, a nineteen-year-old single mother who worked for us while also waiting tables at a restaurant.

Japanese: 元々溝平B団地に住んでいた子だが、十六才のときに、すでにいた子供を連れて街中に引っ越している。
English: She had originally lived in the Mizohira B Housing Complex, but at sixteen she moved into the city with the child she already had.

Japanese: 「向こうの店で働いてる時にキタんだよ。工場の固定回線に向こうの店長さんから電話があった」
English: “She got Hit while she was working at the other place. Their manager called us on the factory landline.”

Japanese: コンタがキちゃっただの、キタだのと言っているのは、つまりタイプBの症状が発露して異常な行動をとってしまったということだ。
English: When Konta said that Rena had been ‘Hit,’ he meant that her Type B symptoms had manifested and made her behave erratically.

Japanese: 直接的な表現を避けるときは、昔からこういう風にそれを表現している。
English: Type Bs had expressed it this way for years whenever we wanted to avoid saying it directly.

Japanese: 「そうか」
English: “I see.”

Japanese: タイプBとして生まれたからには避けられないものだけれど、仲間に起きると胸が重苦しくなるな。
English: It was something no one born Type B could escape, but when it happened to a companion, my heart always grew heavy.

Japanese: レナはもう去年に発症自体はしており、病院に通って幻覚や幻聴を消す薬を飲みながら生活をしていた。
English: Rena’s symptoms had first manifested the previous year. Since then, she had been living on medication from the hospital to suppress her auditory and visual hallucinations.

Japanese: もちろんそれは症状を和らげるためのもので、それによって回復するわけじゃない。だから、さらに悪化、進行してそれが効かなくなったんだ。
English: The medicine could only ease the symptoms; it could not make her recover. Her condition had progressed still further, until the drugs no longer worked.

Japanese: 「病院に行くつもり？」
English: “Are you taking her to the hospital?”

Japanese: 「もう病院には行った後なんだって。保険にも入ってないし、もし入院となったら治療費が払えないから、注射だけしてもらって自宅に帰って来たんだ。店の人達が送り届けてくれたんだけど、彼らも店に戻らなくちゃいけないから、おれが後はバトンタッチしようかと」
English: “She’s already been. She doesn’t have insurance, and if they admitted her, she couldn’t pay the bill. So they only gave her an injection and sent her home. People from the restaurant brought her back, but they have to return to work. I was going to take over from them.”

Japanese: レナは小さな娘と二人暮らしだ。付き添ってくれた店の人が帰ったら、その娘一人で錯乱した母の面倒みなくちゃいけなくなる。それはどう考えても無理ってもんだろう。
English: Rena lived alone with her young daughter. Once the restaurant staff left, that little girl would have to care for her delirious mother all by herself. That was obviously impossible.

Japanese: 「わかった。じゃあ、おれも行こう」
English: “All right. I’ll come too.”

Japanese: 自転車の後ろにコンタを乗せて、おれたちはレナの家へ向かった。
English: I sat Konta on the back of my bicycle, and we set off for Rena’s home.

Japanese: 「こんなんよく有ることだけどさ。やっぱり、自分達より年下がそこまで悪化しちゃうってのは、気持ちが暗くなるね」
English: “This sort of thing happens all the time, but it’s still depressing when someone younger than us gets this bad.”

Japanese: 後ろのコンタの言葉には、まったくおれも同感だ。
English: I agreed completely with Konta’s words behind me.

Japanese: でも、おれたちの気持ちが暗くなったって仕方がないからね。
English: But allowing ourselves to sink into gloom would not help anyone.

Japanese: それに、タイプBの症状ってのは、強いストレスや暗く抑圧された感情に誘発されやすいんだ。だから、おれたちはいつだって明るく、楽しく、夢をみていかなくちゃいけない。だから、みんなをそういう気持ちにさせてやりたいんだおれは。
English: Besides, Type B symptoms were easily triggered by severe stress and dark, suppressed emotions. That was why we had to stay bright, enjoy our lives, and go on dreaming. And that was why I wanted to give everyone else the chance to feel the same way.

Japanese: レナの家に上がり込むと、彼女はベッドに縛り付けられていた。両手両足は大事の時に広げられてベッド柵にロープで結びつけられて、体幹はタオルで巻いた上でロープをベッドごとぐるぐる巻きにされている。
English: When we entered Rena’s apartment, we found her tied to the bed. Her arms and legs had been spread-eagled and roped to the bed rails. Towels were wrapped around her torso, and more rope had been wound again and again around her and the bed together.

Japanese: この街では暴れて手がつけられなくなったタイプB発症者によくやる措置だ。
English: People in this city often resorted to such measures when a symptomatic Type B became violent and impossible to control.

Japanese: 付き添ってくれた二人の男性店員もY地区の出身で、身内にタイプBがいて扱いに慣れているのだと言う。
English: The two male restaurant employees who had accompanied her were also from Y District. They told us they had Type Bs in their own families and were accustomed to handling such situations.

Japanese: 「いやあ、ここに来るまでは大人しかったんですけど、部屋に入った途端スイッチがはいったみたいに暴れましてね。いまは、薬が効いたのかすこし大人しくなりました」
English: “She was quiet enough until we got here. The moment we stepped into the room, though, it was as if someone flipped a switch. She went wild. Maybe the medicine’s finally doing something, because she’s calmed down a little now.”

Japanese: そう笑った店員の腕にはひっかき傷が出来ていた。押さえつけるときに傷つけられたに違いない。
English: The employee laughed as he spoke, though his arm was covered with scratches. Rena must have given them to him when they pinned her down.

Japanese: そして部屋も、その格闘を物語るように、棚が倒れて小物が床に散らかり、カーテンが引っ張られたのか、半分レールから外れてぶらさがっている。
English: The room testified to the struggle. A shelf had fallen, scattering small objects across the floor, and a curtain hung loose with half of it torn from the rail.

Japanese: レナ本人はじっと天井を見つめたまま、口元で独り言をブツブツとつぶやき、そして時々「あっははは」と声を立てて笑った。典型的なタイプBの症状が出ている。
English: Rena herself stared fixedly at the ceiling, muttering under her breath and occasionally bursting into a loud “Ah-ha-ha-ha.” To my eyes, she was showing the typical symptoms of a Type B episode.

Japanese: 「じゃあすいませんけど、帰ります。三人もシフトから抜けちゃってるから、店がきっとメチャクチャになってるんで」
English: “Sorry, but we’d better get back. Three of us left the shift, so the restaurant must be in chaos by now.”

Japanese: 「あ、ありがとうございます！」
English: “Oh, thank you very much!”

Japanese: 部屋を出て行こうとするふたりの店員におれは腰を折って頭を下げた。
English: I bent deeply at the waist and bowed to the two employees as they made for the door.

Japanese: 「いえ。レナちゃん、よろしくお願いしますね」
English: “It’s nothing. Please take care of Rena for us.”

Japanese: 店員達はさわやかに笑いながら出て行く。
English: They smiled cheerfully and left.

Japanese: 「道夫君、このレナなんだけどさ……」
English: “Michio, about Rena...”

Japanese: 「ちょっと、その前に」
English: “Wait. Before that.”

Japanese: おれはそう言って、部屋の隅の方で膝小僧を抱えている少女の前に座り込んだ。
English: I crossed the room and crouched before the little girl sitting in a corner with her knees drawn to her chest.

Japanese: レナが十四才で生んだその子供は、今年で五才になった。髪の毛はモジャモジャの天然パーマで、肌は浅黒い。それらの特徴は母のレナにはなく、誰も知らない父から受け継いだのだろう。
English: Rena had given birth to her at fourteen, and the child was now five. Her hair was a mass of natural curls, and her skin was dark. Rena possessed neither trait; presumably they came from the unidentified father.

Japanese: 彼女の肩は小さく震えている。母親の変貌に怯えているんだ。
English: The girl’s little shoulders trembled. Her mother’s transformation had terrified her.

Japanese: 彼女の服は清潔で、髪の毛からはシャンプーの良い匂いがする。部屋のあちこちには、数字やひらがな、アルファベットを学ぶための張り紙がしている。部屋のいろんなものに、子供が好みそうなこまごまとした飾り付けがされている。
English: Her clothes were clean, and her hair smelled pleasantly of shampoo. Sheets for learning numbers, hiragana, and the alphabet had been posted throughout the room, while all sorts of little decorations a child might like had been added to objects everywhere.

Japanese: 仕事に行く前、そう、ほんの数時間前までのレナは、やさしくて子供の面倒を良く見る素晴らしい母親だったんだ。その素晴らしさは、おれたちもよく知っている。
English: Before leaving for work—only a few hours ago—Rena had been a kind and wonderful mother who took excellent care of her child. We knew very well how wonderful she was.

Japanese: それが、今は失われて、完全な別人になってしまった。
English: Now all of that seemed lost, and she had become like a wholly different person.

Japanese: おれはしゃがみこんでその頭に手を置いた。彼女はびくりと驚き、ゆっくり顔をあげて警戒の目でおれを見る。その目のまわりには、黒い痣が出来、顔中が涙で濡れていた。
English: I crouched down and placed a hand upon the girl’s head. She gave a frightened start, then slowly raised her face and looked at me warily. A black bruise ringed one eye, and tears had soaked her entire face.

Japanese: これもレナがやったのか？　だとすれば、生まれて初めて母親に殴られたに違いない。
English: Had Rena done this too? If so, this must have been the first time in the child’s life that her mother had struck her.

Japanese: 胸が痛くなる。おれはもう、とりわけ子供とか老人には弱いんだ。
English: My heart ached. I had always been especially weak where children and old people were concerned.

Japanese: おれはその頭をなでてやりながら、
English: Stroking her head, I asked,

Japanese: 「大変だったね。おれのことは覚えてる？」
English: “You’ve had a hard day. Do you remember me?”

Japanese: すると彼女は頷き、
English: She nodded.

Japanese: 「みっちゃん」
English: “Mitchan.”

Japanese: 震える唇で言った。
English: She spoke through trembling lips.

Japanese: 「いやあ、こんな美人に名前を覚えて貰えて嬉しいよ」
English: “Well, I’m honored that such a beautiful lady remembers my name.”

Japanese: さすがに、こんな冗談では今の彼女はクスリともしない。
English: Even that joke could not coax the smallest smile from her now.

Japanese: 「今日は大変だったね。怖かったでしょう？」
English: “Today was hard, wasn’t it? Were you scared?”

Japanese: おれの言葉に彼女はゆっくり首を横にふる。
English: She slowly shook her head.

Japanese: 「こわくない……。おかあさんのことすきだから、ぜんせんこわくないの……」
English: “I’m not scared... I love Mommy, so I’m not scared at all...”

Japanese: ああ、もうなんて素晴らしいことを言う子供なんだろう！　おれは涙が出ちゃいそうだよ。
English: Oh, what a wonderful thing for a child to say! I nearly burst into tears.

Japanese: 「そうだね。おれたちも、おかあさんのこと好きだから、平気だよ」
English: “That’s right. We love your mommy too, so everything will be all right.”

Japanese: おれはくしゃっと彼女の頭を撫でると、
English: I gave her hair another vigorous ruffle.

Japanese: 「じゃあ、今日きみはたくさん頑張ったから、向こうの部屋で休んでよう。お母さんのことは、みっちゃんたちが見てるから心配しないでいいよ」
English: “You’ve worked very hard today, so go and rest in the other room. Mitchan and the others will watch your mommy. You don’t need to worry.”

Japanese: そしておれはその子を隣の部屋につれてゆく。寂しくないように棚から玩具や絵本を取り出して彼女の前に並べ、そして部屋に戻ってきた。
English: I took her into the next room, arranged toys and picture books from the shelves before her so that she would not feel lonely, and returned.

Japanese: 一人で残すのは心配ではあったが、それ以上に今の母親を見せたくはなかった。
English: I worried about leaving her alone, but I wanted even less to make her watch her mother in this state.

Japanese: そして、これからは大人の時間だ。
English: Now it was grown-up time.

Japanese: 「状態はどうだい？」
English: “How is she?”

Japanese: ベッドの側でレナと何か会話をしていたコンタに尋ねると、彼は難しい顔で首を横に振る。
English: Konta had been trying to speak with Rena beside the bed. When I asked, he shook his head grimly.

Japanese: 「反応はあるけど、会話は成立しない」
English: “She responds, but you can’t have a conversation with her.”

Japanese: 「そうか」
English: “I see.”

Japanese: 言いながらおれも近づき、彼女の様子を見る。
English: I approached as I answered and looked her over for myself.

Japanese: レナは汗をかき、額に黒い前髪がはりついていた。美人という感じではないが、ほっそりして愛嬌のある顔立ちをしており、みんなに好かれている。
English: Rena was sweating, her black bangs plastered to her forehead. She was not what one would call beautiful, but she had a slender, charming face and was liked by everyone.

Japanese: 普段は真っ黒なその瞳はぎらぎらとした金色に輝き、落ち着きなくぴくぴくと眼球が動いていた。
English: Her ordinarily black irises now shone a glaring gold, and her eyes darted restlessly from side to side.

Japanese: そしておれの顔を認めると、
English: When she recognized my face,

Japanese: 「ああ、みっちゃんじゃない！　こんにちは！」
English: “Oh, it’s Mitchan! Hello!”

Japanese: 普段の彼女ではありえない異常に高いテンションでそう言い、手を動かそうとしてロープがピンと張り、柵がガシャッと音を立てる。彼女はそのロープの方を不思議そうに見る。
English: Her excitement was impossibly high for the Rena we knew. She tried to move her hand, drawing the rope taut and making the rail clatter, then stared at the rope in puzzlement.

Japanese: 「何だか知らないけど、これで縛られてるの。変でしょ？　とってくれない？」
English: “I don’t know why, but I’m all tied up. Isn’t that strange? Will you take these off?”

Japanese: 彼女は子供みたいに唇をとがらせ、縛られた手を動かせる範囲で振る。あまりに強く動かしすぎて、ロープが触れた手首がすりむけている。本来は間にハンカチなどを挟ませていたようだが、それはもう落ちていた。
English: She pouted like a child and waved her bound hand as far as the rope allowed. She had pulled so violently that the rope had abraded her wrist. Someone appeared to have placed a handkerchief beneath it, but that had already fallen away.

Japanese: 「そう言うなよなー。これ、お前を保護するためにやってるんだぜ。落ち着いたらすぐとれるんだから」
English: “Come on, don’t be like that. We only did this to protect you. We’ll take it off as soon as you calm down.”

Japanese: おれはそう言いながら、ハンカチを元通りにしようとその腕に触れたが、
English: As I spoke, I touched her arm to replace the handkerchief.

Japanese: 「やめて！　さわらないで！」
English: “Stop! Don’t touch me!”

Japanese: 彼女が体中をもの凄い力でよじって怒鳴り声を上げたので、おれは慌てて手を引っ込めた。
English: She twisted with astonishing force and screamed, making me snatch my hand away.

Japanese: 「ごめんね、怒る気はなかったの。でもそれはいけないのよ。私は国に帰らなきゃけないんだから」
English: “I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to be angry. But you mustn’t do that. I have to return to my country.”
“Your country?”

Japanese: おれが言ったが、彼女はそれに反応を示さずに一方的に話を続ける。
English: She gave no response to my question and continued talking at me.

Japanese: 「いつまでこの生活が続くの？　私は姫なのに。どうして国に帰らしてくれないのかしら。私をこんなところに縛り付けて……」
English: “How long is this life going to last? I’m a princess. Why won’t anyone let me return to my country? Keeping me tied up in a place like this...”

Japanese: 彼女は焦点の合わぬ目であらぬ方向を見つめて、つぶやき続けている。
English: Her unfocused eyes stared into empty space while she continued to murmur.

Japanese: 「嗚呼、本当にいやらしい！　あなた、きのうの夜私に乱暴したでしょ？　拒んだのに、何度も何度も……。そして嘘ばっかりついて……こんな不誠実な人、みたことがないわ」
English: “Oh, you’re disgusting! You raped me last night, didn’t you? I refused, but you did it over and over... And you do nothing but lie... I have never known anyone so faithless.”

Japanese: 完全に精神が妄想に囚われてしまっている。
English: Her mind seemed wholly imprisoned in delusion.

Japanese: どうしてこんなに苦労人で、頑張ってる女の子がこんなに若く発症しなければいけないんだろう？
English: Why did a girl who had known so much hardship and fought so hard have to develop symptoms this young?

Japanese: 「レナ」
English: “Rena.”

Japanese: コンタがそう呼びかけると、チラとこちらを見たが、またぶつぶつと一方的な妄想を語り、その合間には脈絡のない笑顔を浮かべる。
English: When Konta called her name, she glanced toward us, but soon resumed the one-sided stream I could only take for delusion, smiling at random moments without any connection to what she said.

Japanese: 「注射が効いてないね」
English: “The injection hasn’t worked.”

Japanese: コンタはそう溜息をついた。
English: Konta sighed.

Japanese: 「道夫君、おれ今『ネオ』を持ってるんだ。こいつにつかってもいいか？」
English: “Michio, I have some ‘Neo’ with me. Can I give it to her?”

Japanese: 真剣な顔をしている。おれが『ネオ・ローズ』に対して否定的なことを知っているからだ。
English: His expression was serious. He knew how strongly I opposed ‘Neo Rose.’

Japanese: 「これじゃあどんな治療も効かないぜ。レナには家族も親戚もいないから、ほったらかしていたら親子共々のたれ死にだ。助けたいなら、どこか施設に入れるしかない。レナも、娘もね。……それよりは『ネオ』を使ったほうがいいんじゃないか？」
English: “No other treatment is doing anything. Rena has no family or relatives, so if we leave things as they are, she and her daughter will both die in a ditch. If we want to help, our only choice is to put them in an institution—Rena and the girl both. Wouldn’t using ‘Neo’ be better than that?”

Japanese: おれはすぐには答えられない。
English: I could not answer at once.

Japanese: コンタの言っていることはわかる。でも、おれローズの件がどうしても頭をよぎるんだ。あの時もタイプBの症状を改善することが出来ると、爆発的に流行ったが、その結果は到底「ローズを使わないよりはマシ」とは言えない結果を招いた。
English: I understood Konta’s argument, but I could not keep myself from thinking about Rose. That drug too had spread explosively on the promise that it could relieve Type B symptoms. Yet the result was hardly something anyone could call ‘better than not using Rose.’

Japanese: その頃おれはガキだったが、町中を覆っていた異常な雰囲気は肌ではっきりと感じ取れた。
English: I was only a child at the time, but I had felt the abnormal atmosphere smothering the whole city upon my skin.

Japanese: 「前のやつとは違うんだよ。もう使い始めて二ヶ月以上経つけど、なんのトラブルも出ていない。……そりゃまだ早すぎるっていう道夫君の考えもわかるけど、安全だってはっきりわかるまで、レナをこのままにしておけるのか？　娘はどうする？」
English: “This isn’t the old drug. People have been using it for more than two months now without a single problem. ...I know you think that’s still much too soon, Michio. But can we leave Rena like this until we know for certain that it’s safe? What about her daughter?”

Japanese: コンタも感情的になっていた。彼なりに仲間のことを心から思ってそう提言しているんだ。それはおれにもわかっている。
English: Konta had become emotional. He was making this proposal because, in his own way, he cared for one of our own from the bottom of his heart. I understood that.

Japanese: 「わかった」
English: “All right.”

Japanese: おれが頷くと、コンタはすぐに上着のポケットから道具を取り出し、注射の準備をはじめる。
English: When I nodded, Konta immediately took his equipment from his jacket pocket and began preparing the injection.

Japanese: 「静脈注射用のアンプルを使おう。落ち着いたら今夜にでもデポを打つ」
English: “I’ll use an ampoule for intravenous injection. Once she’s calm, we’ll give her the depot formulation tonight.”

Japanese: アルバイトとして老人たちの下で『ネオ・ローズ』の販売を手伝っているコンタが薬の種類に詳しいのは当然だろうが、元薬物中毒者なのでその手つきも慣れている。
English: Konta helped the Elders sell Neo Rose as a part-time job, so naturally he knew its formulations. As a former drug addict, his hands were practiced as well.

Japanese: アンプルはちょうどこけしの頭が尖ったようなガラス瓶である。コンタはこれを片手で握り、まず軽く回して頭部にたまった薬液を身体の部分に落とす。次にアルコール綿でアンプル全体を拭いたあと、その綿をこけしの首の部分に指で押し当てつつ、もう片方の手でアンプルの頭を掴んで横に力を加える。パキリと音がしてこけしが首の部分で切断される。
English: The ampoule was a little glass vessel shaped like a kokeshi doll with a pointed head. Konta held it in one hand and gently turned it, letting the liquid trapped in the head run down into the body. After wiping the ampoule all over with an alcohol swab, he pressed the cotton against the doll’s neck with one finger, grasped the head in his other hand, and pushed sideways. With a snap, the kokeshi broke at the neck.

Japanese: そのアンプルをテーブルの上に置くと、個別包装された使い捨ての針付き注射器を取り出し、開封する。
English: He set the ampoule on the table, took out an individually wrapped disposable syringe with a needle attached, and opened the package.

Japanese: そして注射針をアンプルに触れないよう首の部分から差し込み、ゆっくりと押子を引くと注射筒のなかに透明な薬液が吸い出されてゆく。
English: Taking care not to touch the ampoule with the needle, he inserted it through the neck and slowly drew back the plunger. The clear liquid rose into the barrel.

Japanese: 薬液を吸い出したところで、注射器を上向きにして窓からの光にすかす。下の方に気泡が入っていたらしく、指先ではじいてそれを上に追い出す。その後で、ゆっくり押子を押し上げて注射筒上部にたまった空気をすべて吐き出させる。
English: Once he had drawn up the medicine, he pointed the syringe upward and held it against the light from the window. An air bubble appeared to have collected near the bottom. He flicked the barrel with a fingertip until it rose, then slowly advanced the plunger and expelled all the air gathered at the top.

Japanese: 普通のヤク中はもっといい加減な手順だが、彼は看護師の女とつき合っていたとかで、ある程度は事故の少ない正しいやり方を踏襲しているらしい。そしてそれを、販売した客にも教えているそうだ。
English: The average addict was much sloppier. Konta had apparently once dated a nurse, however, and so followed a reasonably proper, less accident-prone procedure. I heard he taught the same procedure to his customers.

Japanese: コンタはそしておれを振り返った。
English: Konta turned to me.

Japanese: 「道夫君、おさえてくれる？」
English: “Michio, will you hold her down?”

Japanese: おれは無言で頷き、ベッドに腰をおろすと、
English: I nodded silently and sat on the bed.

Japanese: 「レナ、不安で落ち着かないだろ？　それが見ててもわかるから注射をするよ。ちょっとチクっとするけれど、これでこわいのなくなるからな」
English: “Rena, you’re anxious and can’t settle down. We can see that, so we’re going to give you an injection. It will sting a little, but then you won’t be frightened anymore.”

Japanese: 「近寄らないで！　変態！　あっちに行け！」
English: “Don’t come near me! Pervert! Get away!”

Japanese: 彼女は身体をよじって手足をばたつかせる。
English: She twisted her body and thrashed her arms and legs.

Japanese: 「わるいな。ちょっと我慢してくれ」
English: “I’m sorry. Bear with it for a moment.”

Japanese: おれは柔道の袈裟固めのような格好でレナの上半身を押さえつける。
English: I pinned down Rena’s upper body in something like a judo scarf hold.

Japanese: 「やめて！　殺される！　たすけてえええ！」
English: “Stop! They’re going to kill me! Help meee!”

Japanese: 金色の目になってしまうと、女でもものすごい力を発揮する。すでに暴れ続けて疲労し、病院で鎮静剤を打たれているにもかかわらず、まるで暴れ馬の背にのっているように彼女は激しく動き、おれはその上でぐらぐらと揺れていた。
English: Once a woman’s eyes turned gold, even she could exercise extraordinary strength. Rena was already exhausted from struggling and had received a sedative at the hospital, yet she bucked so violently that it felt as though I were riding an untamed horse. I rocked precariously upon her back.

Japanese: このままでは振り落とされてしまう。
English: At this rate, she would throw me off.

Japanese: やむなくおれも意識を昂ぶらせ、タイプBの力を解放した。
English: With no other choice, I deliberately worked myself into an agitated state and released my Type B strength.

Japanese: 興奮状態や、忘我状態に陥るとタイプBは自然と目が金色になってしまうが、ある程度の才能と訓練があればそれ以外の場面でも任意の瞬間に発動させることが出来る。
English: A Type B’s eyes turned gold naturally upon entering a state of excitement or frenzy. With a measure of talent and training, however, one could also activate the ability voluntarily at any chosen moment.

Japanese: 軍隊などのタイプB部隊には必須のスキルらしいが、コントロール出来るようになると発症自体を遅らせられるそうなので、おれはみんなに訓練を勧めているのだけれど、習得するのは案外難しいようだ。おれは小さい時に老人たちに指導されて、この能力を身につけた。
English: Apparently that skill was mandatory in military Type B units, and people said that learning such control could delay onset itself. I encouraged everyone to train, but mastering it seemed surprisingly difficult. The Elders had instructed me as a child, allowing me to acquire the ability.

Japanese: これでこちらの筋力も増強されるが、体重が増えるわけではないので完全におさえつけるのは難しい。それでも上になったまま彼女の動きを封じていると、相手は段々疲労してゆく。
English: My strength increased, but my body did not grow any heavier, so pinning her down completely remained difficult. Even so, as I stayed on top and blocked her movement, she gradually exhausted herself.

Japanese: 「レナ、大丈夫だから。大丈夫」
English: “Rena, you’re all right. Everything’s all right.”

Japanese: おれは彼女の身体にぴったり密着しながら耳元にそう囁く。
English: I pressed myself tightly against her and whispered into her ear.

Japanese: 彼女は汗ばみ、体中から女のにおいが立ち上っている。
English: Her skin was damp with sweat, and the scent of a woman rose from her entire body.

Japanese: 「はあ……はあ……」
English: “Ahh... ahh...”

Japanese: レナは荒い呼吸を付き、やがて完全に動きを止めた。
English: Rena’s breath came in ragged gasps. At last she stopped moving entirely.

Japanese: するとコンタは近づき、レナに腕を伸ばさせると、その内側をアルコール綿でさする。何もしなくても、血管がうかんでいる。
English: Konta approached, pulled Rena’s arm straight, and rubbed the inside with an alcohol swab. Her veins already stood out without any prompting.

Japanese: 「刺すぞ」
English: “Needle going in.”

Japanese: そう声をかけると、コンタは素早く血管に針を刺し、ゆっくりと薬剤を押し込む。
English: After warning her, Konta swiftly inserted the needle into a vein and slowly injected the drug.

Japanese: すべて投与したところで針を抜き、血がじんわりとにじむ傷口にアルコール綿を押し当てた。
English: Once he had administered all of it, he removed the needle and pressed the swab against the puncture where blood had begun to seep.

Japanese: 「もう大丈夫」
English: “All done.”

Japanese: コンタの合図でおれはレナの身体の上を離れる。
English: At Konta’s signal, I climbed off Rena’s body.

Japanese: 彼女はぐったりとして、天井をぼんやり見つめていた。その口元は小さく動き、何か独り言を囁き続けている。
English: She lay limp, staring vaguely at the ceiling. Her lips continued to move as she whispered something under her breath.

Japanese: 「五分くらいで効いてくる」
English: “It should begin working in about five minutes.”

Japanese: コンタは後片付けをしながらそう言った。
English: Konta spoke while cleaning up.

Japanese: 「これで元通りのレナになるはずだ」
English: “This should restore Rena to normal.”

Japanese: 「元通りね……」
English: “Restore her to normal...”

Japanese: おれが特別な意味もなく呟いた言葉に、コンタは気を悪くしたようだった。
English: I had attached no special meaning to the echo, but Konta appeared to take offense.

Japanese: 「道夫君。そろそろこの現実を受け入れないといけない日が来てるんだと思うよ。道夫君が考えているように、事業をおこして生活を立て直そうってのはすごくまっとうで、最終的にはそれを目指すべきだけどさあ。でも今はそれよりも……」
English: “Michio, I think the day has come when we have to accept this reality. Trying to rebuild our lives by starting a business, the way you want to, is perfectly sound, and ultimately it’s where we should be headed. But right now, more than that...”

Japanese: 「わかったコンタ」
English: “I understand, Konta.”

Japanese: 彼の言葉を遮るって、
English: Interrupting him, I said,

Japanese: 「いろいろと心配させて済まない。その話はあとで聞くよ」
English: “I’m sorry I’ve made you worry about so much. I’ll hear you out later.”

Japanese: おれは立ち上がりドアを開けて隣の部屋へ入った。
English: I rose, opened the door, and entered the next room.

Japanese: そこでは娘が広げてやった玩具や絵本に手をつけずに座り込んでおり、不安げな目でおれを見上げる。
English: The girl still sat without touching any of the toys or picture books I had spread before her. She looked up at me anxiously.

Japanese: 「一人にしてごめんね。もうすぐ、いつものお母さんが帰ってくるからな」
English: “I’m sorry I left you alone. Your usual mommy will be back soon.”

Japanese: そしておれは人形をひとつ手にとって、彼女の前でふざけてみせた。
English: I picked up one of the dolls and made it act silly for her.

Japanese: 薬は１０分ほどで効果を現し、レナは普段の落ち着きを取り戻した。
English: The medicine took effect in approximately ten minutes, and Rena regained her usual composure.

Japanese: 「ごめんなさい。取り乱してしまって」
English: “I’m sorry. I lost control of myself.”

Japanese: ベッドへの拘束が解けたレナはロープの跡がつく手首をさすりながら謝った。
English: Freed from the ropes, she rubbed the marks upon her wrists as she apologized.

Japanese: その顔つきや物言いは先ほど狂乱していた時とはまるで別人で、すっかり憑き物が落ちたようになっている。
English: Her expression and manner of speech were completely different from the frenzy of moments before. It was as though some possessing spirit had left her.

Japanese: これがこの薬の力か。
English: So this was the power of the drug.

Japanese: ローズの時もそうだった。人格が完全に荒廃し、言葉もろくにあやつれず、ほとんど動物みたいな行動しかとれなかった重病人でも、薬を打った途端晴れやかな顔で歩き始めてしまうのだから、それを目の当たりにした人間ならば誰もが奇跡の薬だと叫ぶだろうね。
English: Rose had been the same. Even gravely ill people whose personalities had completely deteriorated, who could scarcely use language and behaved little better than animals, would receive the drug and immediately begin walking about with radiant faces. Anyone who witnessed it would have called the substance miraculous.

Japanese: レナの目はまだ金色だが、これもやはりローズで症状を抑えたときと同じ現象だ。この薬の作用は、精神は正常に戻すが目の色は戻さず、向上した身体能力もそのままなんだ。つまり、症状が去り、メリットだけが残るという寸法だ。
English: Rena’s eyes remained gold, just as they had when Rose suppressed the symptoms. The drug returned the mind to normal without restoring the color of the eyes, and it left the enhanced physical abilities intact. In other words, the symptoms vanished and only the advantages remained.

Japanese: ローズの場合は猛烈な副作用と依存性があったが、ネオの方はそれがないという。その触れ込みが本当ならば、今度こそ本当に奇跡の薬があらわれたと言うことになる。
English: Rose had caused terrible side effects and dependence, but Neo supposedly did neither. If that claim was true, a genuinely miraculous drug had finally appeared.

Japanese: この街はタイプBや特質変異のあるタイプAへの偏見が少ないと、世間では言われている。
English: The wider world considered this city relatively free of prejudice against Type Bs and Type As with trait mutations.

Japanese: 確かにそれはある一面では間違いじゃない。タイプBはありふれているし、他の場所みたいにタイプBだってバレただけで魔女狩りみたいにつるし上げられることはない。
English: In one respect, that was true. Type Bs were commonplace here, and unlike elsewhere, no one was subjected to a witch hunt merely for being found out as Type B.

Japanese: だからって、まるきり平等に扱われるというわけでもない。差別用語はよそよりももっと頻繁に、そして気軽に使われるし、給料で差をつけられるのも当たり前だ。そういった差別はされる方もする方も当たり前になっているから、みな慣れてしまっただけだ。
English: That did not mean they received equal treatment. Slurs were used more frequently and more casually than elsewhere, while wage discrimination was taken for granted. Both those who discriminated and those subjected to it had come to regard such treatment as ordinary. Everyone was simply accustomed to it.

Japanese: もっとも、これはタイプBだから差別する、というよりも、基本的にこの街は弱者や能力のないものに対してシビアだということかもしれない。タイプBというのはやはりハンディキャップと見なされ、安く買いたたかれる。はっきり言って、身体障害者や、人種的なマイノリティも”平等に差別される”。
English: Then again, perhaps the city did not discriminate specifically against Type Bs so much as deal harshly with anyone weak or incapable. Being Type B was still regarded as a handicap, and employers could buy our labor cheaply. To put it bluntly, people with physical disabilities and members of racial minorities were ‘equally discriminated against.’

Japanese: こういった構造はノーマルには気づきにくいだろう。リョウのような聡明なやつでも、そのあたりを肌では理解していないように思う。
English: That structure was probably difficult for Normals to notice. Even someone as intelligent as Ryo did not seem to understand it in his bones.

Japanese: ましてや発症したタイプBなんか、人間扱いされなくても文句は言えない。
English: A symptomatic Type B, in particular, could hardly object even if no one treated that person as human.

Japanese: 『ネオ・ローズ』がなければ、レナのように身寄りのない人間など生きるゴミのようにしか扱われなかったろう。
English: Without ‘Neo Rose,’ someone like Rena who had no family would probably have been treated as nothing more than living refuse.

Japanese: この薬がもたらす奇跡というのはつまりそういうことだ。
English: That, in other words, was the miracle this medicine performed.

Japanese: 「レナ。症状が治ったわけじゃない。これからが大事なんだ」
English: “Rena, your symptoms haven’t been cured. What happens from here is what matters.”

Japanese: コンタは穏やかにそう話す。
English: Konta spoke gently.

Japanese: 彼が今使った薬は効き目が出るのは早いが効果の持続は短い。これからずっと薬に頼って症状を抑え続けるには、持続性の注射を使うべきで、それをどこで手に入れいつ使ったらいいのかを、彼は詳しく説明した。
English: The medicine he had just used took effect quickly but did not last long. If she meant to rely upon medication from now on and keep suppressing her symptoms, Konta said, she should use the long-acting injection instead. He explained in detail where she could obtain it and when she ought to use it.

Japanese: レナは神妙な顔で頷きながら聞いていた。
English: Rena listened with a grave face, nodding as he spoke.

Japanese: 「ホントに、みんなに迷惑かけちゃって……。私、これでお店もクビかしら？」
English: “I’ve caused so much trouble for everyone... Do you think the restaurant will fire me?”

Japanese: おかしくなっていた頃の記憶はあるらしく、彼女は顔を顰める。
English: Apparently she remembered at least part of the episode. Her face twisted with pain.

Japanese: 「そおんなわけないよ！　レナみたいなとびきりの看板娘をクビになんかしやしないさ。店の人たちもそんなに悪い顔してなかったし、あとでおれからも話しておいてやるよ」
English: “Of course they won’t! No one would fire a star waitress like you. The people from the restaurant didn’t look too upset, and I’ll speak to them myself later.”

Japanese: おれは冗談めかしてレナの肩を叩く。
English: I gave her shoulder a playful pat.

Japanese: 「ありがとうみっちゃん……」
English: “Thank you, Mitchan...”

Japanese: 「それより。ほら」
English: “More importantly—look.”

Japanese: 言っておれは、向こうに立ってこちらを見ている娘の方を示した。
English: I pointed toward her daughter, who stood at a distance watching us.

Japanese: 彼女はまだ母親の回復を完全に信じ切っていないらしく、半信半疑の上目遣いで母親を見ている。
English: The girl was not yet fully convinced that her mother had recovered. She peered up at Rena with a doubtful, searching expression.

Japanese: 「ああ、ユリカ、びっくりさせてゴメンね」
English: “Oh, Yurika. I’m sorry I frightened you.”

Japanese: レナが笑顔で両手を広げてみせると、
English: Rena smiled and spread her arms.

Japanese: 「ママー」
English: “Mommy!”

Japanese: 涙をボロボロと流しながら少女は駈け寄ってきて、そして母子はお互いを抱きしめあった。
English: Tears streaming from her eyes, the little girl ran to her, and mother and child embraced.

Japanese: 「ごめんね。もうこんなことしないからね。本当にごめんね……」
English: “I’m sorry. I’ll never do anything like this again. I’m so sorry...”

Japanese: レナも娘に負けないくらい大量の涙を流している。
English: Rena wept every bit as hard as her daughter.

Japanese: 「あやまらないで。大丈夫だから。こんどママが病気になったら、私が守ってあげる……」
English: “Don’t say sorry. It’s all right. The next time you get sick, Mommy, I’ll protect you...”

Japanese: 「なんていいことを言う娘だろう！」
English: “What a wonderful thing for a daughter to say!”

Japanese: 母子水入らずの場面だが、おれはうっかり声を出してしまった。
English: It was an intimate moment between mother and child, but I inadvertently spoke aloud.

Japanese: 「おれにはそんな素晴らしいことは言えなかったよ。きみがそう思っているのなら、誰もお母さんを傷つけることなんか出来ないはずだ」
English: “I could never have said anything so wonderful. If that’s how you feel, then no one will ever be able to hurt your mother.”

Japanese: 「ほんとうに、ほんとうに……」
English: “Truly... truly...”

Japanese: おれの、場の空気を読まない言葉に、レナは何度も頷いた。
English: Despite my failure to read the room, Rena nodded over and over.

Japanese: そして親子は泣きながらいつまでも抱きしあう。
English: Mother and child held each other for a long time, both of them weeping.

Japanese: そろそろ、おれたちも退散したほうが良さそうだ。感動的な場面に、取り出したハンカチで目を何度も拭いているコンタの肩をつついて、おれたちはこっそりとその場を去った。
English: It appeared to be time for us to withdraw. Moved by the sight, Konta kept wiping his eyes with a handkerchief. I nudged his shoulder, and together we slipped quietly away.

Japanese: 「道夫君。薬が好きじゃないのはわかるけど、アレがなければレナを回復させることが出来なかった」
English: “Michio, I know you don’t like drugs, but without that one we couldn’t have brought Rena back.”

Japanese: おれは自転車を押して歩き、コンタは隣を歩いている。
English: I walked my bicycle while Konta kept pace beside me.

Japanese: 彼の目元はこすりすぎて赤かった。こんな、どう見てもその辺りのチンピラにしか見えない姿をしているが、存外に情に厚く涙もろい男なのである。
English: He had rubbed the skin around his eyes until it was red. He looked for all the world like an ordinary street thug, yet he was surprisingly tenderhearted and quick to cry.

Japanese: 「副作用とか依存性を心配するのはわかるけど、使った人間を見てると、ローズとは違うような気がするんだよなあ」
English: “I understand why you’re worried about side effects and dependence. But when I look at the people who have used it, I can’t help feeling this is different from Rose.”

Japanese: 確かにおれはローズのようなに大量に廃人を作り出すことも心配しているが、実はそれだけじゃない。
English: Certainly, I worried that it might ruin people in great numbers, just as Rose had. But that was not my only concern.

Japanese: 薬の効果とはまた別の部分に、とても複雑な問題がある。
English: The drug’s effects were not the only issue. There was another, very complicated problem.

Japanese: それは、ネオの方が本物の奇跡の薬で、人を廃人にするような副作用がなかったとしても同じことだ。
English: That problem would remain even if Neo were a genuine miracle drug and caused no side effects capable of reducing people to wrecks.

Japanese: 一度発症したタイプBは、これがなくては生きていけないことになるだろう。結局依存するしかなくなる。
English: Once a Type B’s symptoms had manifested, that person would no longer be able to live without it. In the end, there would be no choice but dependence.

Japanese: そして、現在この薬を販売出来るのは八龍会しかなく、それはつまり、八龍会が彼らに対して今まで以上の支配力を持つということになる。
English: At present, only Hachiryukai could sell the medicine. That meant Hachiryukai would possess more power over those people than ever before.

Japanese: 前回ローズが流行っていた時は少し事情が違った。ローズはレシピが公開されていたので家庭用製剤器があれば誰でも作ることが出来たし、副作用が酷くてすぐに使い物にならない廃人になってしまう。その点、ネオ・ローズを取り巻く環境は、八龍会がタイプBを支配するためのすべての条件が揃っている。
English: Conditions had been somewhat different during the previous Rose epidemic. Rose’s formula was public, so anyone with a home compounding machine could make it. Its side effects were also so terrible that it quickly turned users into useless wrecks. Neo Rose, by contrast, was surrounded by every condition Hachiryukai required to control the Type Bs.

Japanese: いずれこの薬も製造法が知られてしまうかもしれないが、それまでの間なら、八龍会は街のタイプBたちに、どんなことでもさせることが出来るだろう。
English: Its manufacturing method might eventually become public knowledge. Until then, however, Hachiryukai could compel the Type Bs of the city to do practically anything.

Japanese: 老人たちが『今がチャンス』と言っていたのは、この意味も含まれているはずだ。
English: This too must have been what the Elders meant when they said that now was their chance.

Japanese: 「薬はもしかしたら良いものなのかもしれない。でもなあ……」
English: “Maybe the medicine itself is a good thing. But still...”

Japanese: 結局この薬は街のタイプBたちを、八龍会の奴隷にするだけのことになるのかもしれない。それは、ギャングが人を麻薬漬けにして売春させたり金を搾り取ったりするのと何の違いがあるのか？　八龍会はギャングとは違うんじゃなかったのか？
English: Perhaps the drug would do no more than make the Type Bs of the city Hachiryukai’s slaves. How was that different from a gang keeping people hooked on drugs, then forcing them into prostitution or bleeding them of money? Wasn’t Hachiryukai supposed to be something other than a gang?

Japanese: だから、今この薬を使うのはいやなんだ。レシピが公開されて、ありふれた存在になって、本当に副作用がないことが確認されてからなら何の問題もない。
English: That was why I hated using the medicine now. I would have no objection after the formula was made public, the drug had become commonplace, and we had truly confirmed that it caused no side effects.

Japanese: でも、いまみなが飛びついている状況は危険だ。
English: But the present rush to seize upon it was dangerous.

Japanese: しかし、しかしだ。だからって使うことを完全に否定出来ない。いや、おれだって、この先苦しんでいる人間を見たときに使わずに見捨てることなんかできるだろうか？　レナと娘のさっきの喜びようを見たか？　何の手も打たなければ、一生まともに喋ることも働くこともできないんだぞ？
English: And yet—yet even so, I could not reject its use completely. When I next saw someone suffering, could even I abandon that person rather than use it? Hadn’t I just seen Rena and her daughter’s joy? If we did nothing, she might never again speak coherently or hold a job for the rest of her life.

Japanese: 家族や親しい人が別人になってしまって、それを元に戻したいという気持ちがあるかぎり、我々タイプBは薬の奴隷でありつづけるのかもしれない。
English: As long as we wished to bring back the family and friends who had become like different people, perhaps we Type Bs would remain slaves to the medicine.

Japanese: 「道夫君。さっき言いかけたことだけどさ……」
English: “Michio. About what I started to say earlier...”

Japanese: おれが考えていると、コンタは言った。
English: Konta spoke while I was lost in thought.

Japanese: 「そう言えば、続きを聞くって言ってたな」
English: “That’s right. I said I’d hear the rest.”

Japanese: 「そう。……饅頭屋はいいと思うよ？　でも、成功するまでまだ時間もお金もかかると思う。だから、一旦中止して、手っ取り早く稼げることをまずやって、資金を増やした方がいいんじゃないかな？」
English: “Yes. ...I think the bun shop is a good idea. But it will still take time and money before it succeeds. So maybe we should suspend it for a while, do something that earns money quickly, and build up our capital first.”

Japanese: コンタは前を見ながらそう話す。
English: Konta kept looking ahead as he spoke.

Japanese: 「何かアイデアがあるのか？」
English: “Do you have something in mind?”

Japanese: 彼の言い出すことは大体予想がついたが、おれはそう尋ねた。
English: I could already guess what he would say, but I asked the question.

Japanese: 「うちの工場にも『ネオ・ローズ』が作れる製剤機を置こうよ」
English: “Let’s put a compounding machine in our factory so we can make ‘Neo Rose’ too.”

Japanese: 「コンタ、いくら小麦粉が高いからって、『ネオ・ローズ』じゃグレートホール饅頭は作れないよ」
English: “Konta, however expensive flour gets, you can’t make Great Hole Buns out of ‘Neo Rose.’”

Japanese: 「道夫君、おれは冗談を言っるわけじゃないんだよ……」
English: “Michio, I’m not joking...”

Japanese: コンタは顔をしかめる。
English: Konta frowned.

Japanese: 「わかってるよ饅頭屋から麻薬屋になったらどうかって言うんだろ？　八龍会では『ネオ・ローズ』の生産が追いついてないって聞いてるからね。だからお偉いさんは工場を増やそうと考えてるってわけだ」
English: “I know. You’re asking whether we should stop selling buns and start selling drugs, aren’t you? I hear Hachiryukai can’t make enough ‘Neo Rose’ to meet demand. So the people at the top want to add more production facilities.”

Japanese: 「そう」
English: “Yes.”

Japanese: コンタはうなずく。
English: Konta nodded.

Japanese: 「そりゃあ、どっちも白い粉を扱う仕事だけれどさ……」
English: “I admit both jobs involve white powder, but...”

Japanese: 「確実に金になるよ。八龍会の会員にはこれまでの値段を据え置きだけど、それ以外は値上げして、利益にもしてゆくつもりだろうし。……それなら、レナとか、他の掛け持ちで働いているみんなも、こっちだけに専念出来るようになると思う。それでお金を貯めてから、みんなでまた再開すればいいじゃないか」
English: “It’s guaranteed to make money. They’ll hold the price steady for Hachiryukai members, but I think they mean to raise it for everyone else and turn a profit. ...Then Rena and all the others working two jobs could concentrate on this one. Once we’ve saved some money, we can all start the bun shop again, can’t we?”

Japanese: そういうコンタの顔に、濃い疲労の色が浮かんでいるのに気がついた。
English: I noticed a deep exhaustion in Konta’s face.

Japanese: この疲労は、先の見えない饅頭作りと、仕事を二つ並行しているオーバーワークによるものだろう。
English: That fatigue probably came from making buns with no end in sight while working a second job at the same time.

Japanese: なんだか雰囲気もぴりぴりとしているし、はっきりそう言わないけれど、追い詰められている。
English: There was something raw and tense about him. He did not say so directly, but he had been driven into a corner.

Japanese: きっと、他の従業員も同じような状態なのかもしれない。レナが発症したのも、このストレスが関係しているのだろう。
English: Perhaps the other employees were in the same condition. The stress might even have contributed to the onset of Rena’s symptoms.

Japanese: 「わかった。少し考えさせてくれ」
English: “All right. Let me think about it for a while.”

Japanese: そう返事をすると、コンタはもう気が済んだという風に表情をゆるめて溜息をつく。
English: At my answer, Konta’s expression relaxed as if he were relieved simply to have said his piece, and he released a sigh.

Japanese: 「道夫君、一緒に頑張ろうよ。みんな道夫君のこと大好きなんだからさ」
English: “Michio, let’s keep working together. Everyone loves you.”

Japanese: コンタはそう言ってくれる。おれは複雑だった。
English: Konta was kind enough to say it. My feelings were complicated.

Japanese: おれだって、本当はもう全部わかっているんだ。意地を張って追い続けてきたこの夢は、そろそろ終わりが近づいている。
English: In truth, I already understood everything. The end was drawing near for this dream I had clung to out of stubbornness.

Japanese: もし今から急に売り上げが伸びたとしても、おそらくその運命は変わらない。
English: Even if our sales suddenly began to grow, its fate would probably remain unchanged.

Japanese: 時代が変わろうとしているんだ。
English: The times were about to change.

Japanese: おれたちは食事をとるために暗闇通りを歩いて店を探した。
English: We walked along Darkness Street in search of somewhere to eat.

Japanese: この辺りを昼にうろうろするのは久しぶりだが、少し雰囲気が変わったんじゃないだろうか？　客引きや街娼が前よりも減っているような気がする。
English: It had been a long time since I wandered around this neighborhood by day, and the atmosphere seemed to have changed a little. There appeared to be fewer touts and streetwalkers than before.

Japanese: 「壬生屋が旧義勝に取り込まれたからねえ……」
English: “That’s because Mibuya was absorbed into old Gisho...”

Japanese: おれがふと感想を口にすると、暗闇通り出身のコンタがそう言った。
English: When I casually voiced the observation, Konta, who came from Darkness Street, supplied the answer.

Japanese: 「それで、壬生屋の店もYSの直属って形になったんだ。その時、上から言われて街に立ってる女をかたっぱしから店にスカウトしたんだよ。壬生屋の時だったら面接で断るようなレベルの女も残らずね」
English: “That put all the Mibuya establishments directly under YS. Orders came down from above to recruit every last woman working the streets into one of the shops—even the ones Mibuya would have turned away at an interview.”

Japanese: 「どうして？」
English: “Why?”

Japanese: 「あいつらは悪質な中間業者の食い物になってるケースが多かったからね。そういうのを廃絶したいんだろうな。壬生屋のときはしょうもないちんぴらしかいなかったから、半グレみたいな連中でもいい気になって好き勝手やってたけど、今は何かあると旧義勝の本物の人殺しの兵隊がすっ飛んで来るからね。失業したクズどもも泣き寝入りするしかないのさ」
English: “A lot of them were prey for crooked middlemen. I expect YS wants to wipe that out. Under Mibuya, there were no more than a few worthless thugs around, so quasi-gangsters could strut about and do whatever they liked. Now, if anything happens, genuine killers from old Gisho come running. The scum who lost their livelihood can only swallow it and cry.”

Japanese: かつてその業界で仕事をしていたコンタはこの件が痛快のようで、楽しそうに語っている。
English: Konta had once worked in that industry. He seemed to find the development exhilarating and described it with delight.

Japanese: 「無職になったクズどもは相当第三代龍頭を憎んでいるらしいぜ。いい気味だよ。亮があのYSのボスになるってのはどうも心配な気がしていたが、なかなか良い仕事するもんだねえ」
English: “I hear the unemployed scum hate the third Longtou. Serves them right. I was worried about Ryo becoming the boss of YS, but he does surprisingly fine work.”

Japanese: 「昔からあいつはこれくらいやりそうなやつじゃないか。この通りの立ちんぼも嫌ってたし」
English: “He was always capable of something like this. He hated the streetwalkers lining this road too.”

Japanese: 「そうだけどさあ……。しかし、爺さんたちはどうするんだろうね？　なんだか最近キナ臭いじゃないか。YSのやることにケチ付けたりしてさ。道夫君は何か聞いてない？」
English: “True, but... I wonder what the Elders mean to do. Things have felt dangerous lately, haven’t they? They keep finding fault with everything YS does. Have you heard anything, Michio?”

Japanese: 「何も」
English: “Nothing.”

Japanese: 「そうか。でも、何かもめ事になったらいやだなあ。街歩いてて、YSに気をつけなきゃならないような状況になったらたまったもんじゃないよ。おれ喧嘩弱いし」
English: “I see. I still hope it doesn’t turn into trouble. If things get so bad that I have to watch out for YS just walking around town, I won’t be able to stand it. I’m no good in a fight.”

Japanese: コンタはそう言って苦笑する。
English: Konta gave a wry smile.

Japanese: 暗闇通りは夜は賑やかだが昼は看板をしまっている飲食店も多く、目当てのラーメン屋も臨時休業をして居たのでそのまま滑走路通りの方まで歩いて『Ｐｕｅｒｔｏ』というスペイン風バルの店に足を踏み入れた。
English: Darkness Street was lively at night, but many of its restaurants put away their signs during the day. The ramen shop we had wanted was temporarily closed, so we continued to Runway Street and entered a Spanish-style bar called Puerto.

Japanese: 夜は酒飲みが集まる店だが、昼はランチメニューを提供しており、これがなかなか評判がいい。スペイン在住経験がある店主の手によるオリーブオイルをふんだんに使ったスペイン風料理がメインだが、生まれ故郷であるタイの料理も取り扱っている。
English: Drinkers gathered there at night, while at midday it served a well-regarded lunch menu. The owner had lived in Spain, and his principal offerings were Spanish-inspired dishes prepared with abundant olive oil, though he also served food from his native Thailand.

Japanese: ランチメニューにもグリーンカレーとレッドカレーがあり、おれは鳥肉とタイ産の茄子が入っているグリーンの方を、コンタはエスニック料理が苦手なのでエビとムール貝が入ったシーフードパエリアを注文した。
English: The lunch menu included both green and red curry. I ordered the green, made with chicken and Thai eggplant. Konta disliked what he called exotic food, so he chose a seafood paella with shrimp and mussels.

Japanese: なかなかオシャレな店だけあって、店内には若い客が多かったが、年配の客もちらほらといる。肌や髪の色は多様で、タイプAの特質変異らしい風変わりな容姿の客もいる。よそからの観光客よりも地元の住民が多そうだ。
English: The place was fashionable enough that most customers were young, though a few older people sat among them. Skin and hair displayed every color, and some patrons possessed eccentric appearances that suggested Type A trait mutations. Most looked like local residents rather than tourists.

Japanese: そうしてぼんやり店内を見渡しながら料理を待っていると、ドアを開けて意外な顔ぶれが入って来る。
English: As I idly surveyed the room while waiting for our food, an unexpected pair entered through the door.

Japanese: 年が同じくらいの二人組の女の子で、片方は雨も降っていないのに身体を隠すレインコートを着ており、顔が汗をかいたように濡れている。もう一人のほっそりとした方は白い服をみにつけ、帽子をかぶっている。
English: They were two girls of approximately the same age. Although it was not raining, one wore a raincoat that concealed her body, and her face was wet as though with sweat. The slenderer girl wore white clothes and a hat.

Japanese: 彼女たちは視線をめぐらして空席を探すと、おれの姿を見つけた。
English: They looked around for an empty table and spotted me.

Japanese: 「よう」
English: “Hello.”

Japanese: と手を挙げると、二人は歩いて近づいてくる。レインコートの方は松葉杖をつき、ひょこひょこと頼りない歩き方をしていた。
English: I raised a hand, and they came over. The girl in the raincoat used crutches, proceeding with an uncertain little hop.

Japanese: 「お久しぶりです」
English: “It has been a long time.”

Japanese: 白い服の方がそう言って、頭を下げると、もう一人もそれにあわせて慌てて頭を下げた。
English: The girl in white bowed as she spoke. Her companion hurriedly followed suit.

Japanese: 「あの時以来だね、シウちゃん。それと……さくらちゃんだっけ？」
English: “Not since that day, Siu. And... Sakura, wasn’t it?”

Japanese: そう、そこに入って来たのは亮の妹である謝筱喬と、その友人である熨田さくらだった。
English: Yes—the arrivals were Ryo’s younger sister, Siu-kiu Tse, and her friend Sakura Noshida.

Japanese: 二人と会うのは病院以来だ。あれは二ヶ月前……もう二ヶ月も過ぎているのだと思うとその早さに愕然とするが……グランドタワーを襲撃したサイキック少女に誘拐されたシウを、やはりサイキックであるさくらが救出に向かい、YSのギャングたちが束になっても叶わなかったその相手から、見事奪還に成功したのだ。
English: I had not seen them since the hospital, two months ago. Realizing that two whole months had already passed was startling. A psychic girl had abducted Siu-kiu during the attack upon the Grand Tower, and Sakura, herself a psychic, had gone to rescue her. Where an entire group of YS gangsters failed, Sakura had brilliantly succeeded in taking Siu-kiu back from her captor.

Japanese: ただし無傷というわけにも行かず、彼女は足の一本を相手に奪われ、また落下により体中を打ってしまうこととなったのだ。
English: She had not escaped unharmed. Her opponent took one of her legs, and the fall battered her entire body.

Japanese: まったく勇気のある女の子である。
English: She was a courageous girl indeed.

Japanese: 「知り合い？」
English: “You know them?”

Japanese: コンタがきょとんとした顔でおれと二人の顔を交互に見る。
English: Konta stared blankly from me to the two girls and back again.

Japanese: 子供の頃は定食屋の息子として通していたリョウは、その実の妹のことを仲間には話していない。コンタも当然この目の前の美しい少女がリョウの妹だとは気がつかない。
English: As a child, Ryo had passed himself off as the son of a diner owner. He never told our companions about his real sister. Naturally, Konta had no idea that the beautiful girl before him was Ryo’s sister.

Japanese: かといって、今ここでおれが話すわけにもいかないよな？　あのクリス・ツェーが常に手元に置いていた愛娘であり、現在街を騒がしている新龍頭の妹であると、いくらなんでもここで言うわけにはいかないもの。
English: But I could hardly say so here, could I? I could not possibly announce in a public restaurant that she was the beloved daughter Chris Tse had always kept close and the sister of the new Longtou who now had the whole city talking.

Japanese: 見たところ警備のものも居るわけでもないし、こっそりお忍びでグランドタワーを出て来たんだろう。その正体を、たとえコンタとはいえ教えるわけにはいかないよな。そんなの絶対だめに決まっている。
English: I saw no security personnel. The pair had probably slipped out of the Grand Tower incognito. Even if he was Konta, I could not reveal her identity. Absolutely not.

Japanese: 「おれは田中紺太。この見土君とは昔からの友達だが、きみたちのことは、一度も見たことないけど……」
English: “I’m Konta Tanaka. Michio and I have been friends for years, but I’ve never seen either of you before...”

Japanese: コンタが首を捻りながら言うと、
English: Konta tilted his head as he introduced himself.

Japanese: 「初めまして。私、謝筱喬といいます。謝亮の妹です」
English: “A pleasure to meet you. My name is Siu-kiu Tse. I am Tse Leung’s younger sister.”

Japanese: シウはあっさり答えた。
English: Siu-kiu answered without hesitation.

Japanese: えっ、言ってもいいの？
English: Oh. So it was all right to say it?

Japanese: 「ちょ、ちょっと筱喬。そんなに詳しく自己紹介しちゃって……」
English: “S-Siu-kiu! You shouldn’t introduce yourself in that much detail...”

Japanese: さくらは慌てている。やっぱりダメらしい。
English: Sakura was flustered. Apparently it was not all right after all.

Japanese: 「えっ、謝亮の妹って……」
English: “What? Tse Leung’s sister...”

Japanese: コンタは放心して固まっている。やはりかつての友人とは言え、龍頭の妹をこんなに間近で発見したのはショックだったようだ。
English: Konta froze in a daze. Even though Ryo had once been his friend, discovering the Longtou’s sister at such close quarters appeared to shock him.

Japanese: 「そ、そうなんだ。おれは子供の頃から知ってたんだけど、コンタが会うのは初めてだよな。なかなかややこしい立場なんだから、あんまり大きな声は出さないでやってくれよ」
English: “Y-yes. I’ve known her since we were children, but this is your first time meeting her, Konta. Her position is complicated, so please don’t raise your voice.”

Japanese: おれは場を繕おうとしたが、コンタの耳には入らないようで、相変わらず石像のように凍り付いている。
English: I tried to smooth things over, but my words did not seem to reach Konta. He remained frozen like a stone statue.

Japanese: 少なくとも大きな声を出す心配はなさそうだ。
English: At least I no longer had to worry about him raising his voice.

Japanese: 「まあ、二人ともそこに座りなよ。おれたちと相席だけどいいかな？」
English: “Why don’t you both sit down? Would you mind sharing our table?”

Japanese: 「あ、はい」
English: “Ah, yes.”

Japanese: 「じゃあ遠慮なく」
English: “Then we’ll take you up on the offer.”

Japanese: おれがコンタの隣に移動して、テーブルをはさんで向かいの二つの席を彼女達にゆずる。
English: I moved beside Konta and offered them the two seats across the table.

Japanese: さくらは片足を気遣いながらの着席で、手間取りながら椅子に腰をおろした。
English: Sakura had to take care with her leg. After some difficulty, she lowered herself into the chair.

Japanese: 「大変そうだなあ。足はどういった感じなの？」
English: “That looks hard. How is your leg doing?”

Japanese: 「すごく調子いいですよ。今の技術ってすごいんですね。切断してすぐ義肢つけたのに全然痛くない」
English: “Very well. Modern technology is remarkable, isn’t it? They fitted the prosthesis immediately after the amputation, but it doesn’t hurt at all.”

Japanese: さくらは脇に立てかけてあったランチメニューを手に取りながら答える。
English: Sakura answered as she took up the lunch menu propped beside her.

Japanese: 若い女の子があんな怪我をして家族はなんとも言わなかったのかとか、ちゃんとリョウに支払って貰っているのかとか、聞きたいことは色々あったが、あまり尋ねるとシウに責任を感じさせるかと思い、それ以上は言わなかった。
English: I had many questions. How had her family reacted to a young girl suffering such an injury? Had Ryo compensated her properly? But too many questions might make Siu-kiu feel responsible, so I said nothing more.

Japanese: 「あ、こっちの子は熨田さくらちゃん。シウちゃんの友達なんだ。おれもこの間初めて会ったんだけど、えーと、普段は何をしてる子なんだっけ？　学生？」
English: “Oh, this is Sakura Noshida, Siu’s friend. I only met her the other day myself. Um... what do you ordinarily do, Sakura? Are you a student?”

Japanese: コンタに紹介しようと思ったが、おれもほとんどこっちの子については詳しいことを知らない。
English: I had meant to introduce her to Konta, but in truth, I knew almost nothing about her either.

Japanese: 「えー、あのー、私、学生じゃないです」
English: “Um, well... I’m not a student.”

Japanese: 「じゃあ働いてるの？」
English: “Then do you work?”

Japanese: 「い、いえ……働いてもいません」
English: “N-no... I don’t work either.”

Japanese: さくらは引きつった笑顔を浮かべて顔を横に振り、
English: Sakura shook her head with a strained smile.

Japanese: 「あ、あのー、普段は主に自宅に閉じこもってゲームなどを楽しんでおります」
English: “Um... I ordinarily spend most of my time shut inside my home, enjoying video games and similar pursuits.”

Japanese: 「なるほど！　ゲーマーか。おれ、ああいうのすぐ頭が痛くなっちゃってダメなんだよ。よく眠りもしないで長時間遊んでる人の話とか聞くと、集中力がすごいなって思うんだ」
English: “I see! A gamer. Those things give me a headache in no time, so I’m hopeless at them. Whenever I hear about someone playing all night for hours without sleep, I’m amazed by their powers of concentration.”

Japanese: おれが微笑みかけると、さくらはますます引きつって、
English: I smiled at her. Sakura’s expression grew more strained still.

Japanese: 「あ、ありがとうございます……」
English: “Th-thank you...”

Japanese: と言った。
English: That was her answer.

Japanese: シウとさくらは肩をくっつけあって仲良く一つのメニューを見て、ああでもないこうでもないと言っている。
English: Siu-kiu and Sakura pressed their shoulders together and amicably shared one menu, debating the choices.

Japanese: シウは何だか暗い感じで、さくらはそれを気遣う様子を見せている。不自然な様子だったのでシウの顔をよく見ると、目の縁が少し赤くなり、まぶたがちょっと腫れぼったい。まるで泣いたあとのように見えた。
English: Siu-kiu seemed somehow gloomy, and Sakura was visibly attentive to her mood. The behavior felt strange. When I looked more closely, the rims of Siu-kiu’s eyes were faintly red and her eyelids slightly swollen. She looked as though she had been crying.

Japanese: 一体これは何だろう？
English: What in the world had happened?

Japanese: 「リョウに、こんな凄い美人の妹がいたんだね……」
English: “I never knew Ryo had such a beautiful sister...”

Japanese: さっきまで硬直して何も言えなかったコンタが、おれにそう耳打ちする。
English: Konta, who had been too petrified to speak, whispered into my ear.

Japanese: 「そうだろう。お母さんも美人だったんだ。でも、変な気を起こすのはやめとけよ。リョウはこの妹を溺愛してるからな。ヤツを敵に回すのをいとわないというなら好きにすればいい」
English: “Beautiful, isn’t she? Her mother was beautiful too. But don’t get any ideas. Ryo dotes on his sister. If you don’t mind making an enemy of him, do as you please.”

Japanese: 「いや、ちょっとやめとくよ……」
English: “No. I think I’ll pass...”

Japanese: コンタは情けない顔をして言う。リョウを怒らせた時の相手に対するおそろしい仕打ちを想像したに違いない。
English: Konta’s face went limp with fear. No doubt he had imagined the terrible things Ryo might do to someone who angered him.

Japanese: 昔の仲間なら、きっと誰でもコンタと同じような反応をするだろう。
English: Anyone from our old group would probably have reacted much as Konta did.

Japanese: 苦笑しているところへ、店員がおれとコンタの料理を運んできた。
English: As I smiled wryly, a server brought our meals.

Japanese: 「あ、二人とも注文は決まったか？」
English: “Have you two decided what to order?”

Japanese: 受け取りながら尋ねると、
English: I asked while accepting the dishes.

Japanese: 「私はレッドカレーをお願いします。筱喬はランチセットAで」
English: “I’ll have the red curry, please. Siu-kiu will have lunch set A.”

Japanese: さくらが二人分を注文した。
English: Sakura ordered for them both.

Japanese: やはりシウは表情が暗い。運ばれた水にも手をつけず、ぼんやりそっぽを眺めている。
English: Siu-kiu still looked despondent. She did not even touch the water they brought, but stared vaguely off to one side.

Japanese: 「今日は二人で何をしていたんだ？」
English: “What were the two of you doing today?”

Japanese: おれは彼女の気持ちをほぐすためにそう話しかけたのだが、
English: I meant the question to lighten her mood.

Japanese: 「あ、あの、今日は、友達の服を買ってあげようと滑走路通りを歩いていて。あの……」
English: “Um... today we were walking along Runway Street. I wanted to buy clothes for my friend. Um...”

Japanese: シウはなんとか答えようとしてくれるのだが、途中で言葉を詰まらせてしまう。
English: Siu-kiu made an effort to answer, but her words failed midway.

Japanese: こはよほどのことだな。
English: This had to be something serious.

Japanese: 「筱喬の調子が良くなかったのに、私が無理矢理そとに連れ出しちゃったんです。それでかえって疲れさせちゃったみたいでー。私空気読めないんですよねー」
English: “Siu-kiu wasn’t feeling well, but I forced her to come out. It looks as though I only tired her more. I’m terrible at reading a room.”

Japanese: さくらが苦笑しながらそう説明する。
English: Sakura explained with an awkward smile.

Japanese: 「ねえ筱喬、今日はご飯食べたらもう帰ろっか？　天明と天祥のかわいい洋服選びは、今度にしよう。あの子たちの誕生日まで、まだもうちょっと時間あるし」
English: “Siu-kiu, why don’t we go home after we eat today? We can choose cute clothes for Tin-ming and Tin-cheung another time. There’s still a little while before their birthday.”

Japanese: 「……ご、ごめんなさい。さくらだって大変ななか、元気づけようとしてくれてるのに……」
English: “...I-I’m sorry. You’re having a hard time yourself, Sakura, and you came to cheer me up...”

Japanese: シウは申し訳なさそうに俯いた。
English: Siu-kiu lowered her eyes apologetically.

Japanese: 「私は全然大変じゃないから。何度も同じこと言ってると、スカートめくるよ？」
English: “I’m not having a hard time at all. If you keep repeating yourself, I’ll lift your skirt.”

Japanese: さくらは笑って欲しくてそう言ったのだろうが、
English: Sakura had probably hoped the threat would make Siu-kiu laugh.

Japanese: 「うん、ごめん……」
English: “Yes. Sorry...”

Japanese: シウは乗って来ない。
English: Siu-kiu did not play along.

Japanese: 「一体何があったんだ？　ただごとじゃないぞ？」
English: “What on earth happened? This is clearly serious.”

Japanese: 見るに見かねておれがそう尋ねたが、
English: Unable to watch any longer, I asked her directly.

Japanese: 「すみません。そんな、大したことじゃないんです」
English: “I’m sorry. It is nothing so serious.”

Japanese: と笑ってみせるが、あきらかに無理をしている表情である。
English: She smiled, but the strain upon her face was obvious.

Japanese: 会食は終始そんな調子で、おれやさくらが道化に徹して冗談を飛ばしても変に上滑りするばかりだし、コンタは気を遣って黙りがちになっているし、どうにもならなかった。
English: The entire meal went that way. Sakura and I devoted ourselves to clowning and showered the table with jokes, but every one fell strangely flat. Konta grew quiet out of consideration. Nothing helped.

Japanese: 「申し訳ないです。今日は、私がいるせいで暗くなっちゃって……」
English: “I’m sorry. I made everything so gloomy today just by being here...”

Japanese: 店の外に出てから、筱喬はそう頭を下げる。
English: Once we were outside, Siu-kiu bowed as she apologized.

Japanese: 「私だめなんです。感情がすぐ出ちゃう。いやな気分になると暗くなっちゃうし、悲しいときは顔に出ちゃう。お兄ちゃんにはよく我慢が足りないって言われます」
English: “There is something wrong with me. My emotions show immediately. If I feel bad, I grow gloomy. If I am sad, it shows upon my face. Big Brother often tells me that I have no self-control.”

Japanese: 「謝る理由なんかなにもないよ。おれは楽しかった。久しぶりにシウの顔が見られたからな」
English: “You have no reason to apologize. I enjoyed myself. I hadn’t seen your face in a long time, Siu.”

Japanese: おれはそう言って微笑んでみせると、
English: I smiled at her.

Japanese: 「誰にだって暗く落ち込むときはあるんだ。気にしないでいい。さくらちゃんだって、つらいなかこうしてシウが来てくれただけで嬉しいはずだよ。リョウの言うことは話半分に聞いておけばいいんだ」
English: “Everyone feels gloomy sometimes. You don’t need to worry about it. Sakura must be happy that you came even though things are hard for you. And you only need to take half of what Ryo says seriously.”

Japanese: おれの言葉に、さくらは無言でうんうんと頷いている。
English: At my words, Sakura silently nodded again and again.

Japanese: 「そ、そうだよ。きみのお兄ちゃんは普通の人とはちょっと違うんだから。悪い奴じゃないんだけど、ズレてるっていうか……あっ、これはお兄ちゃんには内緒だからね」
English: “Th-that’s right. Your brother is a little different from ordinary people. He isn’t a bad man, but he’s rather... out of step. Oh, but don’t tell him I said that.”

Japanese: コンタが慌ててそう口止めすると、シウはやっとちょっと笑い、
English: When Konta hurriedly demanded secrecy, Siu-kiu finally gave a small laugh.

Japanese: 「ありがとうございます」
English: “Thank you.”

Japanese: と、頭を下げた。
English: She bowed her head.

Japanese: 一体何があったのだろう？　おれは何度か尋ねてみたが、結局彼女は理由を一言も話さずじまいである。
English: What in the world had happened? I tried asking several times, but in the end, she did not tell us a single word about the reason.

Japanese: YSで起こったことだったら、立場上言えないのかもしれない。
English: If it concerned something within YS, perhaps her position prevented her from speaking.

Japanese: 気になりながら迎えた別れ際、さくらがふっと浮かんで飛んできて、おれの袖を掴むと、
English: The question still troubled me when it came time to part. Sakura suddenly floated over, caught my sleeve, and said,

Japanese: 「あの、連絡先交換させてもらいます？　筱喬のことで相談したいことがあるんです」
English: “Could we exchange contact details? There’s something I want to ask you about Siu-kiu.”

Japanese: 取り出した携帯電話を片手に小声でおれに耳打ちしてきた。
English: She whispered into my ear, holding the telephone she had taken out in one hand.

Japanese: 「もちろん」
English: “Of course.”

Japanese: おれは携帯電話を取り出す。
English: I took out my own telephone.

Japanese: 「助かります。他に、筱喬とお兄さん両方と親しい人がいなくて……」
English: “Thank you. I don’t know anyone else who’s close to both Siu-kiu and her brother...”

Japanese: さくらはさっきみなで喋っているときとは違った深刻なトーンで言う。
English: Sakura’s tone was much more serious than it had been while we all spoke together.

Japanese: そしておれたちは通信機能でお互いの連絡先を、お互いの端末に記憶させ、またポケットにしまった。
English: Using the devices’ communication function, we saved our contact details to one another’s telephones and returned them to our pockets.

Japanese: 「じゃあ、またあとで」
English: “I’ll speak to you later.”

Japanese: さくらはまたふっと飛ぶと、向こうでこちらを不審げに見ているシウの側に着地し、顔にさっきまでの剽軽な笑顔を浮かべる。そして恥ずかしがって避けようとするシウに抱きつくと、そのまま二人で空に舞い上がった。
English: Sakura floated away again and landed beside Siu-kiu, who watched us suspiciously from a distance. The playful grin she had worn before returned. When Siu-kiu shyly tried to evade her, Sakura embraced her and carried them both up into the sky.

Japanese: それを見ていた周囲から、「おお」と驚きの声が上がる。
English: People nearby raised cries of astonishment.

Japanese: 彼女たちが空の向こうの小さな点になってしまうと、おれも、目を丸くして彼女達の背中をみつめているコンタの肩を叩いて、別の方向に歩き出す。
English: Once they had dwindled to a speck in the distance, I clapped the wide-eyed Konta on the shoulder, and we walked away in another direction.

Japanese: 夜、部屋に帰る。
English: That night, I returned to my apartment.

Japanese: 午後からは、いつも通り饅頭の営業のためにサンプルを持ってあちこち歩き回った。
English: I had spent the afternoon walking from place to place with samples, making the usual sales calls for our buns.

Japanese: 可能性が高い場所は初期のうちにあらかたまわってしまったので、最近は新規開拓する場所もなくなって、パラシュート通りの洋服屋などにも足を運ぶ始末だ。もちろん置いては貰えなかった。
English: We had exhausted most promising prospects early on. Lately, there was nowhere left to develop new business, and I had fallen so far as to visit clothing shops on Parachute Street. Naturally, none agreed to stock them.

Japanese: 今日は新しく契約を結べた店はゼロ。つまり徒労である。
English: The number of new contracts I secured that day was zero. In other words, the effort had been wasted.

Japanese: こうなると普段よりも披露は身体を重くするわけで、玄関をはいるとそのまま着替えもせずに街の埃で汚れた姿のままソファーに横になった。頭のなかにグルグルと思考やイメージが飛び回る。やたらとハラも減る。そう言えば、今日は昼以来何も食べていない。
English: Failure made fatigue weigh more heavily than usual. The moment I entered, I collapsed upon the sofa without changing, still covered in the dust of the city. Thoughts and images whirled around and around inside my head. I was ravenously hungry too. Come to think of it, I had eaten nothing since lunch.

Japanese: じりじりと事業が軌道に乗り始めてはいるものの、それ以上に初期の頃からつき合ってくれたみんなの疲労も限界に達しつつある。今は堪え忍ぶときと言ったが、その『今』がいつまで続くのか誰も確答は出来ない。
English: The business was grinding its way onto a stable course, but the companions who had supported me from the beginning were reaching the limits of their endurance even faster. I had called this a period we needed to weather. Yet no one could say with certainty how long ‘this period’ would last.

Japanese: レナのような例もある。はっきりそうだとは断言出来ないが、発症の原因の一端はオーバーワークにあるだろう。
English: There was Rena’s case as well. I could not state it as fact, but overwork had probably been one contributing cause of the onset of her symptoms.

Japanese: 彼女も初期の頃からおれの考えに賛同し、今はそれほどでもないが随分無理をさせた時期もあった。
English: She had agreed with my ideas from the early days. Things were not as bad now, but there had been periods when I demanded far too much from her.

Japanese: シングルマザーとして子育てもしなければならないわけだし、日々の生活に追われてたまった疲れを回復させる時間もなかったはずだ。
English: She also had to raise a child as a single mother. With every day consumed by the necessities of life, she could have had no time to recover from her accumulating exhaustion.

Japanese: 早い段階でああいった協力者には充分な休みと報酬を手渡したいが、今日明日に出来るというようなことでもない。
English: I wanted to give supporters like her sufficient rest and pay as soon as possible, but that was not something I could accomplish tomorrow, or the day after.

Japanese: 溜息が出てしまう。
English: A sigh escaped me.

Japanese: いかんね。これはどうも。
English: This would not do.

Japanese: おれはソファーの上でごそごそと芋虫のように動いて、うつぶせから仰向けに姿勢を変更する。
English: I wriggled over the sofa like a caterpillar and turned myself from my stomach onto my back.

Japanese: ……それにしても、レナは大変だ。
English: ...Rena truly had endured something terrible.

Japanese: あのアパートに辿り着いて縛られている姿を見たとき、おれは昔のことを思い出したね。
English: When I reached her apartment and saw her tied down, it brought back the past.

Japanese: 世間ではおれはほとんど赤ん坊の頃にどこかに捨てられて、八龍会の老人たちに拾われたように思われているが、実際はもう少し大きくなってからのことだ。
English: Most people believed I had been abandoned somewhere as an infant and found by the Elders of Hachiryukai. In reality, I had been somewhat older.

Japanese: 五才くらいまでは母親のところで育ち、母親が育てられなくなってから施設に預けられた。松坊だって知らないが、おれはたった三ヶ月くらいだと思うけれども施設も経験しているのである。すぐに老人たちに拾われ、彼らのもとで育てられるようになったが、もしおれがタイプAでなければそのまま施設にいたろう。
English: My mother raised me until I was approximately five. When she could no longer do so, I was placed in a children’s institution. Not even Matsu knew, but I had spent time in one myself, though I believed it was only about three months. The Elders soon found me and began raising me among them. Had I not been Type A, I would probably have remained in the institution.

Japanese: おれのサイキック能力は便利ではあるが、そこまで大したものではない。が、老人たちは「タイプBでありながらはっきりしたサイキック能力がある」というだけで、何か特別なものを感じてくれたらしい。
English: My psychic ability was useful, but hardly overwhelming. Nevertheless, the mere fact that I was ‘a Type B who possessed a clear psychic ability’ apparently convinced the Elders that I was something special.

Japanese: あと、おれの誕生日やらなにやらが、中国の占いで非常に優れたリーダーとしての資質をあらわしているんだそうだ。意外と彼らはオカルトチックなんだよね。ミスター・チェンの本職は占い師だったと思う。
English: They also said that my birthday and similar details indicated the qualities of an exceptional leader according to Chinese fortune-telling. The Elders were more occult-minded than one might expect. I believe Mr. Chen’s principal occupation was fortune-telling.

Japanese: ということで、五才までの間は母親がいた。スラムで朝から酒を飲んで路上で寝転がっているような連中を当たれば当時のおれたちの暮らしを知る人もいるだろうが、仲間たちには話したことがない。ただリョウだけが本当のことを知っている。
English: In any event, my mother was there until I turned five. If one questioned the people who spent their mornings drinking and lying in the streets of the slums, someone might remember how we lived. I never spoke of it to my companions. Ryo alone knew the truth.

Japanese: あまり言いたくない話だから、滅多なことじゃ口にしなかったんだ。
English: It was not a subject I liked discussing, so I very rarely did.

Japanese: リョウはもっと小さい時の記憶でもはっきり覚えているそうだが、おれはそれほど物覚えがいい人間でもないらしく、五才まで過ごした割りには思い出が少ない。それでも、まるきり記憶がないというわけじゃない。
English: Ryo claimed to remember even earlier childhood with perfect clarity. I did not seem to possess such a good memory. Considering that I lived there for five years, I recalled remarkably little. That did not mean I remembered nothing.

Japanese: 暗闇通りか、他のどこかか、住所ははっきりとはわからないが、ボロボロのアパートに住んでいた。母さんが一人、子供はおれ一人。父親はいなかった。家には大人の男が何人か出入りしていて、もしかしたらそのうちの誰かが父親だったのかもしれないが、そんな感じでもない。
English: We lived in a ruined apartment, either on Darkness Street or somewhere else; I no longer knew the address. There was Mother, and there was me. No father. Several adult men came and went. One of them might have been my father, but it never felt that way.

Japanese: おれの記憶のなかでは母さんはいつもベッドにヒモで縛り付けられていた。金色の目をぎらぎらとさせて、一人でブツブツと喋ったり笑ったりしている。調子が良いときはおれのことが息子だってわかるようだが、それ以外は部屋に出入りする男たちと同じようなものだと認識していた。
English: In my memory, Mother was always tied to her bed with cords. Her golden eyes glittered as she muttered and laughed to herself. On her better days, she seemed to recognize me as her son. Otherwise, she regarded me as no different from the men who entered the room.

Japanese: 丁度、今日のレナのような具合だったのさ。それが毎日続くんだ。
English: She was in much the same condition as Rena that day—except it continued every day.

Japanese: 今思うと、あの状態の母さんが働けるはずもないから、おれたちの生活費は、出入りする男たちのうち誰かが払ってくれたのだろう。遺産などの個人資産はなかったと思う。男たちはおれに優しく、食べ物をくれたり服をくれたりするので好きだった。
English: Looking back, Mother plainly could not have worked in that state. I suppose one of the men who came and went must have paid our living expenses. I do not believe she possessed an inheritance or other personal assets. The men were kind to me and gave me food and clothes, so I liked them.

Japanese: おれの右腕の力が何かの役に立つと思って手懐けただけかもしれないけれど、それだけでもなかったと思うよ。
English: They might have been taming me because they thought the power of my right arm would prove useful, but I do not believe that was all there was to it.

Japanese: 母さんは本当にやかましくて、しかも人の悪口ばっかり言う。ご飯を食べさせてやっても、排泄物を処理してやっても、憎々しく悪口ばかり言う。そして金切り声で叫ぶものだからたまらない。いくら話しかけてなだめようとしても無駄だ。
English: Mother was terribly loud and did nothing but abuse people. They could feed her or clean away her waste, and still she spat hateful insults at them. Then she screamed in a shrill voice no one could endure. Speaking gently or trying to calm her accomplished nothing.

Japanese: だから、母さんのベッドの横には木製のバットが一本置いてあり、あまりにもうるさいときは男がそれで殴った。だからバッドには血がこびりついていた。おれもその殴る光景を見ていたけれど、男たちの方がいつもおれに優しかったし、母さんのうるさいのにも閉口していたから、なんとも思わなかった。
English: That was why a wooden bat stood beside Mother’s bed. Whenever she grew too loud, one of the men struck her with it. Blood had dried upon the bat. I watched them do it, but the men were always kind to me, while Mother’s noise exhausted me, so I felt nothing.

Japanese: 「お前も、本当にうるさかったら使っていいんだぞ」
English: “If she gets too loud for you, you can use it too.”

Japanese: と男たちはおれに言ったが、臆病だったおれは自分で棒を手にとったことはなかった。
English: The men told me that, but I was timid and had never taken the stick into my own hands.

Japanese: その日が訪れるまでは。
English: Not until the day came.

Japanese: テレビではお気に入りのアニメが放送されていて、五才のおれは床に座ってそれを見ていた。なんのアニメだったかな？　超能力者が活躍するやつだったと思う。おれは変身ものとか、特殊な能力をもった人間が活躍する作品がちっちゃなときから大好きだったんだ。
English: My favorite cartoon was playing on television, and five-year-old me sat on the floor to watch. What was its title? I believe it was something about psychics. Even as a tiny child, I loved stories about transformation and people with special powers.

Japanese: それを見ていると、母さんが騒ぎはじめた。最初は我慢していたのだけれど、声がどんどん大きくなる。
English: As I watched, Mother began making noise. At first I endured it, but her voice grew steadily louder.

Japanese: 何を言っても聞いてくれないのはわかっていたが、
English: I knew she would not listen to anything I said, but I tried anyway.

Japanese: 「うるさいよ！」
English: “You’re too loud!”

Japanese: 一応言う。けれども母さんは、何かぎゃあぎゃあと言っている。
English: Mother only continued shouting something unintelligible.

Japanese: ほとんど言葉になっていないけれど、よく聞くとどうも水を飲みたいと言っているらしい。
English: Almost none of it formed words, but listening closely, I gathered that she wanted water.

Japanese: おれは立ち上がってキッチンに行くと吸い飲みに蛇口から水を汲んで、ベッドの側までやって来た。
English: I stood, went to the kitchen, filled a feeding cup from the tap, and brought it to the bed.

Japanese: ろくに風呂にも入れられていない母さんの側に来ると、酸っぱいような汗の臭いと、便や尿の臭いがする。これが、おれが母さんを思い出すといつも感じ取れる臭いだ。
English: As I approached Mother, who was seldom bathed, I smelled sour sweat, feces, and urine. Whenever I remember her, that smell returns to me.

Japanese: 男たちはたまには風呂に入れたり身体を洗ったりしてくれるのだが、すぐにこの臭いに変わってしまう。人間ってのは、みんなが思ってるよりずっとにおいやすいものなんだ。
English: The men occasionally bathed or washed her, but she soon smelled this way again. Human beings produce odor far more readily than most people imagine.

Japanese: 母さんの髪の毛は油で固まってべとべとで、乾いてひび割れた唇のなかには黄色いカスがべっとりとついた歯が見える。ゲッソリとコケ落ちた白い頬。目のまわりは落ちくぼみ、真っ黒なクマが浮かんでいる。まぶたはこれ以上ないくらい大きく見開かれ、まぶたをほとんどしない。白目は充血し、瞳は金色にらんらんと輝き、ぎょろりと動くとおれの顔を見る。
English: Mother’s hair was stiff with grease and clung together. Behind dry, cracked lips, her teeth were coated in yellow grime. Her pale cheeks were hollow and wasted, her eyes sunken into deep black circles. She held her eyelids open as wide as they could go and almost never blinked. The whites were bloodshot, while the irises blazed gold. Her eyes rolled toward me and fixed upon my face.

Japanese: 発症する前は美人で大人しい人だったそうだがその面影は完全に消えている。
English: I heard she had been a beautiful, quiet woman before her symptoms manifested. No trace of that person remained.

Japanese: おれは無言で吸い飲みを差し出し、その唇の端に先端を触れさせる。
English: Without speaking, I offered the feeding cup and placed its spout against the corner of her mouth.

Japanese: 母さんは吸おうとはせず、おれの顔を見ながら言葉にならない言葉をまくし立てる。
English: Mother made no attempt to suck. She stared at my face and poured forth a torrent of speech that was not language.

Japanese: それでも飲ませようと、先端を口に少し差し入れると、首を振ってそれを拒否し、
English: I inserted the tip a short distance into her mouth, still trying to make her drink. She shook her head, refused it, and cried,

Japanese: 「なんてことするんだ！　死ね！　死ね！」
English: “What are you doing? Die! Die!”

Japanese: と繰り返す。
English: She repeated the words.

Japanese: もう慣れきったおれにはその言葉は何も響かない。最初の頃はもっと敏感に反応したらしい。泣いてすがりついたり、興奮したり……そう、今日のレナの娘のような……でも、毎日繰り返されれば人は慣れるものだ。どんなことにも。
English: I was thoroughly accustomed to them, and they meant nothing to me. Apparently, I had once reacted more sensitively—crying, clinging to her, growing upset... like Rena’s daughter that day. But when something is repeated every day, a person grows used to it. One can adapt to anything.

Japanese: もし慣れることが出来なければ、淘汰されてしまう。外の街からやって来て、適応することが出来ずに死んでいった者も、これまで何度も見てきた。
English: Those who could not adapt were selected out. I had watched many people come from the outer city, fail to adjust, and die.

Japanese: とにかく、そのときのおれは、ただ、早くアニメの続きが見たいのにと、そんなことを考えている。
English: At that moment, however, I thought only that I wanted to see the rest of my cartoon.

Japanese: だから、初めてだというのに、そのバットを手に取る動きもスムーズで、迷いも葛藤もなかった。
English: Although it was my first time, the motion with which I picked up the bat was smooth. I experienced neither hesitation nor conflict.

Japanese: 他の大人がやっているようにやればいい。
English: I only had to do what the other adults did.

Japanese: ……当時このようにしてタイプＢの患者をしつけるのは当たり前の方法だった。今でもやっている人はいる。誰にも罪悪感なんかないのは、たとえば熱が出たら解熱剤を飲ませたり、のどに魚の小骨がつまったらご飯を飲み込むときに誰も罪の意識を覚えないのと同じだ。
English: ...In those days, ‘disciplining’ a Type B patient this way was considered ordinary. Some people still did it. No one felt guilty, just as no one felt guilt when giving medicine for a fever or making someone swallow rice to dislodge a fish bone from the throat.

Japanese: おれはバットを振りかぶって、母さんの胸の上に振り下ろした。やせ細ってほとんど肉のない母さんの身体を叩くと、直接骨をバットで叩いたような感触があった。
English: I raised the bat and brought it down upon Mother’s chest. Her body was so wasted that almost no flesh covered it, and the impact felt as though I had struck bone directly.

Japanese: 「げっ」
English: “Guh.”

Japanese: と咳き込むような悲鳴のような声をあげて、母さんは黙り込む。そして怯えた目でおれを見る。
English: Mother gave a sound somewhere between a cough and a scream, then fell silent. She looked at me in terror.

Japanese: おれはやっと静かになったと、またテレビアニメに戻った。
English: Satisfied that she was finally quiet, I returned to the cartoon.

Japanese: しかし、どういうわけかそうまでしてせっかく得られたアニメの時間を楽しむことが出来ないんだ。
English: But for some reason, after going so far to obtain it, I could not enjoy my time with the program.

Japanese: 台詞が耳に入らなくて、内容がうまく理解出来ない。
English: The dialogue did not enter my ears, and I could not follow the story.

Japanese: 胸がざわついて、たまらなかった。
English: My chest churned unbearably.

Japanese: ……そのときはっきりと自覚したわけじゃないんだが、罪の意識ってやつだな。母さんを殴ってしまったのが、恐ろしくて仕方なかったんだ。
English: ...I could not have named it clearly at the time, but it was guilt. The fact that I had struck my mother frightened me beyond endurance.

Japanese: 慣れてすれっからしになってしまったようなおれの心にも、まだ普通の子供みたいな部分が残っていたってことだ。それはきっと本能のように魂に刻みつけられたものなのかもしれない。
English: Some part of my heart remained that of an ordinary child, however hard and calloused the rest had become. Perhaps that part was carved into the soul like an instinct.

Japanese: おれは泣き出してしまって、母さんのところに戻った。
English: I began to cry and returned to Mother.

Japanese: 母さんは怒っていない。少し正気を取り戻していたのかもしれない。
English: She was not angry. Perhaps she had regained some measure of lucidity.

Japanese: おれを穏やかな目で見て、
English: She looked at me with gentle eyes and said,

Japanese: 「道夫。このロープをとって。縛られているところが痛いの……」
English: “Michio. Take off these ropes. They hurt where they bind me...”

Japanese: と静かに言うんだ。
English: Her voice was quiet.

Japanese: おれはうなずき、右腕の力を使ってロープを切断した。
English: I nodded and used the power of my right arm to sever the ropes.

Japanese: 母さんは縛られたところをさすると、ふらつく身体で立ち上がった。
English: Mother rubbed the places where she had been tied, then rose unsteadily.

Japanese: 「ここを出よう。もっと素敵な場所で二人で幸せに暮らそう」
English: “Let’s leave this place. We’ll live happily together somewhere much nicer.”

Japanese: 母さんはそう言っておれに微笑み、おれは引き込まれるように頷いたんだ。
English: Mother smiled at me. Drawn in, I nodded.

Japanese: そしておれたちはアパートを出た。母さんは裸足だった。そして楽しそうに笑っていた。
English: We left the apartment. Mother was barefoot, and she laughed with delight.

Japanese: それはもう妄想の笑いだったのかもしれないけど、そんなに楽しそうなのは例え症状のせいだとしても、久しぶりにそんな顔を見たから楽しかった。
English: Perhaps that laughter already belonged to her delusion. Yet even if the symptoms caused it, I had not seen her look so happy in a long time, and her happiness delighted me.

Japanese: 母さんと手を繋いで街を歩くなんて、それが生まれて初めてだったんだ。
English: It was the first time in my life that I had walked through the city holding my mother’s hand.

Japanese: おれたちはそのまま滑走路通りまで歩いて、そこで母さんは倒れ込んで警察に保護された。
English: We reached Runway Street. There, Mother collapsed and the police took her into protection.

Japanese: 滑走路通りまでいかなければ母さんはアパートへ逆戻りしていただろう。だけど、外からやって来た人間に見つかったおかげで警察が出動し、そして母さんにはこの街の外のルールが適用された。
English: Had we not reached Runway Street, Mother would have been returned to the apartment. Because someone from outside discovered us, however, the police came, and the rules of the outer city were applied to her.
